articles.title: Nobel Committee leaders, Agnés Callamard to speak at Social Good Summit 2026
articles.summary: With the summit's roster of speakers, 'WE, THE HUMANS' aims to make a resounding declaration that human rights should be at the center of any technology, most especially generative AI

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines – A few weeks after announcing this year’s Nobel Peace Prize winner, leaders of the Nobel Committee and Nobel Institute will fly to Manila to speak about the state of peace and human rights at Rappler’s Social Good Summit.
They, along with Amnesty International secretary general Agnés Callamard, have just joined the roster of speakers at the summit, set to take place on November 21 at Shangri-La The Fort, Manila.

Jørgen Watne Frydnes, chairperson of the Norwegian Nobel Committee, and Kristian Berg Harpviken, director of the Nobel Institute, will bring their perspectives on how we protect human rights and democratic values as technology, especially generative artificial intelligence, transforms our societies.

The summit, entitled, “WE, THE HUMANS: Reclaim Our Future,” puts the spotlight on how to protect human values, human creativity, and human communities from the threats posed by unregulated and abused AI systems.

At last September’s United Nations General Assembly, over 100 delegations called for AI to be governed with humanity, human dignity, and human rights at its core — asking who builds these systems, who bears the risks, and who is held accountable when they cause harm.
The message is clear: These are questions that can’t be left to technology companies alone.

The Norwegian Nobel Committee and Norwegian Nobel Institute work together to award the Nobel Peace Prize. Their mission is to promote peace among nations and recognize individuals who have contributed to peace, democracy, and human rights.
Amnesty International is a global organization fighting human rights abuses. Dr. Callamard leads the movement’s human rights work and serves as its chief spokesperson.
With its roster of speakers, “WE, THE HUMANS” aims to make a resounding declaration that human rights should be at the center of any technology, most especially generative AI.

Apart from keynote speeches and panel discussions, the summit will feature mini RappLearn masterclasses, allowing attendees to join two out of six options. RappLearn is Rappler’s learning and training arm, built to equip emerging professionals, leaders, and organizations with global insight and skills shaped by real-world experience. Its hands-on workshops have been in demand since workshops began in 2025.

The mini masterclasses cover vibe coding; personal safety and privacy in the age of AI agents; how to tell compelling data stories; impacts of AI on mental health, learning, and community well-being; the art behind Rappler’s animated editorial cartoons; and how to protect your brands from AI-driven risks to reputation and survival. See all mini masterclasses here:
The Social Good Summit is Rappler’s biggest annual fundraising event, with proceeds going to its investigative journalism and AI literacy initiatives. Tickets are available here.

items: Hear from the people shaping the global AI conversation.​For the first time in the region, members of the UN Independent International Scientific Panel on Artificial Intelligence Leslie Teo, senior director of AI products, AI Singapore, and Amandeep Singh Gill, UN special envoy for digital and emerging technologies, will come together at SGS, bringing global conversations about AI governance closer to the Philippines.​

Maria Ressa × Yuval Noah Harari​SGS participants will also get exclusive access to a recorded conversation between Nobel Peace Prize laureate Maria Ressa and Sapiens and Nexus author Yuval Noah Harari about the state of our world, and where technology is taking humanity.​

Courage panels on AI, mental health, isolation, and anxiety​What is all this technology doing to us as people? Hear from voices including Steph Naval, CEO and founder of Empath, and award-winning actress Iza Calzado, as we examine the human consequences of an increasingly AI-mediated world.​

Take something home with you.​Your SGS ticket includes access to two RappLearn or Nerve masterclasses on human-centered AI, vibecoding, data storytelling, and more, designed to turn the day’s big conversations into ideas and skills you can actually use. Check out the masterclasses here.​

Your ticket goes further​Proceeds from “WE, THE HUMANS” help sustain Rappler’s independent investigative journalism and expand AI literacy programs in schools and institutions across the Philippines through RappLearn. What you learn here helps someone else learn, too.

blocks.text: Each SGS ticket comes with three months of Rappler+, a program that gives members unlimited access to Rappler’s investigative and explanatory journalism, plus invites to exclusive briefings and events. – Rappler.com
If you’re interested in sponsoring the Social Good Summit, please reach out to socialgood@rappler.com.

articles.title: Nord Stream trial: How German police followed the evidence - to Ukraine
articles.summary: After four years, a Ukrainian man is set to stand trial in Hamburg accused of sabotaging the Nord Stream pipelines.

blocks.text: Image source, Swedish Coast Guard
Three of the four Nord Stream pipelines were ruptured by explosions in September 2022
BySarah Rainsford
Eastern and Southern Europe correspondent
Serhii K appeared relaxed as he checked in to the glamping resort near Italy's Adriatic coast with his wife and young children.

Dressed in shorts, sandals and a dark baseball cap, the former Ukrainian Special Forces soldier strolled back and forth, chatting with the receptionist and dipping repeatedly into a bowl of free snacks.
But German police were already closing in on him.

After a painstaking investigation, they had concluded that Serhii K had commanded Europe's biggest act of sabotage in decades: a series of explosions in September 2022 deep beneath the Baltic Sea that ripped through the giant Nord Stream pipelines and ruptured the supply of Russian gas to Germany.

Next week, following his extradition to Germany and months in isolation in a high security prison, Serhii K will go on trial in Hamburg. He is charged with causing an explosion and a war crime – attacking civilian infrastructure – allegedly acting on behalf of "state agencies of Ukraine".
Both he and his country have denied any involvement.
Under Germany's privacy rules, he will be named during the trial only as Serhii K, but during extradition proceedings he was identified as Serhii Kuznetsov.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Police escort Serhii K to a helicopter following a hearing with the German Federal Public Prosecutor

blocks.text: Image source, Reuters
Police escort Serhii K to a helicopter following a hearing with the German Federal Public Prosecutor
It was 02:03 am on 26 September 2022 when the first blast severed part of the Nord Stream pipelines, sending vast quantities of gas gushing through the surface of the Baltic Sea.

There were two further explosions targeting both Nord Stream 2 – not yet in action, but already full – and the original Nord Stream 1 that had supplied around half of Germany's annual demand for natural gas.
Both have been inoperable ever since.
Prosecutors say "high-performance explosives" were planted approximately 80m (260ft) below the surface: four devices weighing up to 27kg each, activated with timers.
They "strongly suspect" that Serhii K led a crew that included four deep-sea divers, using a rented yacht called Andromeda.
Once their complex, dangerous mission was done, the saboteurs slipped back into Ukraine unaware of the DNA evidence some had allegedly left on the boat.
As word of the blasts spread, experts and some governments initially rushed to the same conclusion: they blamed Moscow.
Russia had a history of hybrid attacks, after all, and of using its energy supplies for political pressure.
But as the airwaves filled with commentators citing "suspicious" Russian naval activity near the blast site, German police ignored the noise.
They went on following the forensic crumbs.
Eventually they led to Ukraine.

blocks.caption: A map showing Nord Stream pipelines running through Europe

blocks.text: The case since built by investigators alleges that Serhii K entered Germany for the Nord Stream attack on a forged passport, likely issued by Ukraine's security services.
In the extradition files sent to Italy he is named as Serhii Kulinich.
That might explain why he looked so calm on his holiday in Italy.

He had been travelling widely, and without incident, for the past year. In a copy of his real passport seen by the BBC there are more than two dozen stamps from countries including France, Spain and Canada – all dated after the Nord Stream attacks.
But by 13 August 2025, Germany had identified its key suspect and this time, when Serhii K crossed into Poland, he was detected.

Italian police say the actual arrest warrant was only issued on 18 August after he had travelled south and left Poland, suggesting the Germans were not sure their neighbours would co-operate and detain him.

By the time his wife made a booking at La Pescaccia though, he was officially a "wanted" man. As soon as he showed his passport at check-in at the resort, the local carabinieri got an automatic alert.
Police arrived to make their arrest late that night, leading Serhii K away from the glamping site and his family in handcuffs.
The saboteurs
None of the Nord Stream suspects have spoken publicly and no-one admits any role in the explosions.
But I have talked to some of the Ukrainians caught up in the case, and people close to them.
"Anyone who admits involvement in this mission, they're immediately a target for Russia," one source explained. "Whoever did it can never confirm that."
Nord Stream was a major investment and worth big money to Moscow in fuel sales. But it also made Germany and others dependent, giving Russia immense leverage over Europe.
That is why Ukraine, the US and Poland in particular all loathed it.
Another source I spoke to was "eaten alive by anxiety" over the investigation and baffled that Germany, a close ally of Ukraine, was even pursuing prosecution.
"Many Ukrainians believe that these pipelines, they helped Russia to fight so blowing them up was a good thing for our country," they pointed out.
The German prosecutor's office told me the justice system was outside of any politics. Sabotage is an offence against Germany's constitution.
Equally frustrating for the Ukrainians I met was their own government's silence.
"At the very minimum, he's a military man, so if there are any questions, they should be addressed to the state, not to him," a close contact of Serhii K complained.
Ahead of his extradition to Germany, his lawyer here in Italy told me his client had felt "abandoned".

blocks.caption: Image caption, Volodymyr Zhuravlyov is currently fighting extradition from Croatia

blocks.text: Image source, Omar Marques/Getty Images
Volodymyr Zhuravlyov is currently fighting extradition from Croatia
Germany has a whole list of suspects, but only one other name has been revealed so far.
Volodymyr Zhuravlyov is currently fighting extradition from Croatia where he was arrested in August.
He was there as a consultant on a new thriller film about the Nord Stream blasts, though he denies any role in the real-life operation.
Travelling was a risky move, when he knew Germany was pursuing him.
Zhuravylov has lived in Warsaw with his family since just before Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine and has his own business there installing air conditioning.
He is also a keen and competent deep-sea diver.
But he is a civilian.
Last year, he was arrested in Warsaw on a warrant issued by Germany but a Polish judge refused to extradite him.
In a dramatic twist, he ruled instead that a Ukrainian attack on Nord Stream, if that was what happened, would be a "just" act in a "bloody and genocidal war".
As one source close to the case put it to me: "The Poles don't like Ukrainians, historically, but they hate Russians and Germans even more."
Croatia is a different matter.
Political ripples
The implications of this case reach far beyond the courthouse in Hamburg.

After a slow start, Germany is now Ukraine's biggest supplier of military aid. The far-right AfD party, currently riding high in the polls, has seized on the Nord Stream case to bolster its argument that support for Kyiv needs to stop.
It is awkward, at the very least, for the governments in both Berlin and Kyiv.
It also raises questions about what constitutes a legitimate military target: who can hit what, and where, outside an open war zone.
When asked about the explosions, President Zelensky has previously insisted that Ukraine "definitely didn't do that".
This week, a foreign ministry spokesman went further.
"I find it very unfortunate that this entire discussion has come to focus on who blew [the pipelines] up, rather than who built them," Heorhii Tykhyi told the BBC, forcefully.
He argued that the Nord Stream pipelines had "untied Russia's hands" to go to war, because it no longer needed that to transit Ukraine for its gas to reach Europe.
"Did we warn about this? We did," Tykhyi wanted to know. "Did anyone listen to us? No, no-one did."
First in the dock
Serhii K will shortly become the first suspect to face charges in this high profile trial.
Zhuravlyov's case could be merged, in theory, at a later date, though that would be complicated.
Those who know Serhii K call him a patriot.
He signed up to defend Ukraine when Russia invaded even though he had several children and was exempt - and fought until December 2023.
His military ID shows that he was still in active service when the pipelines were blown up, meaning someone in Ukraine's military command knew exactly where he was and what he was doing.
They are not saying, though.
And in court Serhii K himself will not say a word, either.
His legal team will argue that he is not authorised to reveal details of any activities as a soldier and produce sworn statements from two of his military superiors to back that up.
I am told one of them will be the man widely named as the mastermind of the entire Nord Stream plot.

articles.title: The week in photos: October 3-9, 2026
articles.summary: A recap of news, sports, lifestyle, entertainment, and human interest images from the Philippines and around the globe

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — The Anti-Money Laundering Council (AMLC) flagged the financial transactions of Vice President Sara Duterte allegedly related to the flood control issue and illegal drugs, the House prosecution team said on October 5.

Based on the summary of reports submitted by the AMLC to the Senate impeachment court, Duterte has 373 covered transaction reports (CTRs) and 34 suspicious transaction reports (STRs), while her husband has 363 CTRs and 30 STRs. When combined, the transactions amount to P4.4 billion. The reports however do not imply that the flagged transactions are illegal, and are part of the monitoring process under the Anti-Money Laundering Act.

On October 6, bank representatives took the witness stand to authenticate account records and to verify the accuracy of the veep’s Statements of Assets, Liabilities, and Net Worth (SALNs), which allegedly do not reflect substantial bank balances.

On October 7, House prosecutors presented P96 million in manager’s checks as they sought to establish a “pattern of concealment” involving the year-end balances of the Vice President and her father, former president Rodrigo Duterte. Bank of the Philippine Islands officer Marwin Galvez confirmed the father and daughter had a joint time deposit account opened in January 2010 with a principal amount of P40.65 million.

Alexander Cabrera, a financial forensic analyst called as a witness, told the impeachment court on October 9 that Vice President Sara Duterte’s undeclared wealth tops P800 million. He said that based on his review of voluminous financial records of Duterte and her husband, Mans Carpio, the couple has around P817 million in undisclosed assets and income from 2022 to 2025.

blocks.text: According to Shamsi, interrogations of the 29-year-old pilot revealed he had been inspired by al-Qaeda's 11 September attacks in the US in 2001.

"The findings indicated that signs of his drift towards extremism and terrorism first emerged in 2017, while he was studying in Australia," the attorney-general was quoted as saying by the UAE's state news agency Wam on Friday.
"During that period, he was influenced by takfiri [radical] ideology through reading extremist literature and following online content glorifying terrorist organisations and suicide attacks."

The Wam report also said the pilot had told investigators "he had prepared himself both psychologically and physically to carry out the plot by intensifying his exposure to material promoting terrorism and training in boxing under a private coach".
"He admitted that he had acted alone, without the involvement of others, although investigations are continuing to verify this claim," Wam said.
The Australian Broadcasting Corporation has reported the man was issued an Australian student visa in 2014 and studied in the country in 2015-17, before leaving.

This week, the Sydney Morning Herald unearthed tweets from al-Mammami's now-deleted X account in which he referred to his five years spent studying abroad in Australia, Britain, and New Zealand, as "the golden years of my religious commitment".
More than 170 passengers and crew were on board flight FZ1073 on 30 September.
In the days after the incident, Australian authorities confirmed they were looking into the man's links to Australia.

The Victorian Joint Counter Terrorism Team - made up of the Australian Federal Police (AFP), Victoria Police and the country's security agency ASIO - said it was "investigating the man's links to Australia".

articles.title: Beware of fake Nunelucio Alvarado artworks, wife warns public, art connoisseurs
articles.summary: Counterfeit artwork attributed to Nunelucio Alvarado proliferate after conferment as National Artist

blocks.text: SALLY ALVARADO. The wife of National Artist Nunelucio Alvarado warns the public of fake artworks attributed to her husband
Ambo Delilan/Rappler
Counterfeit artwork attributed to Nunelucio Alvarado proliferate after conferment as National Artist
NEGROS OCCIDENTAL, Philippines – “Beware of fake Nunelucio Alvarado artworks,” warns his wife, Rosalia Alvarado.

In an interview on October 1, Sally said that just days after her husband was proclaimed one of this year’s National Artists, their family received reports on the alleged proliferation of fake paintings attributed to him at high prices.
She said that fake paintings, allegedly labeled as the work of her husband also known as “Maestro Nunelucio” are reportedly being sold in Cebu.
Because of this, they were compelled to issue a Certificate of Authenticity (COA) for all her husband’s creations.

According to Sally, art enthusiasts across the country have already gone to the Alvarado residence in Purok Bougainvillea in Sagay City, Negros Occidental, with their bought artworks just to secure a COA.

blocks.caption: NATIONAL ARTIST. An original Nunelucio Alvarado painting owned by an art connoiseur in Negros Occidental.

blocks.text: As a married couple and art buddies for almost five decades, Sally can easily spot her husband’s original artworks.

Sally said her husband’s artworks mostly focus on social realism and activism, highlighting the plight and struggles of farm workers and other marginalized sectors. It’s this portrayal of social injustice and exploitation that Sally says has allowed her husband’s artworks to stand out.
Sally said they were grateful that Nunelucio was included among this year’s National Artists.
“It was a great honor coupled with great privileges,” Sally said.
As much as they want to bring the 76-year-old artist during the awarding rites at Malacañang, the artist is currently dealing with health issues.

Nunelucio developed dementia during the COVID-19 pandemic, and was recently diagnosed with tuberculosis (TB), which prompted his doctor to forbid any visitors from visiting him at home. Nunelucio is still able to recognize people, but can only say ‘hi’ and “hello,” says the wife, who provides care for her husband. – Rappler.com

articles.title: 'Stain on the country': Trump criticises Norway over Nobel Peace Prize
articles.summary: The US president told a rally he had "never heard of" the winner, former International Criminal Court judge Navi Pillay.

blocks.text: US President Donald Trump has once again made complaints that he did not receive the Nobel Peace Prize, calling this year's decision "disgraceful and embarrassing".
The prize was awarded to former International Criminal Court judge Navi Pillay on Friday. Hours after the announcement, Donald Trump told a rally he had "never heard" of the "mystery person".
"This is an indelible stain on the country of Norway" he said, adding "we will not forget".
Trump has been outspoken about his desire to win the prize, and made similar criticisms in 2025 when it was awarded to Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado.
Last year, Norway's Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre explained to Trump it was an independent committee based in Norway, not the Norwegian government, which decides who will receive the prize.
Speaking to his supporters at a rally in Syracuse, New York, the US president repeated claims that he had settled eight wars and was "about to settle or win two more", without providing evidence.
"The Nobel Peace Prize has been forever discredited by a handful of radical ideologues who are anti-democracy and really enemies of civilisation," he said.

Pillay, a former UN human rights chief and International Court of Justice judge, was recognised "for her efforts to promote peace and international law", which paved the way for a "more comprehensive global legal order", the Nobel committee said.

The South African's work had been "instrumental in ensuring that war crimes, crimes against humanity, and genocide are prosecuted", said the chair of the Norwegian Nobel Committee Jørgen Watne Frydnes.
Shortly afterwards, the 85-year-old reacted to the news from Nuremberg's Palace of Justice by saying "it must be a joke" and thanked those who had gathered to applaud her.
"If you clap a little bit more I may share this prize with Trump," she joked.
Last year, the president openly expressed his displeasure at missing out on the prize, with the White House accusing the committee of placing "politics over peace".
In January, Machado gifted her medal to Trump during a meeting at the White House, which she said was in recognition of his commitment to her country's freedom.
Trump said on social media that the move was "a wonderful gesture of mutual respect".
The Nobel committee later clarified that the prize was not transferable.
"Once a Nobel Prize is announced, it cannot be revoked, shared, or transferred to others," it said in a statement. "The decision is final and stands for all time."

articles.title: Will ALECO reprivatization worsen Albay power woes?
articles.summary: Climate and energy groups claim that privatization will fail to resolve the power crisis and will instead compound the cooperative’s existing debt

items: Public frustration over power outages in Albay has led to renewed discussions about the potential reprivatization of the Albay Electric Cooperative (ALECO).
Lawmakers have shown interest in a private takeover, particularly from Meralco, due to ongoing issues like high power rates and significant debts.

Advocacy groups argue against privatization, citing past failures and advocating for the rehabilitation of ALECO's infrastructure and the use of renewable energy sources to improve reliability and reduce costs for consumers.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

ALBAY, Philippines — Mounting public frustration over unresolved power outages has reignited debates over reprivatizing the Albay Electric Cooperative (ALECO), barely four years after control of the province’s energy distribution operations was reinstated to the cooperative.

Debates over ALECO’s management escalated following Albay Governor Noel Rosal’s 2026 “Ulat ng Bayan (Report to the People),” where he called out the cooperative’s P5.7-billion debt. Clarifying his stance in August, Rosal insisted he is not advocating for privatization, but demanding immediate structural reforms from its management.

“The provincial government of Albay assures everyone that its position on the matter has not changed: the decision on how to rehabilitate and strengthen ALECO’s management and operation shall be left to its member-consumers who stand to be directly benefited or injured ultimately,” Rosal said in a statement.
Rosal has also urged the ALECO board to present all pertinent data at an upcoming Special Annual General Membership Assembly (AGMA) to directly address affected consumers.
“It is important that they prepare a report that is believable, because we need a report from the board for the consumers to be able to decide on the direction that we have to take,” he said.

In 2025, discussions intensified after lawmakers floated proposals for a private takeover — including expressed interest from the Manila Electric Company (Meralco) — prompted by persistent issues such as high system losses, increasing power rates, and ballooning liabilities.

“We already had our first round of talks with a Manila electric company, which is Meralco. That is why we are studying what will be the result of our third and fourth rounds of talks, because the number one priority here is to resolve the debts of ALECO,” said Albay 2nd District Representative Caloy Loria.

Loria initially claimed that he was acting with the support of Rosal, along with Albay 1st District Representative Krisel Lagman and Albay 3rd District Representative Adrian Salceda in discussing Meralco’s possible takeover.

“There will be a round of talks first, and Meralco will study it well. But they are very interested in operating the entire province of Albay,” Loria told DZGB News Online, a local radio station in Legazpi.

The district representative had also filed House Resolution No. 108 in 2025, directing the committee on energy to conduct a legislative inquiry into ALECO regarding its “operational failures” and “frequent power outages.”
However, in August 2026, Rosal clarified that his administration was not in talks with Meralco, nor had it sought the company’s help in strengthening ALECO.

“At this time, however, it must be clarified that the PGA (Provincial Government of Albay) has not made any official request to Meralco. While we continue to explore all viable options, no formal discussions or negotiations with the said electric company have commenced,” Rosal stated in a statement released on July 28.
“We therefore implore Meralco to be more cautious and prudent in releasing statements that might otherwise mislead the public,” he added.

Amid discussions on reprivatizing ALECO, the Philippine Movement for Climate Justice (PMCJ), Albay Renewable Energy Alliance (AREA), and the ALECO Member Consumer Owners Alliance (AMCO) warned that privatization could exacerbate the power woes affecting over 1.3 million household consumers.

“When ALECO was privatized, we saw that it changed nothing and the debt even ballooned. The service they are promising will turn into a nightmare for consumers. It will only become worse if privatization is pushed through,” PMCJ senior energy program officer Larry Pascua said.

AMCO member Virgilio Perdigon also alleged that ALECO’s operations under the Albay Power and Energy Corp. (APEC) — a subsidiary of San Miguel Energy Corp. (SMEC) — resulted in an even more unreliable energy supply distribution and higher electricity costs.

“Under APEC, we experienced higher energy costs. Returning to privatization will only gravely affect residents,” Perdigon said. “It is not true that privatization will solve the issues consumers are experiencing now under ALECO.”
In 2014, ALECO entered into a 25-year Concession Agreement (CA) transferring its operations to APEC to manage the debt-ridden utility, which owed nearly P4 billion to creditors at the time.

However, APEC subsequently accumulated massive debts to power suppliers, including P4.2 billion owed to SMEC. The utility attributed these losses to high system losses and inefficient collection efforts.

In November 2022, ALECO and APEC terminated the CA, citing persistent operational failures, mounting supplier debt, and service deficiencies. Distribution operations were formally returned to ALECO by the end of 2022 under the supervisory management of the National Electrification Administration.

According to Pascua, privatization has also prevented locals from feeling the cost efficiency of renewable energy sources in Albay, such as the geothermal power plants in Tiwi and Manito (along with Bacon in Sorsogon).
He argued that these renewable energy sources could have served as a lifeline for residents reeling from unreliable service and high costs.

“The geothermal power plants in Albay could have provided sustainability and reliability, but unfortunately, because of privatization, power generation does not see public service as its foundation, but rather profit generation,” Pascua added.

blocks.caption: EDC’s Tanawon geothermal plant brings hope to Sorsogon, as locals air gripes

blocks.text: Instead of privatization, advocacy groups are pushing for genuine rehabilitation of ALECO’s infrastructure, including its power lines, substations, and other major facilities.

“There’s a great and urgent need to rehabilitate ALECO’s dilapidated facilities, which are causing these issues. The rehabilitation should also be followed by new and cleaner sources of energy that can increase the efficiency and reliability of energy services in Albay,” Pascua explained.

The Albay power and energy committee held a hearing on Wednesday, October 7, seeking updates on ALECO’s financial statements, as well as its modernization and rehabilitation projects with a combined P1.2 billion budget allocation.

ALECO head of operations Mark Lucilo said that Phase 1 construction of substation rehabilitations in Daraga town and Ligao City worth P367 million is nearing completion and is set to be finished by the end of 2026. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Palace accepted Henry Aguda's resignation as DICT chief -- Ombudsman
articles.summary: Malacañang has accepted the resignation of Secretary Henry Aguda of the Department of Information and Communications Technology (DICT), Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla said Saturday.

blocks.text: Published October 10, 2026 11:52am
Malacañang has accepted the resignation of Secretary Henry Aguda of the Department of Information and Communications Technology (DICT), Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla said Saturday.

Remulla made the announcement when he was asked on his radio program about the fate of Aguda, who had admitted in a statement read during a recent Palace briefing that he was "aware of reports circulating" regarding his position.
"Nag-resign. Tinanggap na 'yung resignation," Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla said in his radio program.
(He resigned. His resignation was accepted.)
GMA News Online has reached out to Aguda, Malacañang, and the DICT for comment on the matter, but they have yet to respond as of posting time.

The development comes just three days after Press Press Officer Undersecretary Atty. Claire Castro said Aguda would stay on as the agency's chief. At the time, she said the Palace has not received information about Aguda's resignation.
Aguda assumed the helm at the DICT in March 2025, succeeding Ivan Uy.

In his statement read by Castro, Aguda said, "As Secretary of DICT, I serve at the pleasure of the President, and I fully recognize and respect the President’s prerogative in matters concerning his Cabinet and his administration. My focus remains on carrying out my responsibilities and serving the Filipino people to the best of my ability." — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: India's 'Cockroach' leaders detained ahead of major protest
articles.summary: India's 'Cockroach' party says its leaders have been detained ahead of a major protest called by the collective. Protesters are calling for India's chief election commissioner to resign.

image.caption: Indian security personnel are out in force in New Delhi, particularly its central areas Image: Adnan Abidi/REUTERS

blocks.text: October 10, 2026
'Cockroach Party' founder Abhijeet Dipke has been detained

Cockroach Janta Party's (CJP) founder Abhijeet Dipke has been detained by Delhi police, Indian media reported, as a preventative measure to block the planned protest against India's election chief in central Delhi.

According to reports by several media outlets, including India Today, authorities detained Dipke on board a flight after he landed in Delhi on Saturday morning. The news outlet quoted Dipke as saying, "I'm not afraid of you," while police officers urged him to cooperate.
The CJP's X handle soon released footage of the detention. "Shame on you Narendra Modi, Amit Shah," the caption read, referring to India's prime minister and home minister, respectively.
Authorities have also detained CJP's co-conveners Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das, as well as the group's legal aid head, Ratna Singh.

Right before being arrested, Dipke posted a video on Instagram, showing tens of Delhi police officers lining up outside his airplane to enter. "Love you, we'll do it together, Inqalab Zindabad," one of Dipke's associate is heard saying in the video's background.

'Inqalab Zindabad', meaning 'long live the revolution,' is a famous slogan used by Indian freedom fighters during their struggle against British rule. It has regularly been used by the Cockroach party against the Modi government.
The preventative arrests are part of a major crackdown on protesters this weekend.
Most of central Delhi, where the government is headquartered, is under an internet blackout and riddled with barricades, which authorities are using to identify and stop potential protesters.

articles.title: ICC allows seven more drug war incidents in Duterte case
articles.summary: The International Criminal Court has allowed prosecutors to add seven killings to the crimes against humanity case against former President Rodrigo Duterte, but struck out an eighth because it fell…

blocks.text: October 10, 2026 | 11:39am

MANILA, Philippines — The International Criminal Court has allowed prosecutors to add seven more incidents to the crimes against humanity case against former President Rodrigo Duterte, but struck out an eighth because it fell outside the time period of the charge it was filed under.

In the same October 9 decision, the ICC Trial Chamber III also rejected a defense request to order the prosecutors to rewrite the charges against Duterte as a closed list of killings. Duterte’s lawyers had argued that because the prosecutors treat the listed incidents as examples, he cannot know which specific incidents he will have to answer for at his trial, which opens November 30.

The ruling brings the Duterte case's incident count to 56. The 49 incidents confirmed by the Pre-Trial Chamber in April charge Duterte with 76 murders and two attempted murders. The public version of this latest decision does not say how many murders or attempted murders are in the seven new incidents.
Police reported at least 6,252 deaths in anti-drug operations during Duterte's presidency, but rights groups estimate the true number is up to 30,000, including vigilante-style killings.
The charges
Duterte faces three counts, or separate charges, of murder as a crime against humanity.

Prosecutors must prove each count on its own and the judges are expected to rule on each separately, so Duterte could be convicted on one and acquitted on another. The counts are divided by time period and by type of killing.

items: Count 1 covers killings in Davao City from 2013 to around June 2016, while Duterte was mayor. Prosecutors attribute these killings to the Davao Death Squad, which it accuses Duterte of having ultimate command over. This count lists 19 people killed in Incidents 1 to 9.
Count 2 covers killings of "high-value targets," or alleged major drug figures, from July 2016 to July 2017, Duterte's first year as president. The count lists 14 people killed in Incidents 10 to 14.

Count 3 covers killings of low-level suspects in police raids to clear barangays of drugs as part of "Oplan Tokhang," from July 2016 to September 2018. It lists 43 people killed and two who survived in Incidents 15 to 49, and is the only count that also charges attempted murder.

blocks.text: The eight new incidents
Prosecutors gave notice of Incidents 50 to 57 on August 31, the deadline the chamber set in May, and detailed them in their trial brief filed September 4.

On September 11, the defense asked the ICC judges to strike them or make prosecutors seek the Pre-Trial Chamber's approval, arguing that all eight involved new locations, victims, perpetrators and dates.

The chamber admitted Incidents 50 to 55 under Count 3 and Incident 56 under Count 2. It found that each falls within its count's time period and within the charges' scope of "locations across the Philippines."
However, the judges decided to reject Incident 57, filed under Count 2, because it falls outside the July 2016 to July 2017 period that Count 2 covers.

Witnesses for the new incidents are not expected to testify in the first months of the trial, and the chamber told both sides to ensure none is called before the defense has had reasonable time to prepare.
Request to refile charges rejected

Lead defense counsel Peter Haynes argued in an August 31 motion that charges built on "illustrative" and "non-exhaustive" incidents violate Duterte's right under the Rome Statute to be told in detail what he is charged with. He called the charges a "moving target" and asked the chamber to order prosecutors to refile them before the Pre-Trial Chamber with a complete list of acts.
However, in its decision, the chamber's judges said they have no power to do that as only the prosecutor can seek to change confirmed charges, and only with the Pre-Trial Chamber's permission.

Trial chambers cannot review pre-trial decisions on appeal and the motion re-argued issues Pre-Trial Chamber I had already settled, including when it refused the defense permission to appeal on May 21, the decision read.

The judges also rejected the argument that prosecutors need pre-trial approval for each new incident. The charges were confirmed as covering "at least" the named victims, and the pre-trial judges had called incident-by-incident approval "practically unworkable."
The chamber found that the confirmed charges, the confirmation proceedings and the trial brief give Duterte enough detail to prepare his defense.
Why the exact number of incidents matter

To convict, prosecutors must prove beyond reasonable doubt that the killings happened, that they were part of a widespread or systematic attack on civilians under a state or organizational policy, and that Duterte is responsible for them.
Each incident names a date, place, victim and alleged perpetrators that the defense must prepare to answer during the trial.
What's next
Prosecutors must file their revised trial brief, witness list and evidence list by October 16. The defense must file its list of contested issues by October 30.
Duterte has been ruled fit to stand trial.

articles.summary: The Department of Justice on Saturday said it conducted a preliminary investigation on Friday, October 9, on the obstruction of justice complaint filed against Senator Robin Padilla.

blocks.text: Published October 10, 2026 11:20am
The Department of Justice (DOJ) on Saturday said it conducted a preliminary investigation on Friday, October 9, on the obstruction of justice complaint filed against Senator Robin Padilla.
The next hearing will be held on Friday, November 6, DOJ spokesperson Polo Martinez said, according to a report by GMA News reporter Katrina Son.

On May 28, the Philippine National Police-Criminal Investigation and Detection Group (PNP-CIDG) filed a complaint for obstruction of justice against Padilla and others with the DOJ over the escape of Senator Ronald "Bato" Dela Rosa from the Senate building.

Former PNP chief Dela Rosa, who is the subject of an arrest warrant from the International Criminal Court for “alleged criminal responsibility as an indirect co-perpetrator” in the crimes against humanity of murder during the Duterte administration's war on drugs, sought refuge at the Senate on May 11 after authorities attempted to serve the said arrest warrant. However, he slipped out of the Senate building on May 14.
Padilla previously maintained that he did not help Dela Rosa “escape” as the former police chief only asked to hitch a ride with him out of the Senate building on May 14. —KG, GMA News

articles.title: How fitterkarma lets Filipinos embrace the horrors of love and life
articles.summary: As fitterkarma reaches new milestones, we look back at the hot streak of successes — and how the four-piece rock outfit made Filipinos wear their (bleeding) hearts on their sleeves

items: Fitterkarma, a four-piece rock band from the Philippines, is experiencing significant success with its debut album release, an orchestral concert tour, and a Record of the Year win at the Awit Awards.
Their song 'Kalapastangan' has become a cultural phenomenon, frequently heard in various public spaces and on social media, showcasing the band's growing influence in Filipino music.
The band's songwriting explores themes of horror and sacrificial romance, with a collaborative creative process that emphasizes emotional depth and vulnerability in their music.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

September is pretty major for four-piece rock band fitterkarma: a debut album (kung tayo’y nasa isang horror na pelikula, tiyak ako ang una mong papatayin) release, an orchestral concert tour spotlighting their fresh record, and its Record of the Year win at the Awit Awards.
But even the events before this already prove how the group has the Philippines in a chokehold.

blocks.caption: How fitterkarma lets Filipinos embrace the horrors of love and life

blocks.text: I hear “Kalapastangan” countless times a week — from a kid I pass by while walking home from my dentist’s appointment, from speakers of ukay-ukay shops and the friendly neighborhood convenience store, and even from the phone of my fellow MRT passenger (because is it even a Filipino commuting experience if you don’t accidentally discover a stranger’s algorithm, thanks to their doomscrolling at a loud volume?).
On TikTok, it has become the sonic background of grief, long-awaited success, or other strangely cathartic stories Filipinos share in their day-to-day lives.

blocks.caption: How fitterkarma lets Filipinos embrace the horrors of love and life

blocks.text: I’m sure nobody would have guessed that the song came out in 2023 — the year that the passion project-turned-band fitterkarma was formed. Before “Kalapastangan” became omnipresent, though, “Pag-Ibig ay Kanibalismo II” was the first to become a nationwide earworm.

During a Valentine’s gig, I was one of the many avid listeners who knew every lyric by heart — and was thrilled to shout it with everybody else. Some time after that gig, I got to talk to the band about its discography’s origin stories.

blocks.caption: How fitterkarma lets Filipinos embrace the horrors of love and life

blocks.text: “I wasn’t even serious when I was writing it,” quipped Joao de Leon, the band’s vocalist and guitarist, in an interview with Rappler. “Nanti-trip lang ako, kaya naging makulit din ’yung lyrics… We had this EP, ’yung ‘pakinggan mo…’ (2022) parang dun ako nag-start maglagay ng dark theme sa lyrics. It just came out naturally, siguro dahil ’yun ’yung hindi ko pa nakita masyado sa OPM that time. But when I was writing stuff sa ‘pakinggan mo…,’ I already saw Bita and the Botflies live. So isa sila sa nagbigay ng inspiration sa akin din sa music.”

(I wasn’t even serious when I was writing it. I was just messing around, which is why the lyrics turned out so playful… We had this EP, pakinggan mo… (2022); that’s sort of where I started incorporating dark themes into the lyrics. It just came out naturally — probably because that wasn’t something I saw much of in OPM at the time. But by the time I was writing material for pakinggan mo…, I had already seen Bita and the Botflies perform live. So, they were among the artists who inspired my music.)

Some of the songs in the pakinggan mo… EP were originally from De Leon’s solo project Joao — a peek into his inkling for dark songwriting themes. It isn’t surprising, given his personal consumption of different media, like video games Resident Evil and Siren.

From the concept of sainthood to purgatory, religious imagery is also present in De Leon’s songwriting, who “highly respects religion” and even has a background in serving his church’s music ministry.

One of the things that stands out in the fitterkarma’s discography is how it treats the concept of horror as something you can acknowledge and even embrace, especially in uncertainty. It’s part of the human experience.
Part of the band’s string of releases this year were “maryclaire” and “Purgatoryo,” which the group had long been performing in gigs before it was released in streaming platforms.

Earlier this year, fitterkarma also dropped “Aswang sa Maynila” featuring Novocrane, which talks about feeling lost and disconnected with the person you love, as implied in the believed absence of an aswang in the city.

Although these songs showcase different worlds, their common thread lies not only in the artistic gruesomeness or sharp vulnerability, but also in the concept of sacrificial romance. It’s not exactly about loving despite suffering — but more of suffering as a form of loving. “Uubusin ko ang sarili ko / Pati ang puso mo (I will let myself be consumed / I will also consume your heart),” the song says.
In tinkering with this topic, their chemistry as a band also shows. According to De Leon, at least 70 to 80 percent of “Aswang sa Maynila’s” initial demo changed compared to its final form.

Their producer, Xergio Ramos, helped in “toning down” the song, as the initial J-rock-inspired version felt a bit difficult to play. But since it was a challenging piece, it also became more collaborative, with each member having the freedom to exercise their creativity.

“Siyempre ako, hindi ako drummer, for example. So si Ders (Sanders Bayas, drummer) kung paano niya didiskartehan ’yung drums. Si Lory (Lory Mendoza, guitarist) daming dinagdag sa guitars, at binawas to make it realistic. Si Soph (Sophia Miranda, bassist and backing vocals), tinone down niya ’yung mga sinulat ko sa MIDI na bass parts para maging mas human.”

(Of course, I’m not a drummer, for example. So Ders took care of the drums. Lory added and also removed a lot in the guitars to make it realistic. Soph toned down what I wrote in the MIDI of the bass parts to make it more human.)
In fitterkarma’s world, love plays like all-consuming devotion.

This is even more evident in the band’s debut album kung tayo’y nasa isang horror na pelikula, tiyak ako ang una mong papatayin. In “999,” someone is willing to take various forms of death in the name of love. It’s even more intense in “Sumpa,” where the person surrenders to their lover, even if it’s the same person who will cause their unspeakable suffering. And while vampires are often treated as emotional parasites, their song “Bampira” becomes a yearner’s wishful thinking anthem.

But to conjure all these feelings — much more onstage — means to prepare for the process properly. Among the band members’ pre-show rituals include moving their body, following the guidance of Bayas, a.k.a. doing a lot of stretching as a warm-up before they hit the stage. Meanwhile, Mendoza is a big pre-show reader. Apart from that, De Leon revealed that they would also shout a lot, as a way to get in the zone.
“Kaya nakakatakot sa holding area namin, akala may galit eh (This is why it’s scary to come near our holding area; people would think we’re angry),” he quipped.
Sophia, who’s described by her bandmates as “quiet and funny,” mentioned how she and her bandmates would find themselves bickering with each other on the way to gigs, especially during longer days.
“IJBOL,” she said. “Hindi pa rin namin nakakalimutang mag-enjoy with our company bago kami maging professional ulit pagbaba ng band at i-meet ’yung fans.”
(We try not to forget to enjoy each other’s company before we become professional again as we go down the stage and meet the fans.)
After all, their listeners have loved seeing them wearing their (bleeding) hearts on their sleeves.

When asked about a memorable fan interaction, the band would recall a time when they performed in Vigan, Ilocos Sur. While the members were having a nighttime stroll, a group of friends — around seven to eight members — immediately stopped the tricycle they were riding and started screaming upon seeing fitterkarma.
Fueled by adrenaline, the band ran away in jest and genuine joy. One of the plastic bags Mendoza was carrying — filled with convenience store-bought items — even got torn, as recalled by De Leon.
“Kung sino man kayo, sana you had fun. We did (Whoever you guys are, I wish you had fun. We did).” – Rappler.com

articles.title: Hurricane Isaias makes landfall on U.S. Gulf Coast as Category 2 storm
articles.summary: Hurricane Isaias crashed into the U.S. Gulf Coast as a dangerous Category 2 storm on Friday, lashing communities in Alabama and the Florida Panhandle with damaging winds, heavy rain, flooding and…

image.caption: An American flag is seen flapping in the wind on Alabama's Mon Louis Island ahead of the arrival of Hurricane Isaias on Friday. (Octavio Jones/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·Updated

Hurricane Isaias crashed into the U.S. Gulf Coast as a dangerous Category 2 storm on Friday, lashing communities in Alabama and the Florida Panhandle with damaging winds, heavy rain, flooding and life-threatening storm surge.
U.S. National Hurricane Center says Isaias made landfall near Destin, Fla., on Friday

The first hurricane of the Atlantic season made landfall near Destin, Fla., the Miami-based U.S. National Hurricane Center said. It had maximum sustained winds of 169 km/h. The storm weakened to just below major hurricane status before it came ashore.

"The storm is here. Buckle down at this point. Don't be getting out on the roads," Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis said at a news conference, adding that flash flooding would be a hazard "throughout the region."

Hurricane-force winds lashed the Gulf shoreline in the low-lying coastal area known for powdery white sand beaches that are dotted with vacation homes, waterfront bars and seafood shacks. Forecasters warned the conditions could also stir up tornadoes.
People are seen leaving a gas station in Mobile, Ala., on Friday, which had been boarded up prior to the hurricane's arrival. (Octavio Jones/The Associated Press)
In Mobile, Ala., officials reported downed trees and power lines, while Emerald Coast Utilities Authority, which serves parts of Florida, issued a boil-water notice for its customers.
More than 400,000 customers in Florida and Alabama were without power Friday evening, according to poweroutage.com.
Residents in Panama City, Fla., braved the rain while filling sandbags Friday to protect their houses.
"I mean, it's just the nature of the beast. It's Florida," said Corliss Stone, who works for the fire department.
A downed tree blocks a road in Pensacola, Fla., on Friday, as Isaias-driven wind and rain approached the area. (Joe Raedle/Getty Images)

One of the biggest concerns is a storm surge that could be as high as 1.8 to 2.7 metres, according to the hurricane centre. Places most at risk include Florida's Pensacola Beach and the Gulf Islands National Seashore.

Anne Petzold, who lives with her husband in the Florida beach community of Gulf Breeze, said everyone in their neighbourhood planned to ride out the storm. The couple installed hurricane shutters and picked up anything in their yard that could turn into a projectile.
"Everybody does what they can do, everybody asks if they need help — they ask for help, they offer help. All good," she said. "It's just another adventure."

Dangerous conditions are expected throughout the western panhandle, southern Alabama and southern Mississippi, the U.S. National Hurricane Center said. Several counties announced mandatory evacuations while Mobile, Ala., imposed a curfew beginning Friday evening until morning.
Dozens of Waffle Houses closed

In a sign of how serious the warnings are, dozens of Waffle Houses in the Florida Panhandle were closed, according to the company's website. The beloved Southern breakfast chain is known for staying open through severe weather and often is a measuring stick of a storm's severity.
Kelsei Frazier, a Florida-native living in Pace who is no stranger to hurricanes, knows all about the Waffle House Index.

"We joke because if Waffle House is still open, then you know it's not a bad hurricane, but all the Waffle Houses that I know of within at least a normal range from us are closed," said Frazier. "Which is a pretty big deal."
DeSantis warned residents to expect power outages, gasoline shortages and closures of bridges and highways.
The state's National Guard deployed about 5,000 soldiers and airmen to help with the response, and search and rescue teams were ready to respond, while some prisons evacuated inmates.

articles.title: Sara Duterte trial recap, Oct. 9: Unexplained wealth pegged at P818 million
articles.summary: The prosecution presented its final witness against Vice President Sara Duterte on Friday, October 9, a forensic financial analyst who claimed before the Senate impeachment court that the Duterte…

blocks.text: October 10, 2026 | 10:31am

MANILA, Philippines — The prosecution presented its final witness against Vice President Sara Duterte on Friday, October 9, a forensic financial analyst who claimed before the Senate impeachment court that the Duterte couple had a whopping P817.87 million in undeclared assets and income from 2022 to 2025.

Alexander Cabrera, a lawyer and accountant who serves as chairman emeritus of PwC’s Philippine member firm Isla Lipana & Co., said the figure was drawn only from bank, tax, anti-money laundering and corporate records obtained through court subpoenas, and excludes documents held by Duterte and her husband, lawyer Manases Carpio.

The figure is the prosecution’s central claim for Article II, which accuses Duterte of amassing wealth beyond her lawful income, misdeclaring her assets and keeping business interests the Constitution bars her from holding. It is more than eight times the P98.66 million net worth the vice president declared in 2025.
The prosecution has announced it would no longer pursue Article III on bribery, making Cabrera the last witness in its presentation of evidence.

The defense, which will cross-examine Cabrera on Monday, questioned his credibility in making a "supposed" forensic report of the vice president's wealth, based on documents it says should not have been handed over to him.
During its turn in presenting witnesses, the defense will also get their chance to call to the stand their own expert witness.

Earlier in the day, a Bureau of Internal Revenue (BIR) official confirmed the agency is auditing Duterte and Carpio under letters of authority covering up to 20 years of taxes, and that Cale 88 Foods Corp., a banana chip exporter with ties to Carpio, is also under audit.
Here are three highlights from the proceedings.
1. How the P817.87 million adds up

The prosecution had billed Cabrera as the witness who would make sense of nearly a month of testimony from several bank executives, land registrars, and representatives from the Securities and Exchange Commission and the Anti-Money Laundering Council.
Among them, they put on record huge sums of funds that prosecutors said were missing from Duterte’s SALNs, but none was in a position to say whether it amounted to wealth beyond her lawful income.

Cabrera built his estimated total from four sources: bank balances missing from Duterte’s SALN, undeclared property, bank deposits that exceeded the couple’s declared income, and their share of undeclared income from companies they own.
Duterte and Carpio's undeclared bank balances alone ranged from P23.17 million to P80.70 million a year, most of it in Carpio’s accounts, Cabrera claimed.

Their alleged undeclared property included 17 insurance policies, firearms, real estate and business stakes, he said. Deposits that counted as income totaled P174.96 million from 2022 to 2025, against P63.11 million declared in the couple’s tax returns, he added.

Cabrera also flagged unusual banking activity by the vice president and her husband, the most damning being the manager’s checks worth P96 million allegedly circulated through the couple’s joint account for years before P80 million went into four life insurance policies.

Certain credit card purchases were also flagged as unusual by the witness, such as an alleged single P205,000 payment at the Ginza Inakaya in Tokyo, Japan, as well as two purchases on the same day at Nike SM Davao, totaling more than P300,000.
Cabrera said he counted each asset only once and left out most dollar accounts.
2. Gencorp: over P1 billion in unreported inflows

Cabrera also alleged that Gencorp Industries, a firm Duterte lists in her SALN as a stockholder but whose corporate filings do not name her, left more than P1 billion in bank inflows off its books from 2023 to 2025, equal to 80% to 94% of the revenue it reported.
“Pag ganyan po kalaki ang tinatago niyo, eh fraudulent po iyan (If what you're hiding is that huge, then that is fraudulent),” he said.

Cabrera had cited receipts showing Gencorp runs five Jollibee branches in Davao City despite a capital of only P1.25 million. He attributed 20% of its undeclared income to Duterte, mirroring her stake in Metro City Chow Foods Corp., which shares directors with Gencorp, and called the estimate conservative.
It's Cabrera's theory that Gencorp intentionally kept Duterte’s name off its records because it does business with the Davao City government.
“Kung si VP Sara po ay nakapangalan po sa GIS ng Gencorp, hindi po pwedeng makakuha ng kontrata ang Gencorp po sa City of Davao,” he said.

Her brother, Davao City Mayor Sebastian Duterte, acknowledged in earlier testimony that the city awarded Gencorp 19 contracts worth about P33.2 million and said he would not have allowed them had he known of her stake.

Several senator-judges themselves had done their own math and raised doubts on the truthfulness of Gencorp's filings in their questions to Anne Garcia Marquez, the chief of staff of the BIR's Office of the Commissioner.

Lacson noted Gencorp reported P520.67 million in 2025 sales but paid only P777,093 in income tax. Sen. Kiko Pangilinan said bank records show Gencorp held P46.19 million at the end of 2023, while its audited statements showed only P924,695.
“They were not being truthful if the bank records show that the ending balance in 2023 is 46 million,” Pangilinan says.
The defense, for its part, drew from Marquez that corporations have separate legal personalities and that their income is not the couple’s.
3. Cale88 and money from China
Cabrera claimed Cale88 understated its revenue by an average of 51% a year, and that P193.95 million of its foreign remittances, more than 80%, came from Chinese companies.

Sen. Risa Hontiveros also revealed that based on her team's research, one Ukrainian remitter to Cale88 matches a company under criminal investigation in Kyiv for fraud and money laundering, and that its last transfer to Cale88 came after that case was opened in May 2025.

Sen. Joel Villanueva noted that Cale88 reported P150 million in sales in 2024 with only two employees on record. Marquez said that seemed "impossible" and guessed it would take several machines to power their operations with such a lean workforce.
The BIR’s audit will check whether Cale88 under-declared sales, which could lead to deficiency taxes or, if evasion is proven, a criminal case, she said.
The AMLC’s executive director testified earlier this week that Cale88 could be a money laundering candidate, subject to further investigation.
Overall, Cabrera laid down five main conclusions from his findings:

items: Duterte’s SALNs from 2022 to 2025 “were untruthful";
She “continued to participate in various businesses” as vice president;
Her unexplained wealth amounts to P817.87 million “based only on the limited documents examined";
The violations “establish the pattern of constitutional violations year-on-year";
Other laws, including the Tax Code, “were violated or may have been violated.”

blocks.text: Presiding officer Sen. Chiz Escudero reminded prosecutors that because no subpoena was issued to Cabrera, they must bring him back for cross-examination on Monday, warning that his testimony “would be useless” otherwise.

articles.title: Some SKs will be ‘trentahin’ by 2028. They’re not happy about it either.
articles.summary: Some will have to sacrifice their careers. Others will have to pick up the slack for council members who cannot afford the same sacrifice.

blocks.text: Angelus Collong ran for Sangguniang Kabataan (SK) chairperson of Barangay Pinili, Abulug, Cagayan, when she was 23 years old — just on the edge of the qualifying age bracket. She only did so because she was told no one else wanted the position.

Three years later, at 26, she had been considering applying for a job abroad once her term ended. “Hindi naman puwedeng ma-stuck lang tayo dito sa barangay,” she said. (I can’t just be stuck here in the barangay.)

Then, the barangay and SK elections (BSKE) slated for this year were postponed to 2028. She will be 28 by then — still technically classified as part of the youth bracket of 15 to 30 years old. But she will already be trentahin, a Filipino slang word describing people in their late 20s to 30s who are starting to feel the first signs of aging.

Despite this new phase in life, she will be stuck in the same place she has been in since she was 23: balancing her SK duties with a full-time software programmer job and selling ukay-ukay (pre-loved clothes) on the side.

“Kung anak-mayaman lang sana ako, eh ‘di kahit hindi muna ako magka-career, maghahanap ng trabaho…. Puwede lang ako mag-serve na ganiyan,” she said. “Kaso, hindi eh. Kailangan ko ring kumayod outside.”
(If only I came from a rich family, then I wouldn’t need to put my career first and look for a job. I can just continue serving as an SK. But I’m not. I need to find work.)

She simply cannot live off the P5,000 to P6,000 per month she gets from her SK post. But she also made a commitment to her barangay — even if she only signed up to do so for three years, the term of office for which she was elected.

She is not the only SK official facing this conundrum. Since SK candidates must be at least 18 years old but not more than 24 by the time of their election, the current batch of officials will be anywhere from 23 to 29 years old when the 2028 polls roll around.
“In our age bracket right now, we already need to start building our careers,” she said in a mix of English and Filipino.

More than 600 miles away in Barangay Piapi, Dumaguete City, Negros Oriental, SK Chairperson Don Ramirez was also 23 years old when he ran for his SK position. Three years later, he is still among the eldest in his batch of youth officials at 26.

But the realization that he was getting older — all while his honorarium remained insufficient — pushed him to find other work to augment his income. He now balances his public official duties with his work as a tutor as well as a freelance photographer and videographer.
As he managed to wear these multiple hats, his council was even awarded the city’s most outstanding Sanguniang Kabataan council in 2025.

But while Ramirez is getting by, not all of his council members can afford the same. He now has one inactive councilor and two more planning to resign because of the BSKE postponement. They cited career priorities — which isn’t all that surprising since they were only being paid P2,500 per month for doing their duties.

He can’t blame them, but it doesn’t stop him from being disheartened. He knows he can’t handle all the preparations alone for the three to five activities that their SK council usually holds every month — such as leadership trainings, clean-up drives, sports tournaments, and scholarship programs.
Now, he has no choice but to limit the programs of their SK council according to the availability of the SK council members.

“If they are not available, who will conduct the activities? It will be me again. But what if I am not available or I am not there because I’m preoccupied with work?” he added in a mix of English and Bisaya.

Poll watchdog National Citizens’ Movement for Free Elections called the BSKE the “most frequently postponed democratic exercises in the country’s history.” Rappler’s own research found that the barangay and SK elections have been moved — either separately or jointly — at least 16 times since 1982.

Why is it an issue that these polls are perennially moved? It’s because the barangay and SK councils are the government units that Filipinos know and feel the most, said lawyer Ona Caritos, executive director of the Legal Network for Truthful Elections or Lente.
“It’s not every day that you get to interact with your mayor, with your congressman, with your senator, but we interact every day with our barangay officials,” she said.

According to the National Youth Commission (NYC), SK officials also have the added responsibility of representing the youth in local governance and policymaking. The commission said these youth councils have control over 10% of their barangay’s budget to create programs that develop neighborhood youth, such as sportsfests, mental health seminars, environmental clean-up drives, and skills training workshops.
These young officials are also being trained to be “future public servants,” according to the NYC. Many may go on to become barangay officials themselves.

Because of this, winning the support of these officials is also key for national politicians who want to consolidate power. Extending terms is a “carrot” these higher officials dangle to earn the loyalty of local leaders, according to Caritos.
And when their loyalties switch from the people who elected them to the politicians who kept them in power, it is the voters who get the short end of the stick.
But not all SK officials want to stay in power.
Caritos told Rappler that Lente had already expected a good number of SK officials to resign in light of the BSKE postponement.
“Because two years is two years — it’s not six months…. It’s a long time for a young person or a young individual to wait and delay his life plans yet again just for the barangay,” she said.
This would exacerbate the existing issue of vacancies in barangay and SK positions across the country.

As of September 29, 13.55% of the 420,100 SK positions nationwide are vacant because the officials who held them have either resigned, died, been removed from office, or been absent without leave during their term. There are also almost thrice as many vacancies for SK councilors compared to their chairpersons.

blocks.caption: visualization

blocks.text: That data only reflects vacancies four days after the postponement was announced — though attempts at the delay had been floated long before it was signed into law. Since then, posts announcing the resignations of SK officials and vacant seats have been all over social media.

blocks.caption: visualization

blocks.text: Caritos said these vacancies can be attributed to the following reasons:

items: a lack of effective communal support for elected SK officials
SK duties taking a back seat in the list of priorities, since most officials are still of student age or at the beginning of their work career
repeated postponement of the BSKE

blocks.text: “When they ran, they were running with the mindset that they would just serve [for] a certain period. If the elections are postponed, then this fixed period is extended — hence, the tendency is to resign or to just not appear,” she added.
SK officials’ honoraria are based on the economic class and financial situation of their barangays. (READ MORE: What are the compensation, benefits of barangay and SK officials?)

Barangay Pinili, where Collong serves, only has a population of just about 754 people based on the 2024 census — plus, it is in the 2nd-class municipality of Abulug. That is reflected in her four-digit honorarium.

Yet even that amount is depleted by the costs she incurs in fulfilling her duties, which include weekly trips to Manila to file reports. Those costs include travel and accommodation, with the fare alone ranging from P1,500 to P1,900 — even though the limit for reimbursements per trip is only P500.

Her other jobs give her the funds to continue her term, but at the cost of her own well-being. She said she barely gets any sleep when she has a night shift right before their morning barangay session.
But that’s not even the last of Collong’s troubles. She also struggles with the minimal budget for SK activities.
“If you want a grand program, you really need to pay out of your own pocket,” Collong said.

Collong and Ramirez are not necessarily against SK officials having a five-year term. In fact, they see the advantages of a longer term — more time to learn the ropes and more opportunities to implement programs.
But, for them, extending their current term so suddenly isn’t the way to go.
Even Lente does not see the five-year term as necessarily a bad thing. There just isn’t enough data to back it up.

“When the first term-setting law was discussed in Congress, the four-year term, most of the stakeholders were in agreement that four years is enough for the implementation of the programs and policies at the barangay level,” Caritos said. “Let’s allow the [initial] law to be implemented — the four-year term — and let’s assess if the four years is enough or not enough. And then, if it’s not enough, then let’s talk about the five years.”
Despite all these reasons to leave, some SK officials choose to tough it out because of their sense of responsibility.
Ramirez is afraid the council would fall into the wrong hands if he resigns. His worries are not unfounded.

Empty SK seats can be handled in three different ways: special elections, mayoral appointments of officers-in-charge, or an election during a Katipunan ng Kabataan (KK) Assembly, which is a gathering of all registered youth voters in a barangay.
But past attempts at special elections have often been deferred or suspended, usually due to funding problems, while KK assemblies have long been criticized for failing to convene regularly.

That leaves appointments as the easiest option. But this method not only deprives voters of the opportunity to choose their own leaders but also opens SK seats to political maneuvering from higher offices.
Collong said she now has no choice but to accept the way things are.
“Ako na lang mag-a-adjust, kasi nandiyan na eh, napirmahan na…. Pero kung hindi na talaga kaya ng mga SK, eh ‘di, pasensiya, magre-resign na siguro,” she said.
(I will be the one to adjust, because it’s there already; the law has been signed. But if the youth council can no longer handle it, then I’m sorry, I have to resign.)
And if she resigns, she said her entire council could follow suit.
The BSKE postponement may seem like a cause for celebration for elected officials. After all, they get to stay in power for two more years without needing to court votes.

But for the young officials who have their whole lives ahead of them, the delay is an added burden they didn’t sign up for. – with reports from Jade Florido, Jedi Rollinas, Jerome Santos, and James Bones/Rappler.com
Jade Florido, Jedi Rollinas, Jerome Santos, and James Bones are volunteers for Rappler’s Research and Data unit.

articles.title: How the trial of two murdered Australian surfers ended in a guilty verdict
articles.summary: The mother of two Australian surfers murdered in Mexico two years ago with their American friend said "accountability matters".

blocks.text: The mother of two murdered Australian surfers, who were killed in Mexico two years ago alongside their American friend, told a court "accountability matters".
Three men have been found guilty of murdering brothers Jake and Callum Robinson, and their US friend Carter Rhoad during a surfing trip in Mexico in 2024.
BBC's Will Grant takes a look at the case.
Read the full story here.

articles.title: Mexico: Court finds three men guilty of murder of Australian, US surfers
articles.summary: The 2024 murders of brothers Jake and Callum Robinson, along with their friend Carter Rhoad, shocked Mexico and drew international outrage.

image.caption: Prosecutors have asked for 210 years of imprisonment for each of the convictsImage: AAP/IMAGO

blocks.text: A Mexican court on Friday convicted three men in the 2024 murders of two Australian brothers and their American friend, who were killed during a botched robbery which sparked international outrage.
Australian brothers Jake and Callum Robinson, aged 30 and 33, and their friend Carter Rhoad, 30, were on a surfing trip to Mexico when they were shot dead in Baja California state.

They were camping in a remote beachside area near the city of Ensenada when they were attacked during a suspected robbery. Their bodies were found days later, in a well, with gunshot wounds to their heads.
What was said in court?
The judge on Friday ruled that the three Mexican defendants had acted with premeditation. They are yet to be sentenced for the murders.
The prosecution has asked for an "exemplary sentence" of 210 years for each of the three convicted, even though the maximum sentence in Baja California is 60 years.

blocks.caption: The brothers' parents were in court to hear the guilty verdictImage: Guillermo Arias/AFP

blocks.text: Debra Robinson, mother to the Australian brothers, burst into tears when the court passed the guilty verdict.

"While no verdict can ever bring back our boys or ease the heartbreak of losing them," the convictions marked "an important step towards justice and accountability," their father Martin Robinson said in a statement on behalf of the family.
Victim begged for mercy
Case prosecutors described the killings of the three surfers during the closing arguments on Thursday, by recalling the testimony of the girlfriend of one of the main suspects.
She had said that Rhoad had begged for his life while her boyfriend had bragged about "how beautifully" his victims cried before he robbed them.
The triple homicide shocked Mexico and drew international attention when it came to light.
Baja California is one of Mexico's most violent states, riddled with organized crime and drug trafficking, although cartel activity doesn't usually affect tourists.
