articles.title: Is active listening to music a lost art, and is physical media bringing it back?
articles.summary: When was the last time you actually paid close attention to the music you're playing?

blocks.text: Tech has made life easier, but it’s left us fatigued from endless doomscrolling and constant notifications. Despite having instant access to everything, none of what we buy or consume actually feels ours.

Even music and streaming have also reached a point wherein it’s also becoming wearisome. Were you one of those people who crashed out when The 1975 got rid of some of their songs on streaming platforms, or experienced firsthand when a song gets pulled out from your playlist and is no longer accessible? Because I have. And it’s funny because I am writing this while mourning the fact that one of my favorite songs from my favorite local bands—who have also recently stopped doing gigs—was removed from Spotify (These Kids Are Only Dreaming by Cheats, I still talk about you).

We are all finding new hobbies and activities that will help us lessen our screen time, hence the rising trend in analog activities such as journaling, reading books, and exercising. And music is a huge part of this conversation, too, as more people are revisiting opportunities to engage more deeply with music.
But where does music fit in this conversation? In an age where almost nothing feels tangible anymore, how do we create an engaging and tactile experience when we listen to music?
When we think about going analog, the same formula applies to music. The common denominator for all of these is intention.

We describe active listening as giving your full, undivided attention to something you are listening to. It encourages you to sit with the music, understand it on a deeper level, and reflect. Sure, you can also do this with songs on Spotify, but physical formats add a layer of action and intent.

Listening to music this way allows you to be purposeful by choosing what you want to listen to and commit to the entire listening journey. When you decide to purchase a record, making time to choose from a variety of genres and artists is itself an act of rejecting the modern impulse of playing and optimizing through algorithms.

In physical formats, you accept an album, or even a custom-burned CD, as a complete and cohesive work and an entirely different form of art. Even the extra bits inside, like the sleeve, notes, and lyrics, are visual assets you can appreciate as you play a track.

Even artists themselves are yearning for an option for their art to be presented in a way it was intended to be consumed. If we can honor Christopher Nolan’s intended way of watching his films – via an IMAX 70mm screen – then we also definitely can with music and physical media.

Just as Adele faced backlash back in 2021 for convincing Spotify to remove the shuffle button as the default for her album 30, she explained, “We don’t create albums with so much care and thought into our track listing for no reason. Our art tells a story, and our stories should be listened to as we intended.”

This was the only request I had in our ever changing industry! We don’t create albums with so much care and thought into our track listing for no reason. Our art tells a story and our stories should be listened to as we intended. Thank you Spotify for listening 🍷♥️ https://t.co/XWlykhqxAy— Adele (@Adele) November 21, 2021

Physical media honors this request in a way that makes skipping a track or optimizing your queue an active and conscious effort. Once you invest the effort into starting an album, you are more inclined to pay attention and justify that effort, rather than letting it fade into the background as noise.

This is also for those who want to physically own what they love because digitally saving it in your library will never hit the same. With physical media, you can rest easy at night knowing that even if your favorites disappear from digital streaming platforms, you will still have a copy of it.
Interested but don’t know where to start? Here’s a short guide and a few starter recommendations:

The first step is to learn about the different types of physical formats (CDs, vinyl records, and cassette tapes) and where you want to start. They all have their own pros and cons, but here’s a short list of what they offer:

items: CDs if you want to prioritize portability and budget;
Vinyl records if you want the immersive experience and are willing to spend on records and a player hooked up to good speakers;
Cassettes if you are into its compact charm and the underground culture it offers

blocks.text: The next step: start with what you love! Make a list of some of your favorites and narrow it down according to your budget. Remember, your collection should feel personal–not curated for an audience. Your only audience is you!

Once you have your list of artists and/or albums, it’s time to hunt! There are still record stores up and running these days, such as Backspacer Records located in Kapitolyo, where you can find CDs and vinyl; Bear‘s Den Records in Legaspi Village, where you can also shop for CDs, vinyl, and even equipment. For cassette tapes, you can find most in thrift stores or in flea markets; United Cassettes PH is also a local webstore you can shop from. These are only a few suggestions, but of course, there are lots of other physical stores if you look around enough.
Of course, your physical media is useless if you don’t have the right equipment for it, so here are some of my curated recommendations:

items: A CD player is the way to go if you want to go down the CD road. There’s also the KC-918, a portable CD player that feeds into the Y2K nostalgia aesthetic if you prefer bringing it around with you on the go.

For your vinyl record needs, the Audio-Technica AT LP60X is a good entry-level turntable. And if you are fully committing to the vinyl lifestyle, lock it in with Big Fudge’s all-in-one cleaning kit for your maintenance needs.
For cassettes, this portable cassette player should do the trick.

blocks.text: The beauty of physical media is also intention through curation: keeping what truly matters to you rather than hoarding every new release. The analog lifestyle is never about overconsumption and feeding into consumerism; it’s about making choices.

This is not a sign for you to cancel your streaming subscriptions and replace them with physical media, and I am not saying that digital streaming should be condemned, not when it makes music and artists easily accessible. I am, however, telling you that there is no harm in taking some time off your screen and letting yourself consume intentionally. Allow yourself to slow down and give your senses a break every once in a while.
So put the phone down, clear your brain, and let the music speak for itself! – Rappler.com

This piece was written by BrandRap volunteer Beatrice Ira Levanza. Bea is a passionate creative whose works revolve around shared experiences and the mundanity of life. She enjoys consuming Philippine media and is eager to try new experiences in the name of art and culture. A fresh graduate with a Bachelor’s degree in Fine Arts, major in Advertising Arts, from the University of Santo Tomas, she hopes to continue creating meaningful work that resonates with people.

articles.title: US country music star Ella Langley cancels show due to 'security threat'
articles.summary: Police say they checked the concert venue in Tulsa, Oklahoma but "could not find any threat".

blocks.text: US country music star Ella Langley has said she had to cancel her sold-out concert in Tulsa, Oklahoma on Friday night, due to a "serious security threat".
The singer made what she called the "incredibly difficult" decision around two hours before the show at the 19,000-seater arena was due to start.
In a post on Instagram, the 27-year-old said the threat involved "the safety of my fans, the venue staff and my team".
Cpt Richard Meulenberg from Tulsa Police Department said a person had called saying "great harm" would be done at the event with "shots fired and bombs."
He stated his team had checked the venue at BOK Center several times before the show and "could not find any threat".
"The event was ready to go," he added, saying officers with sniffer dogs did a sweep of the arena again after the phone call was made.
"We could not find a credible threat," he said, stressing that the person who had made the call "disrupted this entire event" for thousands of Langley fans.
The star - who did not give any further details - also apologised to her fans, saying additional information regarding ticket refunds "will be shared as soon as possible".

BOK Center issued its own statement, saying that "the safety and well-being of everyone involved is our absolute priority, and after careful consideration, we have determined that the show cannot proceed.
"We understand the disappointment this news brings and apologise to fans who planned to attend."
In September, Langley's country smash Choosin' Texas overtook Mariah Carey's All I Want for Christmas Is You to become the longest-running number one single in US chart history.
Its success helped the singer from Alabama to sweep the Academy of Country Music Awards in May.

articles.title: Trump weighs livestream execution amid bipartisan backlash
articles.summary: Donald Trump said he hasn't decided whether the execution of the Fort Hood shooter will be livestreamed, after the Pentagon announced it would do so. The plan has been criticized by both Republicans…

image.caption: Hasan carried out the deadliest mass shooting on a military base in US history [Undated file photo]Image: Bell County Sheriff's Office/REUTERS

blocks.text: US President Donald Trump said on Friday that Fort Hood shooter Nidal Malik Hasan "absolutely" deserves the death penalty by firing squad but told reporters he has yet "to make a determination" on whether it will be livestreamed.
"I don't really care how he goes, as long as he goes," Trump said, referring to Hasan.
What did Hegseth and the Pentagon say about Hasan's execution?

Trump's remarks comes a day after the Pentagon said it would livestream the execution of 56-year-old Hasan, a former US Army psychiatrist who murdered 13 people and injured 32 others in Fort Hood in Texas in 2009.

In a video shared by the Pentagon regarding the execution, US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said "We'll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it's public, because people need to understand that there's serious consequence for these types of things."
Hasan is currently being held on death row in Fort Leavenworth in Kansas. His execution is slated for December 3.
He is paralyzed from the waist down and uses a wheelchair after he was shot by an officer responding to the Fort Hood shooting.
JD Vance says he would not watch livestream of execution
US Vice President JD Vance, speaking to reporters in Cincinnati on Friday, also said he doesn't know whether the livestream is "actually going to happen."
"If it is shown publicly," Vance added, "I'm not going to be watching it." Vance is a devout member of the Catholic Church, which opposes the death penalty.
"Whatever the controversy is about the method of the execution, I hope that people don't forget that this is a guy who brutally murdered a lot of innocent people," the US vice president said.

blocks.caption: Hasan is incarcerated at the United States Disciplinary Barracks [FILE: September 16, 2026]Image: Paul Hennessy/SOPA Images/IMAGO

blocks.text: Livestream plan faces bipartisan backlash
The Pentagon's plan to broadcast the execution has been met with a fierce backlash from within Trump's own Republican Party and the opposition Democrats.
"I absolutely support the sentence of death, but livestreaming executions is what jihadists do. America is better than that," said Republican Representative Austin Scott of Georgia.

Public executions are common in Taliban-controlled Afghanistan and the so-called Islamic State (IS) also engaged in public beheadings when the group controlled large swathes of Syria and Iraq in the 2010s. Iran is another country that carries out public executions.
Republican Congressman Rob Bresnahan of Pennsylvania said "an execution shouldn't be a livestreamed spectacle."
"The focus should be on justice for the victims and their families, not turning an execution into entertainment," he said in a statement posted on X. "Their pain deserves respect, not a public show."

Democratic Congressman Eugene Vindman of Virginia, who said he oversaw legal proceedings following the Fort Hood attack, said livestreaming Hasan's execution "is what terrorists and authoritarian regimes do. It's un-American."
Democratic Senator Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut said Pentagon chief Hegseth is "turning the Fort Hood execution into a gruesome inhumane spectacle."

The UN human rights office (OHCHR) also strongly condemned the ideaof a livestreamed execution, while the president of the United States Conference of Catholic Bishops called the plana "barbaric promotion of a culture of death."

articles.title: Life-threatening Hurricane Isaias makes landfall in Florida
articles.summary: The storm took direct aim at Florida and is expected to impact Alabama, Georgia, and Louisiana.

blocks.text: Hurricane Isaias has made landfall in the US state of Florida and is expected to bring life-threatening flooding and winds that have forced thousands to evacuate.
The storm weakened slightly to a category 2 hurricane, with 110 mph (175 kph) winds, before ramming into Florida's western panhandle on Friday evening.
Florida, Alabama, and Georgia have each issued states of emergency as meteorologists warned of life-threatening storm surge that could cause up to 9 feet (2.7m) of flooding in some areas.
Isaias is one of three storm systems affecting North America this weekend, with the two others hitting Mexico and Southern California in the El-Niño fuelled warm waters of the Pacific Ocean.
Both Florida and Alabama instituted mandatory evacuations due to the storm.

In Florida, those evacuations includes coastal communities in direct aim of the powerful storm. Florida Senator Rick Scott encouraged residents in designated areas to evacuate as soon as possible, as he warned in a social media post: "DO NOT WAIT! Get out NOW!"
Governor of Alabama Kay Ivey issued a mandatory evacuation for all non-residents, tourists and visitors in key counties likely to be heavily affected by the storm.
Hurricane Isaias is the first hurricane in the Atlantic's hurricane season, which largely has been delayed due to El Niño conditions in the Pacific.
It marks the first time in more than 30 years that a hurricane did not form till October.
The storm is likely to bring "life-threatening storm surge" to the US Gulf Coast, the National Hurricane Center warned.
After hitting Florida, the centre of Isaias is forecast to move across Alabama and into the Tennessee Valley on Saturday and Sunday, the National Weather Service said late on Friday.
As of Friday evening, hurricane-force winds extended outward up to 35 miles (55 km) from Isaias' centre, and tropical storm-force winds extended as far as 205 miles (335 km).
John Guoth, a resident of Navarre, Florida, told the BBC that he and his wife will remain in their home despite the rest of his street having already left.
"It's a hurricane, we get them all the time... we kind of knew that when we moved here," he said.
"Pretty much everything that can fly and will fly is battened down, and everything that cannot fly is really, really secured," he said,
Guoth said he put his ducks and chickens in the bathroom and weighed down his boats and trailers so "nothing flips over".
A few households have remained in the area, describing them as "long-term locals" who are "going to protect our homes".
Pensacola resident Brandin Ruth told the BBC that they have been turning the gas off to the buildings, icing down product and trying to get team members home.
People in the Florida city have "seen bad storms before" but are "bunkering up", he said, adding: "You don't want to underestimate a storm like this".
Two other storms are also forecast to batter North America this weekend.

Hurricane Simon is bearing down on the Pacific coast of Mexico as a category one hurricane. It is set to pick up speed and become category four by Saturday, eventually making landfall near Puerto Vallarta on Sunday, according to Reuters.
Further north, Tropical Storm Rachel, a downgraded hurricane, is heading toward landfall around the US-Mexico border, along the Pacific.
While, Rachel is expected to reach the coast late on Saturday, the impact of the storm is already being felt due to high tides in southern California.
Video footage and photos show several streets under water in Newport Beach, California, through a combination of the tropical storm swells at sea and high tide.
Posting on its account on X, the City of Newport Beach advised people to "avoid the Balboa Peninsula due to street flooding caused by recent storm conditions and elevated tides".
It also urged people not to drive through flooded streets. Bulldozers have been shoring up the beach to try and prevent further flooding.
With additional reporting by Simon King.

articles.title: Trump fumes over Nobel peace prize snub and criticizes Norway
articles.summary:
President complains about not winning prize in year he started war with Iran and says: ‘We will not forget, Norway’

Donald Trump complained Friday about not winning the Nobel peace prize for…

blocks.text: Donald Trump complained Friday about not winning the Nobel peace prize for 2026, a year in which he started a war with Iran.
At what was supposed to be a rally for other Republican candidates in Syracuse, New York, the US president devoted a long portion of his speech airing his grievances with the Nobel committee.

“The United States of America, represented by me as your president, should have received the Nobel peace prize, but didn’t. And this is an indelible stain on the country of Norway, and those people that made such a disgraceful and embarrassing decision,” Trump said.

“The Nobel peace prize has been forever discredited by a handful of radical ideologues who are anti-democracy and really enemies of civilization,” Trump went on. “We will not forget, Norway, that you didn’t give this prize.”

Trump also recited a list of wars he claims to have settled, some of which were not wars and some that are still not settled, before adding: “I’m about to settle or win two more: Iran and Russia-Ukraine.”
Trump said he would be ending both wars “quickly”.
“I will tell you what,” he added, darkly. “Iran will be very quick one way or the other: that they give us everything or they don’t exist any longer.”

“Additionally, I stopped Iran from having a nuclear weapon and blowing up the entire Middle East and ultimately far beyond the Middle East, including Europe, perhaps the US and I saved more lives than anyone in history,” Trump claimed, despite the fact that US intelligence agencies reported to Congress in 2025 that Iran had actually suspended its pursuit of nuclear weapons in 2003.

“Despite all of this and all of these unbelievable accomplishments, the Nobel prize was given out today to a liberal person who works at the United Nations, who nobody has ever heard of,” Trump said of Navi Pillay, the South African former UN human rights chief who chaired the UN commission that concluded Israel was guilty of genocide in Gaza.

articles.title: Key things to know about Hurricane Isaias as millions under evacuation orders
articles.summary:
The hurricane is first in the Atlantic in what has turned into a very late season. Here’s what forecasters are saying about where Isaias will hit and how hard

Hurricane Isaias, which made…

blocks.text: Hurricane Isaias, which made landfall on the US Gulf coast Friday night, was forecast to bring a dangerous storm surge, significant rainfall, flooding and strong winds across the US Gulf coast this weekend. Millions of people across several states, including Florida, Georgia and Alabama, were under evacuation orders as officials prepared for the storm. All three states issued states of emergency.
The hurricane, the first in the Atlantic in what has turned into a very late 2026 season, made landfall as a category 2 storm, with sustained winds of 105 mph.

The National Weather Service warned that Isaias could produce a “life-threatening storm surge” along parts of the northern Gulf coast, which occurs when rising ocean water moves inland from the coastline.

items: 1. What are forecasters saying about where Isaias will hit and how hard?Isaias made landfall along the northern Gulf coast late Friday as a category 2 storm.The National Hurricane Center (NHC) warned it would bring a “life threatening” storm surge and “devastating winds likely across the Florida panhandle and Alabama coasts”.Isaias could bring 4-8in of rain, with locally higher totals up to 15in (380mm), across parts of the Gulf coast. Forecasters warned of significant flash and river flooding, especially in southern Alabama, the Florida Panhandle and south-western Georgia.Hurricane-force winds were expected to spread inland as far as 100 miles (160km) from the Alabama coast, the NHC said. There were also warnings of possible tornadoes late Friday or Saturday in its outer band of rains.The NHC said: “Across much of the remainder of the Southeast, rainfall amounts of 2 to 5 inches are expected. Localized higher amounts up to 10 inches are possible, especially across the Southern Appalachians and coastal Carolinas.”

2. What do the emergency response preparations look like?Florida, Georgia and Alabama have declared states of emergencies, with mandatory evacuations ordered in some coastal communities. Numerous evacuation shelters have opened across Florida, Louisiana, Alabama and Mississippi, with more than 370 trained American Red Cross (Arc) disaster workers supporting the response. The Arc is also pre-positioning cots, blankets, shelf-stable meals and other emergency supplies across the region.About 5,000 national guard troops were expected to mobilize in Florida, where at least four school districts cancelled late-week classes.Before the storm, oil and gas producers shut down a significant share of offshore production in the Gulf, which accounts for almost 15% of crude pumped annually in the US.

3. How come this season’s first Atlantic hurricane is so late? Is El Niño a factor?The El Niño climate pattern is a factor in this year’s quieter Atlantic hurricane season. While it warms sea surface temperatures in the Pacific where storm activity has been greater, it also increases wind shear – changes in wind speed and direction with height – over the Atlantic, which can disrupt tropical storms before they strengthen into hurricanes.The hurricane season begins 1 June and runs up to the end of November with the height of the season usually from the middle of August to the middle of October.The last hurricane to make landfall in the US was Hurricane Milton, which came ashore near Florida’s Siesta Key on 9 October 2024. It followed Hurricane Helene a month earlier, which killed more than 250 people and was the deadliest hurricane to hit the mainland US since Hurricane Katrina in 20o5.

4. What are storm surges and where are they expected to hit?As a hurricane approaches a coast, the churning winds force ocean water up on to land; atmospheric pressure from the storm also helps squeeze the water ashore. The shallower the continental shelf, the higher the threat of a dangerous surge. The water may take a couple of days to fully subside.Storm surge was expected from south-east Louisiana to Suwannee, in north-east Florida, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (Noaa).Up to 9ft of storm surge is forecast between Dauphin Island, Alabama, and Indian Pass, Florida.chart

5. How ready are local officials and Fema?Although state officials have declared their preparedness, Isaias will be a key test of the Federal Emergency Management Agency’s (Fema) ability to respond to a major hurricane after significant staffing cuts and an overhaul of the agency under the Trump administration. About 17% of Fema’s workforce left in fiscal year 2025, following Trump’s push to downsize the agency and shift more responsibility to states.The agency’s staffing reductions were not carried out systematically to ensure Fema could still meet its statutory obligations, said Chris Currie, director of homeland security and justice at the GAO. “It’s not whether Fema is going to respond. They’re going to respond. It’s more about the depth,” Currie said.Fema, however, said: “FEMA Incident Management Assistance Teams are deploying to Alabama and Florida, and FEMA personnel are embedded in state emergency operations centers. FEMA is also prepositioning emergency supplies at Maxwell air force base in Montgomery, Alabama, to supplement state resources if requested.”

articles.title: Hurricane Isaias makes landfall in Florida with severe effects expected across several states
articles.summary:
Governors of Mississippi, Alabama and Florida declared states of emergency as a downsized Fema faces first major test

Hurricane Isaias made landfall near Destin, Florida, on Friday evening,…

blocks.text: Hurricane Isaias made landfall near Destin, Florida, on Friday evening, sweeping ashore from the northern Gulf of Mexico as the first Atlantic hurricane of the 2026 season.
The National Hurricane Center (NHC) in Miami said the center of the cyclone made landfall at 9.30pm ET as a category 2 hurricane.
Forecasters had expected Isaias to weaken from its peak earlier on Friday as a major category 3 hurricane due to shifts in wind speed.
But even as high-end category 2 storm, the NHC said, severe impacts would be felt across a wide stretch of the northern Gulf coast from Louisiana to Florida, and far inland.
They included a “life-threatening” storm surge of up to 7ft (2.1 meters) along the Alabama-Florida line, and powerful wind gusts reaching parts of northern Georgia.

“Weakening will occur after landfall, but sustained hurricane-force winds will likely occur near and along Isaias’s track up to 100 miles inland,” wrote Robbie Berg, an NHC hurricane expert, in a Friday advisory.

The governors of Mississippi, Alabama, and Florida all declared states of emergency ahead of the storm’s arrival, urging some residents of coastal communities to evacuate and many more to prepare for the storm’s likely violent arrival.
The Mobile office of the National Weather Service warned parts of Florida could see “extremely dangerous” tornado-like winds.
By Friday evening, more than 400,000 customers had lost power across Alabama and Florida, according to poweroutage.com.
“Things are going to get really, really treacherous,” Jamie Rhome, deputy director for the National Hurricane Center, told the AP.

Florida’s national guard deployed roughly 5,000 soldiers and airmen to aid with the response, the AP reported. Some prisons were also evacuating their incarcerated populations. Most flights were grounded at several airports in Florida’s Panhandle.

Isaias is notable as one of the two latest-forming Atlantic hurricanes on record, tying a record set on 8 October 1905. None of the eight previous named storms of the 2026 Atlantic season intensified above tropical storm status.
Ahead of the storm, oil and gas producers shut down a significant share of offshore production in the Gulf, which accounts for almost 15% of crude pumped annually in the US.

The storm could also be the first major test of the ability of the Federal Emergency Management Agency (Fema) to deploy a large workforce after huge cuts and restructuring, emergency management experts warned.

The Trump administration has said it wants to eliminate, or drastically downsize, Fema. More than 4,300 employees left the agency in fiscal year 2025, about 17% of the workforce, according to a recent US government accountability office (GAO) report.

articles.title: [Vantage Point] Landbank’s P182-million belated retreat
articles.summary: Prolonged financial paralysis is never a harmless administrative technicality

items: Landbank has finally moved to deposit over P182 million in disputed funds with the court after nearly six years of freezing the account of PPI-JKG Philippines Inc., raising questions about its delayed action.

The bank's decision to withhold the funds was influenced by an internal legal directive despite having verified documentation of the account holder's authority, leading to significant commercial harm for PPI-JKG.

Landbank's recent court motion to consign the funds does not address the years of financial damage caused by its inaction, and there are concerns about its adherence to proper banking protocols compared to other institutions.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

This column and mounting legal pressure could have pushed Landbank to consign over P182 million in court after a nearly six-year freeze. But surrendering custody today cannot erase the unmitigated commercial injury caused yesterday—nor explain why a state lender sat on client funds for so long under the guise of neutrality.

Landbank has finally chosen to act. On August 10, nearly six years after it froze PPI-JKG Philippines Inc.’s corporate bank account and initiated an interpleader, Landbank asked the Manila Regional Trial Court to let it deposit the disputed funds with the court.

Only after Vantage Point (click here or click story below) exposed this ongoing paralysis did the state lender suddenly declare itself “ready, willing and able” to surrender physical custody of the balance. Landbank may attempt to frame the timing as purely coincidental. Readers, however, can decide for themselves whether that self-serving explanation deserves any credence.

blocks.caption: [Vantage Point] When Landbank’s prudence becomes punishment

blocks.text: The obvious question remains: Why only now? Landbank possessed the clear legal mechanism to deposit the funds the moment it filed its complaint for interpleader on October 2, 2020. Instead, it retained P182,760,217.77 inside its vaults for almost six years while insisting in open court that it harbored no beneficial interest in the money.

The institutional intervention began on September 23, 2020, when Christian Calalang wrote to Landbank claiming majority authority over PPI-JKG and requesting an immediate suspension of all corporate transactions pending an accounting.
That exact same day, PPI-JKG president Annabelle Arcilla submitted an official request for a P182-million manager’s check payable to Omniprime Marketing Inc. to meet pressing commercial obligations.

Landbank initially processed the application, formally debited the amount from the company’s account, but then withheld the physical release of the manager’s check immediately upon receiving Calalang’s letter.
The December 15, 2023 court testimony of Landbank Pearl Drive branch manager Nenita Camposano reveals the extraordinary nature of that stoppage.

Under cross-examination, Camposano confirmed that Arcilla’s transaction was already completed, that Arcilla had signed the received portion of the manager’s-check form, and that the only remaining operational step was handing over the check for deposit with Asia United Bank. Camposano then abruptly changed course after consulting Landbank Legal.

She identified Cesar Cabañez as the in-house lawyer she contacted. In her sworn testimony, she confirmed telling Cabañez that Arcilla was the fully documented, registered account signatory. Asked what Cabañez instructed, she answered: “He told me to not release the check”.
Under further questioning, she agreed that he issued that binding legal directive without ever seeing the corporate documents and board resolutions she held in her hands.
Landbank neither called nor emailed the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) that day to verify whether Calalang was indeed PPI-JKG’s legitimate majority shareholder or president.

That courtroom testimony dismantles any suggestion that the branch arrived at a balanced, prudent judgment based on verifiable facts. Asked about the devastating commercial injury caused by the stoppage, Camposano answered: “It was not my decision”. She admitted on the stand that this was the very first time in her banking career that she refused to release a recognized depositor’s funds without a formal court order.

She also acknowledged under oath that losing an account holding P182 million would inevitably impair the branch’s current-account and savings-account (CASA) performance targets, though she denied wanting the money retained for that specific reason.

items: [Vantage Point] DOTr: Jaime Bautista’s cross (Part 1)
[Vantage Point] DOTr: Jaime Bautista’s cross (Part 2)
[Vantage Point] Conclusion | DOTr: Jaime Bautista’s cross

blocks.text: I am certainly not inferring illicit motive from that admission. But it underscores the urgent need for Landbank’s senior leadership to explain who made the call, upon what verified records, and with what internal consideration of the bank’s own institutional targets.

Its recent four-page motion explains none of this. Landbank merely reiterates that Calalang and Arcilla asserted conflicting claims over corporate representation. While that might have justified a brief administrative pause to seek clarity, it cannot justify how an emergency precaution turned into a six-year commercial deprivation.

Landbank continues to maintain it has “no actual or personal interest” in the account. Precisely. Under Rule 62 of the Rules of Court, a special civil action for interpleader is provided so that an innocent stakeholder can consign disputed property with the court and step aside while rival claimants litigate.

If Landbank truly stood as a disinterested stakeholder, why did an internal bank lawyer urge Arcilla to “settle” with Calalang, when it was Arcilla who was the recognized, documented client of the branch?

Furthermore, if Landbank harbored no beneficial interest, why did it hold the money for nearly six years rather than consign it when the litigation commenced? While the funds sat idle in Landbank’s books, vendors remained unpaid, financing charges escalated, and binding contractual commitments accumulated.

The bank continually cites the legal doctrine of shielding itself from possible “double vexation or double liability”. Yet repeatedly invoking that legal doctrine does not mean the competing claims possessed equal evidentiary weight. Landbank possessed Arcilla’s formal account-opening records, verified signature cards, and established corporate mandate.

Calalang presented only a private letter accompanied by disputed corporate claims—wholly devoid of a temporary restraining order, an injunction, a final judicial decree, or an Anti-Money Laundering Council (AMLC) freeze order.

Arcilla responded within twenty-four hours with a formal secretary’s certificate repudiating his authority, followed later by an amended General Information Sheet (GIS) establishing her status as president and 75% owner.

The contrasting behavior of other universal banks makes Landbank’s conduct impossible to justify. Records and representations supplied to Vantage Point reveal that Asia United Bank, Security Bank, and UnionBank all received comparable intervention letters from Calalang. Unlike Landbank, those institutions strictly adhered to established Know-Your-Customer (KYC) rules and honored the company’s verified signatories.

Philippine National Bank likewise protected roughly P8 million in company funds from Calalang’s extrajudicial demands. Those banks recognized that Calalang was not an authorized signatory on the corporate accounts and held no court order, and they properly released the funds to Arcilla.

This does not prove that every institution received identical documentation, but it demands an answer to a disturbing question: What did Landbank know that four other major banks did not—or what did those private banks diligently verify that Landbank chose to ignore?

Landbank’s requested relief creates an additional irregularity. In its motion, the bank notes that the account contains P182,760,217.77, yet it petitions the court for permission to deposit an even P182 million.

What happens to the remaining P760,217.77? After immobilizing the company’s working capital for nearly six years, Landbank now seeks to consign the bulk of the balance to the court and secure a blanket judicial discharge from all further liability.

Arcilla has vigorously opposed this maneuver because consigning the funds at this late date would merely shift the freeze from Landbank’s vaults to the judiciary’s registry. Instead, she seeks the release of the funds under a court-approved counter-bond—a recognized procedural remedy that would allow PPI-JKG to fund its ongoing government license-plate production commitments while completely securing whatever lawful stake Calalang might establish in the future.

Vantage Point tried but failed to reach Arcilla, but a confidential source close to her confirmed that, beyond utilizing her own capital, she personally secured a US$4-million loan in May 2019 at an average of 7% annual interest to fund the license-plate project. Because confidential loan files were not disclosed, her accounting cannot be independently audited under Philippine bank secrecy statutes.

Nevertheless, releasing that P182-million check in September 2020 would have eliminated approximately 86% of the original loan balance. Applying her timeline, interest rate, and prevailing dollar-peso exchange metrics, compounding interest charges and currency depreciation have added an estimated P141 million in financing costs onto the company by September 2026.
That figure is an unadjudicated estimate, but it illustrates why prolonged financial paralysis is never a harmless administrative technicality.
Landbank’s latest court motion confirms that consignation was an available remedy all along. Moving the capital today cannot erase the years of commercial injury inflicted yesterday. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Passed from hand to hand, Paete’s taká tradition looks to its next generation
articles.summary: While Paete, Laguna is renowned for its woodcarvers, its papier-mâché craft remains far less recognized

blocks.text: LAGUNA, Philippines – Horse-shaped forms sat on a table inside a cafe in Paete, surrounded by glue, brushes, oil, and strips of paper. Around them, participants in the Matutong Magtaká workshop were learning how taká is made, one layer at a time. Guiding them was Ka Ichu, a magtataká who has spent decades making taká by hand.

Taká is Paete’s traditional papier-mâché craft. The workshop was among the activities of the Taká ng Paete Festival and Exhibition on September 27. Taká ng Paete is an initiative that local artist Rizia Adao and her family launched in 2022 under the advocacy #KeepTheTakaAlive.

But the people who have kept the craft going are growing older. Ka Ichu said many magtataká her age already have great-grandchildren, and the younger members of their families no longer want to take it up.
“Yung mga apo nila, yung mga anak nila, ayaw na. Kasi hindi madali gawin,” she said.(Their grandchildren, their children, no longer want to do it. Because it isn’t easy to make.)
Around the table that day, though, people had come to learn.
Paete is widely known as a town of woodcarvers or mag-uukit. Taká rarely comes up in the same breath.
Pieces of taká are often seen as souvenirs, decorations, or goods sold in town. Less visible are the people who make them, and the long process behind each piece.
Rizia sees this whenever she faces a crowd during her workshops. She asks who knows ukit, and people raise their hands. When she asks about taká, hardly anyone does.
“Pero pag sinabi ko na yung name na ‘taká,’ wala nang nagtataas ng kamay. So that’s the recognition na need ng taká,” she said.
(But when I say the word ‘taká,’ no one raises a hand. So that’s the recognition taká needs.)

blocks.caption: UNFINISHED. Unpainted taká animals, including a pig, a goat, and chicks, sit on a shelf in their plain brown finish. Photo by Arabella Grace Sta. Ana/Rappler

blocks.text: Rizia said there may be just as many magtataká in Paete as there are woodcarvers, if not more, despite the difference in recognition. Yet beyond the town and the people already familiar with it, the craft fades from view. The Ukit Taká Festival has started to help, she said, as more people now see taká through social media.

Behind Taká ng Paete is a family that has lived with the craft for much of their lives. Rizia’s parents, Ka Jong and Ka Ichu, have been making papier-mâché for almost four decades, and Rizia grew up surrounded by it.

Ka Ichu was already making taká before her pieces reached buyers. By her recollection, it took shape as a business around the 1990s. She started with large ducks, mallards shaped in different poses with their wings spread, using molds she got from another maker in the area. She and her family even attached the wings themselves.

Soon after, they began displaying their pieces in town. Buyers who came to look included exporters from Manila, who asked her to bring samples. She delivered them, and orders followed, slowly at first. By around 1991, she recalled, the orders had grown enough that they needed their own gawaan, or production space.

blocks.caption: KEEPING TRADITION. Ka Jong and Ka Ichu have been making papier-mâché in Paete for almost four decades. Photo from Rizia Adao

blocks.text: Local buyers came first. She supplied large decorative pieces to Rustan’s and SM, sourcing at the start from other taká producers in Paete since they did not yet have a production of their own. Taká was in its heyday then.
“Kasi talaga naman noon, parang boom na yung taká noon eh,” she said.
(Back them, taká was really booming.)

Prices were better, she recalled, and materials were cheaper. By 1992, she was supplying exporters. The orders were good from then until 2000 and stayed fairly strong until around 2005, before things began to slow down.

Some unfinished pieces were exported to Europe, including the UK, shipped in a plain brown finish. Abroad, they were sold as do-it-yourself kits with paint and brushes, with students among the target buyers.

What she misses most from those years are the papier-mâché leaves and flowers, attached to sticks and painted into flower arrangements. She would like to bring them back. Buyers have since moved toward animals, she said.

When lockdowns began, Ka Ichu said, they still had export orders to finish. They went to the workshop one at a time and asked the barangay for passes, since the space was open-air. Their priority, she said, was their workers, who were paid through bank transfers.
It was after the pandemic that the difficulty of the work was felt the most.

Competition added to the pressure. Ka Ichu said buyers began moving toward items that were difficult to copy, while other importers imitated pieces and lowered prices. She relayed an exporter’s view that cheaper and faster production from China had pulled prices down, a comparison to fast fashion and slow craft.
For makers, that leaves little room to set a price.
“Kasi may mga target price, target na ito lang yung kaya ibayad,” she noted.
(Because there are target prices, buyers who can only pay this much.)
They want to raise the value of taká, she said, but there is a limit.

Rizia described what she sees as a disconnect between the value the makers produce and what actually reaches them. Based on her own experience, she said only about 10 percent of a piece’s selling price goes to the makers, while the rest goes to middlemen and business people.
This, she shared, is part of the reason the younger generation hesitates. There are young people who want to learn the craft. They just will not take it up as a livelihood if it does not pay enough.
Rizia herself paints on taká, but she points out that the creative process begins long before the painting. A magtataká prepares, shapes, layers, dries, and finishes the forms that she paints on.

Her exhibit at GITNA Art Studio, which she curated, puts those makers at the center. Pictures of the magtataká are displayed in the exhibit, so visitors meet the people behind the pieces as well as the finished work.
It is also tied to her Taká Registry Project, an ongoing effort to document Philippine papier-mâché as an art form, including its people, processes, and traditions.

blocks.caption: ARTISTS. Photographs of the magtataká on display at the Taká ng Paete exhibit at GITNA Art Studio in Paete, Laguna. Photo by Arabella Grace Sta. Ana/Rappler

blocks.text: For some of the magtataká, being part of the exhibit changed how they saw their own work. Ka Ichu said many of them long had a low appreciation of their craft since they were paid minimally.
“Kasi nga, ang baba nung amount, ang baba nung binabayad sa amin,” she said.
(Since the amount is low, what we get paid is low.)
After Rizia invited them, Ka Ichu heard something new from her fellow magtataká: “Ah, artist pala rin kami (Ah, so we’re artists too).”
Rizia recalled that the exhibit opening left many of them in tears, seeing the craft and the people behind it side by side.

Rizia hopes taká will receive enough recognition and value, as other crafts in the Philippines have, so that the younger generation would want to take it up, and see it’s valuable enough to be paid enough.

Not everyone was sure of that at the start. According to Rizia, Ka Ichu hesitated when they began teaching workshops, wondering if anyone still wanted to learn taká. Ka Ichu herself said she was against the idea at first. Today, she shared, she is glad that their stock is finding its way to people and that schools have started to show interest.
How the craft is passed on and who will take it up next remain open questions.
But at the workshop, participants pressed paper onto the forms under Ka Ichu’s guidance, going through a process that generations of Paete artisans had learned through years of work and repetition.
For at least that afternoon, taká was passing into new hands. – Rappler.com
Arabella Grace Sta. Ana is a Rappler intern studying BA Philosophy at UP Los Baños.

articles.title: Powerful 7.7 magnitude earthquake rocks Panama
articles.summary: A magnitude 7.7 earthquake struck southern Panama on Friday, damaging buildings and sending thousands into the streets, but the country appeared to escape widespread destruction or deaths.

blocks.text: World·New
A magnitude 7.7 earthquake struck southern Panama on Friday, damaging buildings and sending thousands into the streets, but the country appeared to escape widespread destruction or deaths.
Country appears to have escaped widespread destruction or deaths
Powerful earthquake hits Panama, triggers tsunami warnings

The ‌U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) said the earthquake hit at a depth of 12.6 kilometres, with an epicentre in a sparsely populated area about 200 kilometres from the capital, and that some casualties were possible.

In the following hours, even as more than 40 aftershocks rattled the isthmus nation, the Panama Canal and Cobre Panama copper mine reported normal operations and the Tocumen International Airport lifted ​a suspension on flights.
Office workers in the upscale business hub of downtown Panama City ​fretted about how to get home in the snarl of traffic, after the quake sent thousands into the streets.
Juan Sanchez, a 37-year-old Economy Ministry employee, waited for a bus he said he doubted would arrive.
Canadian in Panama experiences aftershock live on air | Hanomansing Live
"They evacuated all of ​these buildings. Everyone is outside. Now the problem is, how do we get home?"
President Raul Mulino travelled to Penonome, ⁠a city about halfway between the epicentre ⁠and Panama City, where some buildings collapsed and a church was damaged.

items: Some TV meteorologists want to talk about climate change. Not everyone wants to hear it

blocks.text: Despite the ‌force of Friday's tremor, the country appeared to have been spared the destruction of other recent powerful quakes in the region, with no deaths or injuries immediately reported.
Back-to-back quakes in Venezuela in June killed several thousand people, while a quake in Colombia in August killed more than 300.
Cars are seen crushed under a collapsed building after an earthquake in Penonome, Panama, on Friday. (Martin Bernetti/AFP/Getty Images)

An exposure report by the USGS estimated about 43,000 Panamanians lived in areas with at least severe exposure ⁠to the quake. This compares with nearly 1.4 million in the area of the twin quakes in Venezuela and over 1.6 million in the quake-hit zone of western Colombia.
Nestor Luque, director of Panama's geosciences institute, attributed the quake to the Azuero Sona Fault System that he said contained a massive buildup of pressure ‌that is occasionally released.
"The seismic signals have travelled throughout the national territory and that is why it could be felt everywhere."
People gather on a street in Panama City after an earthquake on Friday. (Enea Lebrun/Reuters)
In Panama City, Luque said he counted 40 seconds of vibrations, though other areas may have felt even longer tremors.
Sabina Rios, who was on the sixth floor of an old U.S. military-era building in Panama City, said the shaking was unusually strong and prolonged.
"The quake felt strong ​and lasted a long time, the longest I've felt in years," Rios said.
People look at a damaged government building in Penonome on Friday. (Martin Bernetti/AFP/Getty Images)

Victor Pinzon, a 48-year-old maintenance worker, told Reuters he had watched high-rise window cleaners ride out the shaking. "It's a miracle they didn't ⁠get killed," he said. "They looked like they were swinging in a hammock."
Strong earthquakes are not common in Panama, and some elderly residents were in ⁠tears as they evacuated into the streets.

"We're scared. It's just the two of us old folks here. The house has cracked, and we're afraid ⁠it ⁠could fall on us," said Ricardo Brown, 74, in Herrera ​province in southern Panama, where he said he saw a number of damaged homes.
A statue is seen by the earthquake in Penonome on Friday. (Martin Bernetti/AFP/Getty Images)

Omar Smith, who heads Panama's civil protection agency, told news outlet Telemetro Reporta ​that impacts had also been reported in Chitre, ⁠the capital of Herrera, and along the coast in Los Santos province.
The USGS estimated economic losses could amount to 1 to 10 per cent of Panama's gross domestic product, and electricity provider Naturgy reported power outages in six provinces.
Panama was due to hold a national evacuation drill on Monday of next week to test the country's emergency response.

articles.title: Questions remain over Ebola patient who travelled across three nations undetected
articles.summary: Fresh details reveal how the 40-year-old businessman flew and crossed regional borders while seriously ill.

blocks.text: Image source, EPA
Nearly 70 potential contacts have been placed under quarantine in Nairobi
A Kenyan businessman was able to spend time in one of the regions worst-affected by Ebola, then travel to two more countries before his illness was identified.

The 40-year-old - who was only diagnosed with the deadly infectious disease after arriving seriously ill at a Nairobi hospital - became Kenya's first confirmed case. He died two days later on 5 October.

That his infection went undetected at multiple health facilities in the Democratic Republic of Congo and two airport health screenings in Uganda and Kenya has raised serious questions about these nations' biosecurity during a significant outbreak.
More than 4,000 people have died from Ebola in DR Congo this year, in what is the second most deadly known outbreak to date.

Africa CDC, the continent's leading public health agency, has now reconstructed the Kenyan patient's movements across nearly six weeks, revealing several missed opportunities to detect his infection and potentially preventing dozens of people from coming into contact with the deadly virus.
DR Congo

The account, presented by the agency's emergency director, Dr Wessam Mankoula, provides the clearest picture yet of how the businessman travelled thousands of kilometres while growing increasingly unwell.
The man, whose identity has not been made public, had lived in DR Congo for seven years and had travelled across three of its provinces on business.
Exactly when or where he contracted Ebola remains unclear - but it was present in all three provinces he went through by early October, according to the World Health Organization (WHO).
The man had spent much of late August and early September in the province of Bas-Uélé, visiting towns including Buta, Aketi and Likati.

blocks.caption: A map showing the man's journey from DR Congo through Uganda to Kenya

blocks.text: The WHO confirmed an Ebola case in Buta in August, prior to his visit, though there is no evidence he contracted the virus there.
His symptoms first emerged around 15 September. He was given antibiotics and sent home.
Two days later, he was admitted to the Tongo Etandi Health Centre in Bondo, where he remained until 19 September.
Despite suffering from fever and a rash, he was diagnosed with a skin infection.

Without an Ebola test being taken at any point during his travels, it is hard to say exactly when he contracted the virus. Those symptoms are consistent with the early stages of the disease, but also other infections common to the region, such as malaria.
On 20 September, he flew to Kisangani, a city with a population of about 1.5 million people on the Congo River, where he spent more than 10 days seeking medical care.
We do not know which hospitals or clinics treated him there, nor what medications they gave him. Kisangani is the capital of Tshopo province which has only recorded 51 Ebola cases.
Uganda
However, on 1 October, more than two weeks after first becoming ill, the businessman boarded another domestic flight to Beni, before continuing his journey to Kasindi, a busy border town.
Both Beni and Kasindi are in North Kivu, which has recorded 1,755 Ebola infections and more than 1,000 deaths, making it one of the Congolese provinces worst-hit by the disease.
But he did not stay there long, crossing into Uganda later that day.
Uganda imposed restrictions on movement across its border with DR Congo shortly after the outbreak began in May.

The country has experience containing several Ebola outbreaks, including through surveillance, contact tracing and the isolation of suspected cases. It has had some cases this year - mostly among people travelling from DR Congo - but was declared free of the disease in August.
But the border between the two nations stretches for hundreds of kilometres through remote terrain, making it difficult to police.
It remains unclear whether the businessman passed through an official health checkpoint when he crossed the border.

blocks.caption: Image caption, The man's funeral was held under strict safety protocols

blocks.text: The man's funeral was held under strict safety protocols
Once he had, he travelled by road to the capital, Kampala, and then Entebbe International Airport, where he boarded a flight to Nairobi on 3 October.

Ugandan officials said his temperature was normal when he passed through airport screening. Health experts say his case highlights the limitations of relying on temperature checks and self-declarations.
Mankoula said investigators were examining whether the man's medication could have suppressed his temperature. He may have also not had a fever when he passed through the checks.
Kenya

Similarly, he was not flagged as a suspected Ebola patient when he reached Nairobi's Jomo Kenyatta International Airport, where a relative collected him and drove him directly to Nairobi Hospital, a private medical facility in the Kenyan capital.
By then, he was suffering from fever, chills, muscle pain, a sore throat and bleeding.
Laboratory tests confirmed that he had contracted the Bundibugyo species of Ebola - the same one responsible for the outbreak in DR Congo.
He was placed in isolation while his condition deteriorated. He died on 5 October and was buried the following day under strict infection-control measures.

The Kenyan government says it has now identified 66 people who may have been in contact with him after he arrived there. The WHO says the number is likely to rise as contact-tracing in Uganda and DR Congo continues.
The quarantine arrangements have also raised concerns among some healthcare workers, amid questions about how the patient was handled at Nairobi Hospital.
Kenya's health ministry says more than 652,000 travellers have been screened and nearly 5,000 healthcare workers trained to deal with Ebola, with five facilities designated to handle cases.
Ebola spreads through direct contact with the bodily fluids of an infected person who has developed symptoms, or through contaminated materials.
Its incubation period ranges from two to 21 days, meaning someone exposed to the virus may not become ill until several weeks later.
CDC advice
Mankoula urged travellers experiencing symptoms of Ebola to report them, saying early medical attention could improve their chances of survival.
"When you reveal any Ebola-related symptoms early, you're not only preventing the virus spreading to other countries but you're also protecting yourself first," he said.
The WHO has warned that stigma surrounding Ebola could discourage people from reporting symptoms or seeking medical care, potentially allowing the virus to spread undetected.

The agency says it is stepping up efforts to encourage this by reducing fear and misinformation about the disease - something that is a big problem in DR Congo, where some health workers have been attacked by people who claim Ebola doesn't exist.
