articles.title: Russian search engine Yandex struggles after Ukrainian strikes on data centres
articles.summary: Often dubbed "Russia's Google", the tech firm admits customers may experience disruption to digital services due to the attacks.

blocks.text: Russian tech giant Yandex has said it was struggling to maintain services after two of its five data centres were struck by Ukrainian drones in the past two days.
Often dubbed "Russia's Google", the company runs the country's most popular search engine, as well as a food-ordering and taxi app used by tens of millions of people.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said the attacks were in response to weeks of Russian strikes on Ukrainian data centres.

Both sides have stepped up attacks on infrastructure in recent months as the war between the two drags on. Kyiv says its strikes are aimed at revenue streams for Moscow's war machine, and that the latest attacks could force Russia to divert resources to Yandex.
Yandex said that its data centre in Sasovo, in the Ryazan region, had been "seriously damaged as a result of a drone attack" overnight into Thursday, with its operations "completely suspended".
Another data centre in Kaluga, a region south-west of Moscow, had also been attacked on Friday morning, it said, with part of that site's infrastructure "taken out of service".
Yandex said on Friday that its data centres were "critical" for the normal operation of its services and that it was "very difficult to predict" when they would be back online.
It said teams were working "day and night" to keep services running, but "unfortunately it is not a simple task".
The tech giant said none of its employees had been injured in the strikes. The regional governor in Kaluga said nine people had been injured in a drone attack on the city's infrastructure.

The exact scope of the disruption to the company's services is unclear - though it told state news agency Tass that some of its AI chatbot functions were temporarily unavailable, while its smart home devices may also experience problems.
Yandex previously said its Kaluga data centre was one of Russia's largest - covering an area of 130,000 sqm (1,399,000 sq ft) and consuming as much electricity annually as 220,000 UK households.
Its data centre in Sasovo, meanwhile, houses two of three supercomputers used to develop the company's AI model. It is unclear whether the supercomputers survived the attack.
Ukraine's defence ministry confirmed the data centre attacks, saying they could "force Russia to divert resources to repair the damaged capacity".
Zelensky said Kyiv was responding to similar Russian attacks on Ukrainian data centres in a "mirror-like fashion".

Last month, a Russian drone hit a business centre in Kyiv, killing four people and damaging a data centre. Due to the strikes, about 100,000 households in Kyiv and the region suffered internet outages.
Some Ukrainian firms have already begun moving data from damaged servers to facilities abroad.
Moscow has justified the attacks by saying the data centres were used by Ukrainian military intelligence.

But Ukraine accuses it of deliberately targeting civilian infrastructure. Russia has stepped up strikes on energy infrastructure ahead of the winter, as it has done in previous years of the full-scale invasion, which began in 2022.

articles.title: Residential school denialism shouldn't be illegal, Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew says
articles.summary: Residential school denialism is detestable but not illegal, and that shouldn't change, says Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew, who disagrees with federal Manitoba NDPer Leah Gazan's efforts to add it to the…

image.caption: Premier Wab Kinew speaks during an event at the Brandon Residential School site on Sept. 30. (John Woods/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Manitoba

Residential school denialism is detestable but not illegal, and that shouldn't change, says Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew, who disagrees with federal Manitoba NDPer Leah Gazan's efforts to add it to the Criminal Code.
Education, not criminalization, needed to combat those who don't believe, premier says

"I have a lot of respect for MP Gazan, but I don't think we can criminalize this. I think we have to just do the continued work of educating people and trying to combat misinformation," Kinew told CBC Manitoba Up to Speed host Marcy Markusa on Friday.

Gazan first introduced Bill C-254, her private member’s bill to amend the Criminal Code regarding the promotion of hatred against Indigenous people, in October 2024, but it died when the spring 2025 election was called.
"If the government is serious about reconciliation, then they need to protect survivors and their families from hate," Gazan said when she first introduced it.
"The residential school system was a genocide designed to wipe out Indigenous cultures, languages, families and heritage. To downplay, deny or justify it is cruel, harmful and hateful."

She reintroduced it in October 2025. The bill seeks to make it illegal for anyone to condone, deny, justify or minimize the Indian residential school system in Canada through any statements beyond a private conversation.

items: Bill before Parliament would outlaw residential school 'denialism'
SCO condemns Winnipeg Sun and its CEO for column questioning residential school 'murder and concealment'

blocks.text: All bills must go through three readings, which also involves committee reviews and final debates, before being granted royal assent and enacted into law.
The introduction was the first reading. The bill has yet to reach a second reading.

For a period of more than 150 years, from the 1830s until 1997, First Nations, Inuit and Métis children were taken from their families and communities to residential schools, often far from their homes. Most were government-funded and run by Christian religious organizations.

The schools were designed to assimilate Indigenous children into Euro-Canadian culture. An estimated 150,000 children across Canada attended the schools and the National Centre for Truth and Reconciliation has documented more than 4,000 who died while attending them.

On Sept. 30, the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation, Kinew announced the province partnered with the City of Brandon to buy a popular campground property that was once part of the Brandon Residential School, which ran from 1895 until 1972.
The site that became the campground included a former school cemetery, used from 1895 to 1912, the province said in a news release on the day the purchase was announced.

This sign is at the site of the Brandon Residential School cemetery. Historical records indicate the cemetery, where children from the school were buried, was used from 1895 to 1912. The area later became a park and then a privately owned campground. (Jaison Empson/CBC)
The property still contains the remains of children, the province said.
Kinew, who dedicated a memorial at the site on Sept. 30, said on Friday that such events help educate the public on residential schools.
"It's very well-documented. It's very historic. So let's make sure that we keep that history alive in our living memory as a province," he said.

Sioux Valley Dakota Nation, which owns the land where the school once stood, will guide decisions around the former cemetery and is working with university researchers to identify the more than 50 children it believes are buried at the site.

Rev. Stan McKay, who said his maternal grandparents were forced to attend the Brandon Residential School for a good part of their life and never talked about it, called the purchase of the cemetery land a “very important piece” of reconciliation.
"It was not a good place," McKay said the day of the province's announcement.

Kinew participates in a ceremony on the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation after the Manitoba government announced it partnered with the City of Brandon to purchase the private campground land. (Jaison Empson/CBC)
His eldest sisters also attended the Brandon school for two years, while he is a survivor of the Fisher River and Birtle residential schools.

The United Church of Canada was one of three church organizations that operated the Brandon school during its long history. Later, McKay later made history as the first Indigenous person to lead that church.

He said he nearly left the church after an "awakening" that he had been colonized by it. Elders, who also "had some difficulties with the church," encouraged him to stay and work within the system and be a part of helping it change, McKay said.
McKay would like to see more education in Manitoba schools around the residential school experience and have it localized to stories about the 18 schools that operated in the province.
Kinew, on Friday, agreed that would be a good idea and said much more is being done in schools now than in previous decades.
"How much did we learn about residential school in K-12 versus what a kid today learns? It's night and day in terms of being so much more," he said.

items: Manitoba's purchase of site of unmarked residential school graves a historic moment: Sioux Valley chief
Large crowd marches to former Brandon residential school site to honour survivors

blocks.text: There is a need for those no longer in school to be educated as well, Kinew said.

"As we were preparing for Brandon … I was talking to some of my staff that I work with very closely — very smart people — and I pulled out the volume of the Truth and Reconciliation Commission that documents the child deaths. People were shocked. They didn't know [the number of deaths]," he said.

"So for sure there's more needs to be done in the K-12 system, but I think there's also a lot in the workplace, in churches, in sports, all the venues where we gather as Manitobans, where we need to keep this thing alive.
"The thing that we don't want to happen is for this to fade from our living memory, and then we forget, and then maybe some of the the negative lessons we should have learned start to re-emerge."

items: Kids are learning more about residential schools than their parents, but experts say it can't be a 'one-off'

blocks.text: ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Darren Bernhardt has been with CBC Manitoba since 2009 and specializes in offbeat and local history stories. He is the author of two bestselling books: The Lesser Known: A History of Oddities from the Heart of the Continent, and Prairie Oddities: Punkinhead, Peculiar Gravity and More Lesser Known Histories.

articles.title: China, EU reach deal to 'moderate' China's car exports to EU
articles.summary: An agreement between the EU and China would reduce exports of Chinese electric and plug-in hybrid cars to the 27-member European bloc by up to 50%, according to the EU trade envoy.

image.caption: China's increased exports of electric vehicles to the EU have become a problem for European carmakersImage: Avalon/IMAGO

blocks.text: European Trade Commissioner Maros Sefcovic announced on Friday that China and the European Union had reached a deal that could cut Chinese exports of hybrid cars to the EU by more than half.
This announcement followed two-day talks in Beijing aimed at reducing the EU's growing trade deficit with China.
Earlier, Sefcovic said this week's talks were the culmination of three months of intensive work.
What do we know about the EV deal?
According to Sefcovic, the deal would "moderate China's export of hybrids and plug-in hybrids to the EU."
He added that this opens the prospect of cutting China's exports by more than half, based on projections over a four-year period.
"By this step, we're actually preventing several millions of cars exports from China to the European Union," Sefcovic said.
Although he did not offer details on how the agreement will be implemented, Sefcovic said he believed the two sides had achieved a very good result.

blocks.caption: Sefcovic said he believes the EU and China have achieved a very good result in trade talksImage: Johannes Neudecker/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: What else was decided?
Sevcovic added the two sides also reached an agreement to reduce Chinese import duties on €4 billion ($4.5 billion) worth of EU exports, including car parts, olive oil and footwear.
They also agreed to simplify China's process for granting export licenses for rare earths and permanent magnets.
The agreement will require approval from the leaders of all 27 EU nations, who will discuss the outcome at the start of their summit in Brussels on Thursday.
How China is upping pressure on German businesses
Rebalancing EU-China trade

According to UN Comtrade data, Chinese exports to the EU totaled $560 billion (€500 billion) last year, up from $517 billion in 2023. Exports to major economies, including Germany, Italy, Spain, and Poland, each rose approximately 10% from a year earlier. Shipments to Hungary increased by 43%.
Meanwhile, China imported $268.3 billion (€240 billion) worth of European goods last year, down from $269.4 billion the previous year. Purchases from Denmark, Ireland, and France led the way.

Last month, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen warned lawmakers at the European Parliament that the trade gap had reached a tipping point. She said the EU would use all available tools to rebalance the relationship.

articles.title: EXPLAINER: What is the role of Cardinal Tagle as Dean of the College of Cardinals?
articles.summary: Tagle"s election marks a historic milestone for the Catholic Church in Asia and the Philippines. But what does the Dean of the College of Cardinals do, and why is the position important?

blocks.text: Published October 10, 2026 12:53am
VATICAN CITY —Filipino Cardinal Luis Antonio Gokim Tagle has been elected Dean of the College of Cardinals, becoming the first Asian cardinal to hold the position.
Pope Leo XIV approved the election on October 8, 2026, following the acceptance of the resignation of Italian Cardinal Giovanni Battista Re. The Vatican announced the development on October 9, 2026.
Tagle’s election marks a historic milestone for the Catholic Church in Asia and the Philippines. But what does the Dean of the College of Cardinals do, and why is the position important?
What is the College of Cardinals?

The College of Cardinals is composed of senior Church leaders who advise the Pope and, when the papacy becomes vacant, elect his successor in a conclave. Only cardinals who meet the requirements under Church law may vote in the papal election.
What is the role of the Dean?
The Dean serves as the head of the College of Cardinals in a coordinating and representative capacity. The position is often described as primus inter pares, meaning “first among equals.”
Although the Dean does not govern the Church in place of the Pope, the role becomes particularly important when a Pope dies or resigns, and the Church prepares for a new pontificate.
What happens when a Pope dies?
Under the Vatican’s apostolic constitution Universi Dominici Gregis, the Dean has several key responsibilities during a papal vacancy, known as sede vacante.

The Dean must notify and summon the cardinals to meetings called General Congregations, where they discuss the Church’s needs and prepare for the conclave. The Dean also plays a central role in coordinating the process leading to the election of the next Pope.
If eligible to participate as a cardinal elector, the Dean presides over the conclave. If the elected Pope is not already a bishop, the Dean is responsible for ordaining him a bishop.
Meanwhile, the Cardinal Camerlengo has separate responsibilities concerning the administration and safeguarding of the Holy See’s temporal goods and rights during the vacancy.
Why is Cardinal Tagle's election historic?

Cardinal Tagle is the first Asian cardinal to serve as Dean of the College of Cardinals. His election is a significant development for the Catholic Church in Asia and the Philippines, a predominantly Catholic country with a large Filipino community overseas.
His new position places a Filipino Church leader in a key coordinating role within one of the Catholic Church’s most important institutions.
However, becoming Dean does not automatically make Cardinal Tagle the next Pope. The Pope is elected by eligible cardinal electors in a conclave, and the Dean does not choose the successor alone.
What happens next?

Cardinal Tagle will assume the title of the Suburbicarian Church of Ostia while retaining his existing title of Albano. He will also continue his work as Pro-Prefect of the Section for First Evangelization and New Particular Churches within the Vatican’s Dicastery for Evangelization.

His election is both a historic milestone for Filipino Catholics and an important responsibility in coordinating the College of Cardinals, particularly during a future transition of papal leadership.—LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Man named Hitler Mussolini elected mayor in Peru
articles.summary: The left-wing candidate won a narrow victory in a remote district in the Peruvian Andes, exit polls show.

blocks.text: A man named Hitler Mussolini Simeon Flores has secured a narrow victory in Peru's local elections, exit polls show.
The candidate for the centre-left Ahora Nación party was elected mayor of Queropalca, a remote district in the Peruvian Andes.
Some 229 residents voted for the 45-year-old, putting him ahead of the second-place candidate from right-wing Renovación Popular Perú by just 25 votes.
Despite being elected to represent fewer than 1,000 people, his forenames being those of two notorious fascist dictators has drawn outsized international attention to the small corner of the country.
Data from Peru's elections office showed a little over 700 people had participated in the election, with Simeon securing around 34% of the vote.
He was born in the district in the central department of Huánuco, some 360km (224 miles) from the capital, Lima, according to his candidate profile.

That he shares his name with Adolf Hitler and Benito Mussolini - "two of the most well-known figures of 20th-Century European totalitarian regimes" - has made his candidacy a "striking event", local outlet Peru21 reported.
Despite the curiosity generated by his name, local media noted that Hitler Guesclin Alba Sánchez had been elected mayor of Yúngar in 2018.
He reportedly beat rival candidate Lenin Vladimir Rodríguez Valverde after campaigning on the slogan "I'm the good Hitler".

A politician named Adolf Hitler Uunona attracted similar attention in 2020 after winning local elections in Namibia - a former German colony where Adolf and other Germanic first names are not uncommon.

articles.title: Tornado rips through Sicilian town and city
articles.summary: Dramatic footage shows huge tornado moving through Marsala and Petrosino, causing damage to buildings and cars.

blocks.text: Dramatic footage shows the moment a tornado ripped through the city of Marsala and nearby town Petrosino, in Sicily.
The tornado injured two people and caused damage to buildings with the strong winds flipping cars according to local media.
Thunderstorms moved across the island on Friday, and while conditions have eased across Sicily, more are forecast across parts of the central Mediterranean.

articles.title: Ombudsman inspects vacated office of Jinggoy Estrada
articles.summary: Representatives from the Office of the Ombudsman inspected the office vacated by Senator Jinggoy Estrada, according to a GMA News report, quoting Senate Secretary Renato Bantug.

blocks.text: Published October 10, 2026 12:18am
Representatives from the Office of the Ombudsman inspected the office vacated by Senator Jinggoy Estrada, according to a GMA News report, quoting Senate Secretary Renato Bantug.
“I was informed of the Ombudsman inspection yesterday and of the GSIS ocular the other day," Bantug said.
He added that he did not receive a request from the Commission on Audit for an inspection, but the Commission asked the Senate to clarify the chamber's policies on such matters.
On Monday, the office was seen bare and stripped of furniture, sockets, and tiles.
Senator Vicente Sotto III was supposed to take over the room after replacing Estrada as Senate President Pro Tempore.
The room was missing most of its floor tiles, and there was no furniture such as tables and chairs.
Also noticeable were exposed and hanging electrical wires and the removal of wall sockets throughout the office.
The office’s comfort room was also stripped of tiles from the ceiling, walls, and floor, while the shower and toilet bowl had been removed as well.
In response, Estrada's staff said dismantling fixtures and other materials from a Senate office previously occupied by a senator is an established and accepted practice.
"It must also be emphasized that similar instances of dismantling fixtures and materials from a vacated senator's office have occurred in the recent past," Estrada's office said.

"This is neither new nor unusual — it is an established and accepted practice within the institution, and singling out this particular transition for scrutiny is both unfair and misleading," it added.
In June, Estrada was detained at the Quezon City jail after the Sandiganbayan Fifth Division ordered his arrest on non-bailable charges of plunder.
Since then, he has been unable to attend Senate hearings due to his ongoing detention. —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: US imposes sanctions on International Criminal Court
articles.summary: The US says the measures are aimed at restricting the tribunal's resources and ability to operate.

blocks.text: The Trump administration has imposed sweeping sanctions on the International Criminal Court (ICC), saying it wants to restrict the tribunal's resources and ability to operate.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the measures - which include a ban on US entities making transactions with the ICC - were intended to "defend US sovereignty" and accused the court of seeking to prosecute Americans.
The ICC said the measures were an assault on the rule of law and the foundations of the international legal order.
The announcement comes just hours after former ICC judge Navi Pillay was awarded the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize for her efforts to promote peace and international law.

US President Donald Trump has reacted sourly to the Norwegian prize's choice of winner this year and last, after having expressed a desire to receive it himself. He criticised Pillay for being part of a panel that accused Israel, as well as Hamas, of war crimes during the 7 October conflict.
The US says the ICC has no jurisdiction over it as it never ratified the statute founding it - but the international court has investigated US actions elsewhere.
Rubio said Trump would not allow the ICC to prosecute Americans, adding: "Either the ICC will end its threats, or we will end the ICC."
The US sanctions will stop US companies from providing goods or services to the ICC, such as banking or software.

Rubio said Washington had delayed imposing the sanctions in the hope that the ICC and its member countries would address US concerns. He said the measures had been structured to allow other countries to negotiate a possible solution.
He also called on US allies that were ICC signatories to "rein in" the institution.

articles.title: Trump administration hits International Criminal Court with sweeping sanctions
articles.summary: The Trump administration imposed sweeping new sanctions Friday on the International Criminal Court, which it says is politicized and attempting to illegally prosecute Americans and Israelis. The…

image.caption: The International Criminal Court (ICC) is seen on Dec. 9, 2025, in The Hague, Netherlands. (Peter Dejong/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·New

The Trump administration imposed sweeping new sanctions Friday on the International Criminal Court, which it says is politicized and attempting to illegally prosecute Americans and Israelis. The court denounced the U.S. move as "an assault on the rule of law" aiming to prevent its work.
ICC denounces the move as an 'assault on the rule of law'

The Trump administration has imposed sweeping new sanctions on the International Criminal Court (ICC) as part of its campaign to dismantle the tribunal that the United States believes has become politicized and attempted to unfairly and illegally prosecute Americans and Israelis on war crimes charges.

U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced the sanctions on Friday, after the Nobel Peace Prize was awarded to South African prosecutor Navi Pillay, a former judge at the ICC and other international courts.
U.S. President Donald Trump has coveted that prize for himself. The move, however, long predated the Nobel Prize announcement.

"We will ban transactions with this rogue court, cutting off their resources and crippling its ability to operate against us," Rubio said in a video address posted to social media. "The United States and the American people are not subject to the jurisdiction of this fake ICC."
Why the ICC is in the fight of its life with Trump

The sanctions block any assets that the ICC as an institution might have in U.S. jurisdictions and set a six-month timeline for U.S. companies and individuals that have business with the court to wind that business down.

Rubio said both Republicans and Democrats have deep reservations about the court, which was established to prosecute war crimes and crimes against humanity that might not otherwise be handled by the parties involved.

items: Netanyahu is flying freely over Canada as his international arrest warrant remains in place
The Trump administration sanctioned ICC judges. A Canadian judge is fighting back

blocks.text: But he said that only Trump was willing to move against the court.

"Both parties agree on this, but only President Trump has the resolve to take the action needed to end this threat once and for all," Rubio said. "Either the ICC will end its threats, or we will end the ICC."
ICC denounces 'assault on rule of law'

The ICC denounced the step as an attack on the rule of law and the foundations of international order, themes that Rubio had appeared to embrace only two days ago in a speech in front of the Acropolis in Athens.

"It is an attempt to obstruct the course of justice and to prevent the court from doing what it was created to do," the court said in a statement. "It is an assault on the rule of law and on the very foundations of the international legal order which strikes at the simple principle that no one stands above the law."
U.S. sanctions Canadian judge on International Criminal Court

ICC President Tomoko Akane, a citizen of U.S. ally Japan, said the court would "continue to fully discharge its mandate, with independence and impartiality, acting only on the basis of the law and the evidence, for the sake of the countless victims of grave crimes."
She also appealed to other ICC members for support. "This is not just about defending a single institution, but about safeguarding the international order grounded upon the rule of law."
Rubio had said that the U.S. expects its allies to join in the actions against the ICC. Those include many NATO members in Europe and Japan.
"If they do not, the United States will continue its campaign to dismantle the ICC, piece by piece, until Americans are threatened no longer," he said.
Dutch Foreign Minister Tom Berendsen, posting on X, called the sanctions announcement "a deeply regrettable step. We stand firm in defence of the court."
He said the six-month window before the sanctions take effect "creates scope for dialogue."
As host state of the court, the Netherlands is a strong defender of the ICC.

articles.title: Palace: President Marcos to attend F1 race in Singapore
articles.summary: President Marcos is attending the Formula 1 Grand Prix here this weekend, a move that Malacañang said would allow him to have face-to-face interactions with potential investors, but is…

blocks.text: October 10, 2026 | 12:00am
President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.
Bongbong Marcos / Facebook Page

SINGAPORE — President Marcos is attending the Formula 1 Grand Prix here this weekend, a move that Malacañang said would allow him to have face-to-face interactions with potential investors, but is assailed by critics who view it as insensitive to Filipinos facing economic hardships.
“He will attend,” Palace press officer Claire Castro said at a media briefing yesterday here.

“According to the President, it would be better for transactions if there are face-to-face meetings... The attendees see each other’s body language. Most of those who will attend are business executives, world leaders,” Castro added.
She said Marcos had seen leaders like the late Lee Kwan Yew and key investors during the Formula 1 race.

Marcos is in Singapore for a five-day working visit, his 47th foreign trip since becoming president in 2022. It is also his sixth visit here, two of which saw him watching the luxurious sporting event in 2022 and in 2023.
Castro said Marcos would not pay for his ticket to the race because he was invited by Singaporean Prime Minister Lawrence Wong.
“You can meet anybody, anyone you want, even some of the businessmen from the Philippines, I had meetings with them because they were there for the F1. So… happy coincidence” Marcos said.

While officials claimed that the race – which began yesterday and ends tomorrow – would allow the President to boost ties with fellow leaders and seize investment opportunities, critics described attendance to the event as a “shameless” act that would do nothing to alleviate the plight of the poor. ?

articles.title: Prosecution drops bribery case vs VP Sara
articles.summary: The prosecution panel for the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte will no longer present its bribery case in order to further expedite the proceedings.

blocks.text: October 10, 2026 | 12:00am
Vice President Sara Duterte arrives before the start of the impeachment trial at the Senate of the Philippines in Pasay, Metro Manila on July 7, 2026.
Noel Celis, pool / AFP
MANILA, Philippines — The prosecution panel for the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte will no longer present its bribery case in order to further expedite the proceedings.

House prosecutor and Bukidnon Rep. Jonathan Keith Flores said they have already filed the manifestation to drop the bribery charge, which is under Article III of the Articles of Impeachment, before the Senate impeachment court on Oct. 6.
He explained the decision to drop the charge “had nothing to do with the strength of the case,” but on the prosecution’s general timetable for its presentation of evidence.
“It no longer fits into the timetable we set for ourselves,” Flores, who leads the team on the bribery case, said.
With this, the prosecution will end its presentation of evidence with its case on Duterte’s alleged unexplained wealth.

It initially requested eight trial dates to present its bribery case and listed four potential witnesses, including those who allegedly received or were offered bribe money from Duterte’s office in the Department of Education.
These include former DepEd undersecretary Gloria Jumamil-Mercado and former bids and awards committee chair Resty Osias.

The bribery charge stemmed from the admission of then-DepEd special disbursing officer Edward Fajarda, who claimed that when Duterte was department secretary, she ordered him to give cash to school superintendents through their bank accounts.

Mercado likewise admitted that she received envelopes containing money – supposedly from Duterte – in September 2024. She said she saw it as a means to influence her since she used to be DepEd’s head of procuring entity.

The prosecution has so far finished presenting Article I which covers Duterte’s alleged misuse of P612.5 million in confidential funds from DepEd and the Office of the Vice President; and Article IV which tackles the alleged grave threats against ranking government officials.
It is currently wrapping up its presentation of evidence for Article II on the supposed unexplained wealth and non-disclosure in Duterte’s statement of assets, liabilities and net worth.
Trial resumes Monday
Meanwhile, Duterte’s Senate impeachment trial will resume on Monday for the cross-examination of the prosecution’s final witness.

Presiding officer Francis Escudero adjourned yesterday’s proceedings with no rulings other than setting the Monday schedule and reminding financial forensic analyst Alexander Cabrera to return for cross-examination.
House prosecutor Chel Diokno confirmed that Cabrera is the final witness for the prosecution’s “case-in-chief.” — Neil Jayson Servallos

articles.title: Online scams cost Filipinos P121.8 billion in one year
articles.summary: Filipinos lost an estimated P121.8 billion to scams over the past year, with digital wallets emerging as the primary channel used to transfer money to fraudsters, according to a new report.

blocks.text: October 10, 2026 | 12:00am
Stock image of an attempted scam.
Pixabay / File

MANILA, Philippines — Filipinos lost an estimated P121.8 billion to scams over the past year, with digital wallets emerging as the primary channel used to transfer money to fraudsters, according to a new report.

The State of Scams Philippines 2026 report, conducted by Global Anti-Scam Alliance (GASA), in collaboration with Mastercard and Gogolook, estimated that about 11.7 million Filipino adults suffered financial losses from scams, averaging P10,427 per victim.
The P121.8-billion figure was based on a survey of 1,160 Filipino adults conducted from March 16 to April 13, 2026, with the findings extrapolated to the country’s adult population.
It is a survey-based estimate rather than an official tally of money reported stolen to authorities.
The report found that 84 percent of Filipino adults encountered at least one scam attempt in the past 12 months, up from 77 percent in 2025.
Respondents were estimated to have encountered an average of 151 scam attempts annually.
Overall, 44 percent of respondents interacted with a scam, while 15 percent reported losing money directly or through the theft of personal information that resulted in financial losses.
Among those who interacted with scams, 34 percent ended up losing money.
Shopping scams were the most commonly encountered schemes that prompted interaction, accounting for 24 percent of cases, followed by investment and employment scams at 22 percent each.

Digital wallets were the dominant payment channel used by scammers, with 73 percent of respondents who suffered financial losses saying the fraudsters received payments through e-wallets. This was substantially higher than the Asian average of 34 percent.

articles.title: Defense to dispute wealth claims vs VP Sara
articles.summary: Vice President Sara Duterte’s camp on Friday night vowed to present its own expert to contradict the claim of the House prosecution witness that Duterte and her husband Manases Carpio failed to…

blocks.text: October 10, 2026 | 12:00am

MANILA, Philippines — Vice President Sara Duterte’s camp on Friday night vowed to present its own expert to contradict the claim of the House prosecution witness that Duterte and her husband Manases Carpio failed to declare at least P817.8 million in her statement of assets, liabilities and net worth.
At a press conference, defense spokesman Michael Poa reacted after expert witness lawyer Alex Cabrera presented his report on the total undeclared assets of Duterte.
“Our work is, we will confront him with all these figures he released through cross-examination on Monday,” Poa said. “We will also have our own expert.”
“We will not rest because the team will definitely have to work on cross-examination on Monday,” he added.
90 witnesses
Poa added the defense has listed over 90 witnesses, as the House prosecution team decided to drop the bribery charges in the ongoing impeachment trial against her.

“That means these are the identified and reserved witnesses. So as to the number of witnesses that we will be presenting, again, I can’t give a number right now because that will be something that we will have to discuss within the team depending on what we feel will be best for the defense,” Poa said.
He said that the defense has been preparing for their turn to present evidence.
‘Not proof of fraudulent activity’

The issuance of a letter of authority (LOA) against Vice President Duterte and Carpio under the Bureau of Internal Revenue (BIR)’s Run Against Tax Evaders (RATE) does not mean they are already engaged in fraudulent activities, the defense said yesterday.
“We did not say there is fraud. What I said was prima facie fraud,” BIR lawyer Anne Loraine Garcia-Marquez said in reply to defense counsel Kristine Ferrer.
Ferrer added that in case there is a finding of possible tax evasion, a criminal case for alleged tax evasion will still have to be tried before the court.
“So, you confirmed that the person that is being issued a LOA under the RATE is only presumed to have engaged in fraud, correct?” Ferrer said.
“Prima facie fraud, yes,” Marquez added.
Marquez likewise testified that the Vice President and her husband earned only a total of P85.3 million as lawyers in a span of 18 years, from 2007 to 2025.

Private prosecutor Erwin Matib tried to reconcile the P85.3-million earnings of the couple with the P98.6-million total conjugal assets Duterte declared in her 2025 statement of assets, liabilities and net worth, but found no match.

The testimony forms part of the House prosecution’s presentation under Article II of the impeachment complaint, which concerns Duterte’s alleged unexplained wealth and discrepancies in her asset declarations.
The defense defended the inclusion of the legal profession in Vice President Duterte’s income tax return in 2023.

During direct examination of Matib, it was also pointed out that Duterte, having been elected as vice president in mid-2022, should not have practiced her legal profession as this directly violates the 1987 Constitution.
BIR records show Duterte still received lawyer’s fees in 2023, when she was already the vice president.
Duterte’s camp also vowed to present evidence that the income from the legal profession was included in the filing of income tax return in 2024.
Arraignment
The arraignment of Vice President Duterte’s grave threats case at the Quezon City Regional Trial Court Branch 98 has been deferred anew, her lawyer Paul Lawrence Lim said yesterday.
“The judge decided to study all of these first and reset, cancel the hearing today and reset it to some other date,” Lim told reporters outside the court.
“Now that other date, I will not disclose it for now, I am sorry. I would rather have the court announce it,” he added.

Lim said the presiding judge made the decision to study Duterte’s pending motion for partial reconsideration ad cautelam before the court as well as a petition for certiorari before the Supreme Court. — Josiah Antonio, Janvic Mateo

articles.title: Palace denies hand in Mark Villar’s move to majority
articles.summary: Malacañang yesterday distanced itself from Sen. Mark Villar’s decision to join the majority bloc even as it dismissed notions that the alliance shift is a step closer to the conviction…

blocks.text: October 10, 2026 | 12:00am

SINGAPORE — Malacañang yesterday distanced itself from Sen. Mark Villar’s decision to join the majority bloc even as it dismissed notions that the alliance shift is a step closer to the conviction of Vice President Sara Duterte.
The number of senators in the majority bloc increased to 14 after Villar decided to leave the minority led by Sen. Alan Peter Cayetano, which is now down to 10 members.

There are views that the transfer of alliance will boost the chances of Duterte being convicted in her impeachment trial, but Senate Majority Leader Juan Miguel Zubiri claimed that no politics was involved in the development.
However, Cayetano linked Villar’s move to Malacañang, saying it is important for the administration to “maintain a closely allied working majority in the Senate.”
Speaking to reporters here, Palace press officer Claire Castro said the administration cannot impose its will on senators.

Castro added that Cayetano has been blaming the administration for several developments, including his removal from the Senate presidency, the ruckus in the chamber and the escape of minority bloc member Sen. Ronald dela Rosa, who continues to evade arrest for alleged crimes against humanity.
“This was not dictated by the administration. Senators have their own minds and decisions. They cannot be dictated upon,” Castro said.

“If they can be dictated upon and they do not have their own minds, the people should not vote for them. We should tell that to Sen. Alan Cayetano because if he thinks like that, did he experience it under former president (Rodrigo) Duterte?” she added.
Asked about the possible implication of Villar’s switch on the impeachment trial of Vice President Duterte, Castro said there is no assurance that the majority bloc would vote uniformly.

“We cannot say that. As I said, each senator will decide based on their evaluation, their beliefs, their alliances. Even if many join the majority of the Senate, it does not mean that they would not side with VP Sara Duterte. So it still depends on their decision,” she said.

“Our prayer is, and perhaps this is also the prayer of our countrymen, that they decide based on evidence, not on their alliances. It should be based on evidence because the winner there is not the Senate, not the impeached official, but the people,” she added.
The Marcos administration, nevertheless, is convinced that a bigger majority could help advance the legislative agenda of Marcos.
“If more people believe in the programs of the President, it would be better for the country and our people,” Castro said.

articles.title: Mixed price adjustment for gas, diesel next week
articles.summary: Domestic gasoline prices are expected to rise further next week following China’s brief halt of refined fuel exports, while diesel prices are set for another rollback.

blocks.text: October 10, 2026 | 12:00am
Gasoline prices could rise by P2 to P2.20 per liter on Oct. 13, based on the four days of trading in the regional benchmark Mean of Platts Singapore.
STAR / File
MANILA, Philippines — Domestic gasoline prices are expected to rise further next week following China’s brief halt of refined fuel exports, while diesel prices are set for another rollback.
Diesel prices, meanwhile, could go down by P1.80 to P2 per liter.

Rino Abad, director of the Department of Energy (DOE)’s Oil Industry Management Bureau, said the expected diesel price rollback follows the G7 countries’ decision to release 100 million barrels of crude oil and diesel from their emergency reserves.
For gasoline, Jetti Petroleum president Leo Bellas said markets remain under pressure due to continued supply strain amid China’s fuel export suspension.
Reuters, citing unnamed sources, reported that China could resume refined fuel exports this month following a brief suspension.
Transition plan
In order to cut the Philippines’ oil dependence by half, major infrastructure shifts need to happen, Bellas said.
Under the Fuel Transition Plan, the country targets reducing its oil dependency by 30 percent by 2030, 50 percent by 2040 and more than that by 2050.
Energy Secretary Sharon Garin this week said the country will aggressively adopt electric vehicles to achieve these goals.
This means EVs should take up 80 percent of automobile production between 2040 and 2050, according to the plan.
However, in his 5th State of the Nation Address, President Marcos sees electric-powered vehicles making up just half of the cars on the road by then.
The plan also puts great emphasis on the use of high-blend biofuels, sustainable aviation fuels and alternative maritime fuels, among others.
Bellas said the Philippines can achieve these, but the focus shouldn’t be only on automotive fuels.

“If the government would push through with renewable energies and those sources of electricity that would not be using fossil-based fuels, I think that could be realistic,” Bellas told “Money Talks” on One News yesterday.
Marcos aims to raise the share of renewables in the country’s energy mix to 50 percent by 2040.

Patrick Aquino, director of the DOE-Energy Utilization Management Bureau, said EV registrations surged 130 percent year-on-year from January to August, as the Middle East war drove people toward electric-powered vehicles. — EJ Macababbad

articles.title: DBM pushes quality education for better doctors, nurses
articles.summary: Free tuition may open the doors of universities to more Filipino students, but what happens inside those classrooms, laboratories and training facilities will ultimately determine how well they can…

blocks.text: October 10, 2026 | 12:00am
Acting Budget Secretary Kim Robert de Leon (right) inspects medical and nursing education facilities at the University of the Philippines-Manila yesterday.
UP MANILA

MANILA, Philippines — Free tuition may open the doors of universities to more Filipino students, but what happens inside those classrooms, laboratories and training facilities will ultimately determine how well they can serve the country.

This was the central message of acting Secretary Kim Robert de Leon of the Department of Budget and Management (DBM) during his visit to the University of the Philippines-Manila yesterday, as he inspected modern medical and nursing education facilities that demonstrate how public investment can translate into better learning, stronger clinical training and ultimately, better health care for Filipinos.
“Free tuition opens the door. Quality education determines how far our students can go once they enter,” De Leon said.
For the DBM chief, expanding access to higher education must go hand in hand with ensuring that students have the facilities, equipment, competent educators and practical training needed to succeed.
“In health care education, the quality of training today can determine the quality of care tomorrow,” he stressed.

Accompanied by UP Manila chancellor Dr. Michael Tee, DBM Undersecretary Goddes Hope Libiran, Assistant Secretary Gerald Janda and other UP officials, De Leon inspected the College of Medicine’s Surgical Knowledge Intensive Learning Laboratory thru Simulation (SKILLS) and the College of Nursing’s skills and simulation laboratory, where future Filipino doctors and nurses develop essential clinical competencies before attending to actual patients.
These facilities allow students to develop technical competence, sound clinical judgment and confidence in environments designed to prepare them for the demands of actual health care delivery.
“When we invest in the education of one future doctor or nurse, we are also investing in the lives of countless patients that professional will someday serve,” Kim said.
The budget chief underscored that the value of these investments extends beyond UP Manila’s campus.

In January 2026, for instance, 37 faculty members from other nursing institutions participated in a simulation-based education workshop, gaining teaching techniques they can apply in their respective schools.
This demonstrates how investments in one institution can help strengthen the quality of instruction in other higher education institutions and ultimately benefit more Filipino students.

As the country’s National Health Sciences Center, UP Manila also contributes to national development through medical research, health policy and specialized health care services delivered through the Philippine General Hospital.

Chancellor Tee underscored that government support for UP Manila creates a multiplier effect by strengthening education, research and health care while building the country’s capacity to respond to the health needs of its people.

He also emphasized the university’s responsibility to share its expertise and best practices with other higher education institutions so that the benefits of public investment can reach communities beyond UP Manila.
De Leon also stressed that world-class facilities can deliver their full value only when supported by capable professors, researchers, technical personnel and dedicated university staff.

articles.title: Duterte found fit to stand ICC trial
articles.summary: Former president Rodrigo Duterte is fit to stand trial for crimes against humanity before the International Criminal Court (ICC), judges ruled on Thursday, clearing a major hurdle ahead of the trial…

blocks.text: October 10, 2026 | 12:00am
Former president Rodrigo Duterte

MANILA, Philippines — Former president Rodrigo Duterte is fit to stand trial for crimes against humanity before the International Criminal Court (ICC), judges ruled on Thursday, clearing a major hurdle ahead of the trial proceedings scheduled to start on Nov. 30.

“The Chamber is satisfied that the expert panel’s reports are sufficiently conclusive to make a determination on the accused’s ability to participate in the trial proceedings and to effectively exercise his procedural and fair trial rights,” the 17-page redacted decision read.
The decision was signed by Presiding Judge Joanna Korner and Judges Keebong Paek and Nicolas Guillou, who compose the ICC’s Trial Chamber III.
They also rejected the defense’s request for additional medical examination and the conduct of an oral hearing on Duterte’s fitness to stand trial.
The finding was based on the reports of the three-member panel formed to assess the medical condition of the former president.
According to the decision, the experts found “no new evidence” that would alter their previous opinion submitted ahead of the pre-trial proceedings earlier this year.

They also observed that Duterte’s health even improved since its previous report, attributing it to “the high standard of medical and nursing care, including diagnostic rigor and pharmacological rationalization.”

Although there were some evidence of “pre-clinical” disease, the experts said the “any reduced mental capacity present is not such as to render Mr. Duterte unable to fulfill the necessary capacities.”
The experts found Duterte has the capacity to understand the charges, the purpose and consequences of the proceedings and the evidence presented during the trial.

They said Duterte is also capable of following the course of the proceedings, including the nature and implications of entering a plea, as well as instruct his counsel in the preparation and conduct of his defense.
The trial judges also noted the panel’s recommended measures in light of Duterte’s advanced age and condition.

These include using over-ear headphones or hearing aids during hearings; provision of care and support in relation to food, rest and exercise; taking hourly breaks; starting hearings no earlier than 11 a.m. and having a member of nursing staff available to assist with medication. — Alexis Romero

articles.title: Brussels: Rioters clash with police at anti-austerity rally
articles.summary: Violent rioters, many of whom were masked, confronted police at the edge of an anti-austerity march in Brussels. Police responded with water cannons and tear gas.

image.caption: Rioters, who were mostly young and masked, confronted police in the central tourist district of BrusselsImage: Geert Vanden Wijngaert/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Hundreds of protesters clashed with police in the Belgian capital on Friday during an anti-austerity march organized by trade unions.
Masked protesters dressed in black threw rocks and other projectiles at police in Brussels. Anti-police slogans echoed through the streets, and similar graffiti covered nearby walls.

An AFP reporter witnessed two buses being attacked after the passengers were evacuated. The rioters smashed the windows and ripped out the seats. Meanwhile, youths set fire to trash cans, rental bikes, and scooters.
According to Reuters, firefighters extinguished several fires, including those on buses.

blocks.caption: The police responded to the violence by using water cannons and tear gasImage: Yves Herman/REUTERS

blocks.text: How did police respond to protests in Brussels?
The police said officers used water cannons and tear gas after young people on the outskirts of the protest targeted them with sticks and bottles.
"Several hundred youths gathered along with the demonstrators," police said in a statement. "The atmosphere gradually became more tense and there were serious disturbances to public order."
In a preliminary update, the police said they had arrested approximately 20 people, mostly minors.
Police also said the main trade union march had gone ahead peacefully. Before the rally, union head Bert Engelaar called on rioters to stay away from the protest.
"Those individuals have nothing to do with the message with which thousands of others come out on the streets," Engelaar wrote on Facebook.

blocks.caption: Despite organizers urging rioters to stay away from the protests, violent youths confronted police and vandalized propertyImage: Yves Herman/REUTERS

blocks.text: What are the government's goals?
Chaotic scenes of violence occurred during a demonstration in which between 30,000 and 50,000 people participated. It was one of many nationwide union protests against planned austerity measures.

Belgium is burdened by substantial public debt and a persistent budget deficit. Led by Prime Minister Bart De Wever, the center-right government aims to find €10 billion ($11.2 billion) in savings by the end of its term in 2029.
Rather than imposing cuts in areas like health and hiking VAT, trade unions are pushing for the government to increase taxes on the highest earners.

The clashes in Brussels came after a week of tension in Liege, where authorities banned public gatherings after students clashed with police and vandalized shops. Over 200 people were arrested in Liege, and dozens of police officers were injured.

articles.title: PCG repels Chinese militia vessel, 22 fishing boats from Kota Island waters
articles.summary: The Philippine Coast Guard said it drove away a Chinese maritime militia vessel and 22 fishing boats from the territorial waters of Kota Island on Friday.

blocks.text: Published October 9, 2026 11:52pm
The Philippine Coast Guard said it drove away a Chinese maritime militia vessel and 22 fishing boats from the territorial waters of Kota Island on Friday.

Rear Admiral Jay Tarriela, PCG spokesperson for the West Philippine Sea, identified the Chinese mothership as CMMV 9622, which is the same vessel it repelled, along with 24 sampans, from Kota Island on Sept. 28, 2026.

“At approximately 3:00 PM, PCG personnel stationed on Kota Island sighted and monitored the Chinese sampans conducting unauthorized fishing activities approximately 0.55 nautical miles northwest of the island, with the nearest sampan observed only about 250 meters from the shoreline, well within the 12-nautical-mile territorial sea of Kota Island,” Tarriela said on X.
The PCG’s operation was carried out by Coast Guard Station Kota under the Coast Guard District Kalayaan Island Group, in coordination with the Philippine Marine Corps and the Philippine Navy.
He noted that the Chinese vessels were also seen dumping waste into the sea.

“At 3:30 PM, two rubber boats departed Kota Island manned by a joint team of PCG personnel from the Special Operations Group, Maritime Law Enforcement Group, Coast Guard District Kalayaan Island Group, and medical personnel, together with three (3) Philippine Marines. On shore, Philippine Navy personnel provided radio and communications support, while Philippine Marines maintained monitoring and situational updates throughout the operation,” Tarriela added.

According to Tarriela, during the agency’s operation, the Chinese mothership was encircling the two PCG rubber boats deployed, while its master was using hand signals, claiming the area and directing its team to leave.
Over a period of two hours, the PCG said it expelled the sampans one by one.
“One sampan refused to leave, resulting in minor contact, with no injuries or damage sustained. The sampan eventually complied and departed,” Tarriela said.
“By 5:30 PM, all Chinese vessels had been pushed back to approximately 3.5 nautical miles from Kota Island and departed toward the northwest, and the operation was terminated,” he added.
The PCG emphasized that Kota Island is an integral part of the Municipality of Kalayaan, Province of Palawan.

The agency stressed that under international law, the Philippines exercises full sovereignty over its territorial sea. Consequently, unauthorized fishing by foreign vessels constitutes a direct violation of Philippine laws, including the Philippine Fisheries Code and the Philippine Maritime Zones Act. —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: The U.S. plans to livestream an execution. Here's how that compares to global practice
articles.summary: For about nine decades, executions in the U.S. have been private affairs, often shrouded in secrecy. If carried out as planned, death penalty experts said it would mark the first known broadcast or…

image.caption: United States Army soldiers stand outside the First Calvary Monument during a guided media tour of the Fort Hood Army Post in Fort Hood, Texas, on Nov. 7, 2009. (Jessica Rinaldi/Reuters)

blocks.text: World·New

For about nine decades, executions in the U.S. have been private affairs, often shrouded in secrecy. If carried out as planned, death penalty experts said it would mark the first known broadcast or livestream of a lawful execution.
Experts say it would mark the 1st known broadcast or livestream of a lawful execution

The U.S. military plans to livestream the Dec. 3 execution by firing squad of Nidal Hasan, the former Army psychiatrist convicted of killing 13 people and injuring 32 others in the 2009 Fort Hood shooting.
He's due to become the first person executed by firing squad by the U.S. military since 1945.

Hasan, a former U.S. army officer, walked into a medical building where soldiers were getting checkups, shouted Allahu akbar — Arabic for "God is greater" — and opened fire with a laser-sighted handgun.
Executions are generally conducted behind prison walls, and internet platforms and governments have spent years trying to limit the circulation of violent execution footage.
How does the Pentagon's stunning announcement that his execution will be livestreamed compares to global practice, and to the history of U.S. public executions?
We explain below.
Firing squad execution to be livestreamed, Pentagon says
Will this be the first livestreamed lawful execution?
Death penalty experts consulted by Reuters said they were unaware of any previous lawful execution that had been livestreamed or broadcast to a public audience.

Execution footage has occasionally emerged after the event. The hanging of former Iraqi leader Saddam Hussein in 2006, for example, was seen around the world after official and unofficial recordings circulated online and through broadcasters, though it was not shown live.
Broadcasts and livestreams today are common for court proceedings, parliamentary debates and other state functions, but not for judicial executions.
How unusual is this compared with modern execution practices?
Public executions have become rare worldwide, with most countries that retain the death penalty carrying out executions away from public view.
According to Amnesty International, public executions recorded in recent years have largely been concentrated in Iran and Taliban-run Afghanistan.

The execution would also be notable in the United States. Public executions largely disappeared during the 20th century, and death penalty experts cited by Reuters said the last legally sanctioned public execution took place in 1936.
Hasan's execution would be the first carried out by firing squad by the U.S. military since the 1945 execution of Eddie Slovik, who was convicted of desertion during the Second World War.

Nidal Hasan, charged with killing 13 people and wounding 31 in a November 2009 shooting spree at Fort Hood, is pictured in an undated handout photo obtained by Reuters on June 29, 2012. (Bell County Sheriff's Office/Handout/Reuters)
How has the internet changed this?
The internet has transformed execution imagery from a local event into content capable of reaching global audiences within minutes.
Militant groups such as Islamic State became notorious for producing professionally edited execution videos that were distributed online as propaganda and recruitment tools.
Criminal organizations, including Mexican drug cartels, have also circulated violent footage to intimidate rivals and project power.
The ability of users to rapidly copy, repost and redistribute content has made it more difficult for governments and technology companies to control the spread of such material.
What's the global reaction so far?
The UN human rights office on Friday said the planned livestreaming would violate the absolute prohibition on torture and amount to a form of public execution.
"Public executions constitute a form of cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment," Shabia Mantoo, spokesperson for the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights, told reporters in Geneva.
Amnesty International's U.K. CEO Kerry Moscogiuri said Friday that the U.S. plans are a "grave step," considering that the death pentalty is already "so inhumane."
"To create some kind of theatre around the State taking someone's life is barbaric and deeply shocking," she told Reuters.

items: Pentagon says firing squad execution of Fort Hood shooter will be livestreamed
What happened in Tennessee's failed execution of Christa Pike and what comes next?

blocks.text: Governments and technology companies have generally moved in the opposite direction, attempting to reduce rather than expand access to graphic execution footage.
Major social media platforms have spent years removing execution videos linked to extremist organizations and other violent groups.

One of the first public governmental reactions came from New Zealand, whose chief censor said authorities would have little practical ability to prevent residents from accessing a livestream while it was taking place.
Christa Pike's lawyers demand answers, transparency over botched execution
Livestreams pose particular challenges for platforms because footage can be viewed, copied and redistributed before moderation systems can intervene.

Even countries that still conduct public executions have often restricted filming and broadcast rights. Saudi Arabia historically carried out public executions before spectators, but recording them was prohibited and such public executions had largely ceased by 2019.
Did the U.S. used to do public executions?

The livestreamed execution is reminiscent of a bygone period in America’s history in which public executions were seen as deterrents to crime as well as popular ceremonies, said Michael L. Radelet, professor emeritus at the University of Colorado Boulder, who has done extensive research on executions.

Parents and teachers would often bring children along to teach them a lesson. The events would sometimes feature a choir, a preacher giving an "execution sermon" and the condemned, who was typically a man being hanged, giving a long speech to the crowd.
The 1936 hanging in Kentucky of Rainey Bethea is often considered the last public execution in the country, said Radelet.

Bethea was a Black man who reportedly confessed to the rape and killing of a 70-year-old white woman, but was never charged with murder, according to the Death Penalty Information Center. Thousands of people attended the event, which was held in a parking lot so the courthouse lawn wouldn’t be damaged by the crowd, according to the centre.
As NPR points out, the last time the U.S. military executed someone by firing squad was in 1945, when Private Eddie Slovik was shot for desertion in France.
A United States Army Specialist prays near a makeshift memorial for victims of the shootings at Fort Hood Army post in Fort Hood. (Jessica Rinaldi/Reuters)
With files from The Associated Press

articles.title: Eritrean troops in Ethiopia raise fears of a regional war
articles.summary: Ethiopia and Eritrea are trading blame for confrontations in Tigray amid international calls for restraint. Their respective allies have the potential to catapult the conflict into a regional war.

image.caption: ENDF patrol on October 7: The airport of Mekelle is under Ethiopian government control. But witnesses have reported Eritrean troops towards Tigray's northern border.Image: REUTERS

blocks.text: Various sources have confirmed the presence of Eritrean armed forces in Ethiopia. An AFP report quoted a foreign security source, speaking on condition of anonymity, as estimating that 5,000 to 8,000 Eritrean soldiers were present in Tigray.
Meanwhile, Ethiopia and Eritrea are ramping up their war talk.
According to Reuters, the government of Ethiopia has written to the UN Security Council, calling for the immediate withdrawal of Eritrean troops from its territory.

In the letter, dated ‌Oct. 8, Ethiopia's ‌Foreign Minister Gedion Timothewos said the Eritrean troops' presence left Ethiopia with "no option but to defend itself against Eritrea," the news agency reported.
Eritrea's Minister of Information Yemane Meskel, in a post on X on October 7, had accused Ethiopia of "incessantly beating the drums of war."
"The sovereign state of Eritrea is bound by blood and law," Yemane wrote in the national Tigrinya language on October 9. "Woe to those who touch it."
The war talk by Ethiopia and Eritrea comes amid a conflict that is seen to be deteriorating rapidly in recent weeks.

Some experts have suggested that Ethiopia may have intentionally triggered the escalation. Just last week, it expelled diplomats from Eritrea and Egypt, causing Eritrea to sever diplomatic ties altogether.

On Monday, when Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed was sworn in for another five years, he stated that access to the sea was a priority. The statement fueled fresh speculation that he intends to take Eritrea's strategic port of Assab by force and prompted fierce reactions from the Eritrean side.
Why can't Ethiopia and Eritrea be friends?
Abiy's internal opposition: Tsimdo and the Alliance for Survival

While the Ethiopian National Defence Forces (ENDF), aided by the Tigray Peace Force milita, have made significant advances and notably recaptured the Tigray federal state capital of Mekelle, opposition to Ethiopia has found new formats for collaboration.
One is the so-called Tsimdo movement, a Tigrinya term that loosely translates as "engagement."

"The Tsimdo concept initially surfaced through cross-border peace initiatives involving activists, religious figures, and local communities in the Tigray and Eritrea border villages in 2025," Dr. Jalale Getachew Birru, senior East Africa analyst with the US-based conflict monitor ACLED, told DW.
It has since undergone several reconfigurations and now encompasses diverse groups within Ethiopia, mostly defined along ethnic lines and with long-standing grievances against the federal government.

The Ethiopian Peoples' Forces Alliance for Survival, or simply Alliance for Survival, that was proclaimed in September, stems from this movement. According to Jalale, the alliance aims at removing the current government and initiating a constitutional dialogue.
The new rebel alliance transforming the Tigray conflict
The new alliance says a lot about the long history of unresolved conflict in Ethiopia, said Abdurahman Sayed, an analyst at the Horn of Africa Centre for Regional Integration.
"The fighting inside Ethiopia has never stopped," Sayed told DW.

"With the Oromo Liberation Army, it's been going on for decades, with the Amhara, it's been going on for the last three years, at least. With the Tigrayans, the Pretoria agreement about three years ago was just a cessation of hostility that would have led to some kind of sustainable peace by addressing the root causes of the conflict — but it failed to do that, so they're back to the conflict situation now."

However, of the seven groups in the alliance, ACLED data shows that only three were involved in recent fighting: The Tigrayan Defence Forces (TDF), the Amhara Fano National Movement (AFNM), and a fairly recently formed ethnic Afar group called Ugugumo.

blocks.caption: Amhara Fano fighters (pictured here in 2021) who fought in the two-year Tigray War are part of the new Ethiopian Peoples' Forces Alliance for Survival Image: Solan Kolli/AFP

blocks.text: Joint declaration by Sudan, Egypt, Eritrea, Somalia

The success of the Alliance for Survival would depend in large part on the support they get through external actors, according to ACLED. Those could include neighboring Sudan, Egypt, Eritrea, and Somalia.
"All these four countries have grievances against Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's government," Sayed said.

"The Egyptians have issues with the Nile River and how it should be administered, including the dams that are already there and those planned to be built around the Nile River. The Sudanese also have their own concerns that Ethiopians are supporting the [Rapid Support Forces] militia, which is fighting the Sudanese army."

In the case of Somalia, the issue of sea access has sparked tensions. Landlocked Ethiopia has negotiated access to the port of Berbera in Somaliland . In 2024, it signed a memorandum of understanding with the breakaway region, causing uproar in Somalia, which considers the deal a violation of its national sovereignty. Turkish mediation was needed to calm things down.
Somaliland: Somalia's breakaway 'nation'
"So all those neighboring countries have their own concerns and they feel this threat that is coming from Ethiopia needs to be tackled collectively."

On October 4, the leaders of the four countries issued a joint declarationthat didn't mention Ethiopia but seemed to send a strong signal. The leaders stressed the importance of international law, "particularly respect for the sovereignty, independence and territorial integrity of the states of the region."
And it maintained that "the governance of the Red Sea is the exclusive responsibility of the littoral states."
Although the leaders of Sudan, Egypt, Eritrea and Somalia vowed to promote "peaceful solutions to conflicts," the reality on the ground may prove otherwise.

articles.title: Macron and Steinmeier struggle to revive Franco-German ties
articles.summary: Presidents Frank-Walter Steinmeier and Emmanuel Macron are about to step down from their offices. Their meeting in France made it clear how urgently the Franco-German partnership needs new momentum.

image.caption: Presidents Steinmeier (l) and Macron and their wives met in Paris for a farewellImage: Bernd von Jutrczenka/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: The German delegation passed through Paris without being hindered by the student strikes taking place on the streets of Paris. The motorcades moved through the French capital without disruption. Around the Arc de Triomphe and the Champs-Elysees, however, traffic was at a standstill for hours. Due to the high-profile visit, the streets were cordoned off over a wide area.

Emmanuel Macron had decided on a special gesture to send off Frank-Walter Steinmeier, his German guest: The military honors took place under the Arc de Triomphe. And so, early in the morning, the German national anthem rang out in the heart of Paris — amid sunshine and bitter cold.

It was a generous gesture of friendship and symbolism, yet it seemed to be from a bygone era. In both countries, populists on the political fringes are gaining support. In Germany, the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) ranks first in nationwide polls. In France, Emmanuel Macron could soon be succeeded by either Jean-Luc Melenchon of the far left or Marine Le Pen of the far right.

Added to this is an economic crisis that threatens prosperity. Unresolved issues of social justice are driving younger generations into the streets. At the same time, social media is increasingly becoming a tool of disinformation and "accelerating doubts about democracy," Macron said in Paris.

While the AfD may soon form its first state government in Saxony-Anhalt, President Steinmeier remained confident. He insisted that Germany would continue to "play a leading role in Europe" in the future and that Germans would remain good Europeans. But he did not say where he drew this certainty from. Questions from journalists were not permitted at the joint press conference at the Elysee Palace.
A future, but no plan

Political scientist Jacob Ross isn't surprised by this. Both Macron and Steinmeier lack a "genuine agenda for Germany, France, and Europe." Both represent political systems that "seek to respond to 21st-century crises with 20th-century solutions," said the expert on German-French relations at the German Council on Foreign Relations (DGAP).

Even though Steinmeier and Macron have different political styles, Ross sees parallels — especially where their policies have failed. One example of this is strategic foreign policy issues, such as dealing with Russia. "For a long time, they pursued a policy based on integrating Russia into Europe, and then both were overwhelmed by the events of 2022 and had to adjust their course," said Ross. Since then, both have merely reacted to current affairs, according to the political scientist.
Little support for Macron's ideas
Emmanuel Macron has made some bold moves for Europe, but without support from Berlin, says Ross. Germany's political leadership has long reacted with caution to proposals from Paris.

A joint initiative that both countries recently promoted to the European Commission is aimed at combating unfair competition. Countries that gain an advantage through unfair practices should face strict European measures.

Macron joined German Chancellor Friedrich Merz in speaking out in favor of this. Although China was not explicitly named, the initiative is seen to be primarily aimed at that country. Beijing uses enormous subsidies to support its companies, whose products flood the European market, while European firms continue to face barriers when trying to access the Chinese market.
How Europe's defense sector is trying to gear up

Germany and France have also long sought greater cooperation in the defense sector. Yet major joint defense projects are making little progress. When the planned joint fighter jet, the FCAS, fell through in June, officials emphasized ongoing cooperation on the future MGCS main battle tank. And yet differences on this became apparent during the state visit.

As German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius arrived in Paris, French Chief of the General Staff Fabien Mandon stated during a hearing in the French National Assembly that Germany had decided to withdraw from the tank project. A day later, Mandon clarified that he had expressed himself ambiguously. But some observers believe that such misunderstandings are a sign of dissatisfaction on both sides — below the political level — regarding cooperation with the other partner.

It is this political level that often ends up having to set the record straight in such cases. This time was no exception: Pistorius firmly refuted the claim that the project was on the verge of being scrapped. "The MGCS project is not over; it is not dead; it has not been terminated by anyone — quite the contrary. It is a core project of Franco-German cooperation on land systems," said the German defense minister.

The focus is primarily on digital information processing in combat, as well as unmanned and automated systems. Germany and France would continue their cooperation, Pistorius insisted, and MGCS is an important future project for both countries and their armed forces.

blocks.caption: The French and German Presidents took part in a ceremony in the heart of ParisImage: Abdul Saboor/REUTERS/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: The future of defense and space

On Friday, the presidents of France and Germany visited several facilities near Bordeaux that are closely linked to space exploration and nuclear deterrence. These include ArianeGroup, a Franco-German company that, among other things, manufactures the nuclear-capable M51 missiles for French nuclear submarines. The itinerary also included visits to startups that are looking far into the future.

It was unofficially reported during the visit that this focus of the trip was a personal priority for Macron. The French president has long spoken of a European dimension to France's nuclear deterrent. Considering announcements from the US saying it would reduce its commitment to Europe, his views are gaining increasing traction.

As early as 2020, Macron proposed a strategic dialogue on the role of French nuclear weapons in European security. Several countries, including Germany, have since expressed interest. Now, further steps are being considered. The focus is on what Macron once called "forward deterrence," such as joint military exercises and visits to strategically important locations. A permanent deployment of French nuclear weapons in other countries remains off the table. Furthermore, according to French nuclear doctrine, France always retains sole decision-making authority over the use of its nuclear weapons.

Steinmeier's two-day state visit to France ended on Friday afternoon. So far, there has been little sign of new momentum in Franco-German relations. This makes it all the more urgent for the successors to the two presidents to develop a shared vision for the future of the relationship between the two countries starting next year.

Macron and Steinmeier will step down from their posts almost simultaneously in 2027 after ten years in office. The state visit to France thus also served as a final joint meeting, marked by some ceremonial farewells.
This article was originally written in German.
