articles.title: China agrees to ‘halve’ hybrid car exports to EU in landmark deal
articles.summary:
Brussels says Beijing’s shipments could fall by more than half over four years, cutting millions of vehicles amid fears for European jobs

The EU said it has reached a landmark deal with…

blocks.text: The EU said it has reached a landmark deal with China to “halve” its sales of hybrid cars in the bloc amid fears surging sales could kill off parts of the European car industry.

Trade commissioner Maroš Šefčovič said the deal was the first of its kind and the result of “intense” negotiations with China since June to curb a trade deficit of €1.18bn (£1bn) a day, which has caused mounting tensions between the two economic powers.

The deal “opens the prospect of cutting China’s export [of hybrids] by more than a half”, Šefčovič said, adding that this would translate into a reduction in exports of plug-in and battery-powered hybrid cars by “several millions” over the next four years, said Šefčovič said Šefčovič at a press conference in Beijing on Friday.

“It is the first time that China has accepted to moderate its exports without going through the phase of prior trade tension,” he said, a reference to the usual investigations that must take place before safeguards under WTO trading rules are put in place.

China has been flooding Europe with cars, including hybrids and pure battery electric vehicles (BEVs), threatening European manufacturers. Hybrids combine an internal combustion engine with a small battery. They are sold by carmakers as a transitional step towards BEVs.

Šefčovič said the Chinese had recognised the political pressure building in every member state in Europe with “literally thousands of job losses” at risk because of the flood of cheap imports from China across many sectors including chemicals and textiles.
He said EU leaders were “clearly expecting very fast action” from the European Commission and the Chinese recognised that.
“I am glad to say that the Chinese partners appreciated this very strong political argument, and therefore, we can proceed through the negotiated solution,” he said.
“This ‌is far from the end. It’s a crucial first step, but only a first step,” Šefčovič told ‌reporters in Beijing where he had travelled to hold ​talks with his Chinese counterpart.

Earlier this week senior EU officials said they were heading to Beijing to seek what they called a “proof of concept” or pilot scheme with one sector which they hoped could then be expanded to other areas under pressure from Chinese competition.
Šefčovič said he put “so much emphasis” on the negotiations because it was “very difficult to stop” a trade war once it was declared.
As part of a 16-point agreement, Beijing and Brussels will continue negotiating on cars, export restrictions on rare earths and access to China for more food and drink from the EU.
after newsletter promotion

China said both sides would adhere to “procedures concerning company price undertakings” for hybrid cars suggesting one method of curbing sales would be to set higher minimum price tags for Chinese cars sold in Europe.
The EU commissioner will brief EU diplomats in Brussels on Sunday ahead of a leaders’ summit on Thursday.
A statement from the Chinese ministry of commerce said China is “willing … to continue facilitating the approval of export licenses for rare earths and permanent magnets destined for the EU”.

It added that both sides had “reaffirmed their commitment … to properly handle differences within the framework of WTO rules, and to continuing to stabilise and balance bilateral trade and economic relations”.
While China and the EU acknowledged “differences” between them it appears that China has accepted the EU’s request to create a new model for trade balances starting with a pilot on hybrid cars.

articles.title: Author or artificial intelligence? Literature in crisis
articles.summary: AI is a hot topic at this year's Frankfurt Book Fair. An international literary scandal raises questions about machine-generated texts.

image.caption: The pavilion of the Guest of Honor, the Czech Republic, at the 2026 Frankfurt Book FairImage: Hannes P. Albert/AFP

blocks.text: It's the hot-button topic at the Frankfurt Book Fair: How profoundly will artificial intelligence transform the book industry, and how can this transformation be regulated?

Given the warnings about the technology's long-term risks to humanity as a whole, such debates might seem rather narrow in scope. In reality, however, they concern very concrete issues — copyright protection, the power of major tech corporations and the future of creative work. Many of those involved agree that the political measures taken don't go far enough.
This year, however, another aspect has entered the debate: Can we actually recognize when a text has been written with the help of artificial intelligence, and how can it be proven?

These are the questions being asked in the current literary scandal surrounding Haitian-Canadian author Thélyson Orélien. His debut novel, "C'était ça ou mourir," (It Was Either That or Die) was published in Canada in the spring and then in France in late summer.

blocks.caption: The controversy around Thélyson Orélien's book has sparked a larger debate on AI and authorshipImage: Joel Saget/AFP/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: The migration story was universally acclaimed, with translation rights sold in more than 20 languages. The book even made the longlist for the prestigious Prix Goncourt.

Then, suddenly, allegations emerged that the book had been written almost entirely using AI. Orélien, until then a rising literary star, suddenly found himself branded a fraud, despite denying all the allegations. His nomination for the Prix Goncourt was withdrawn.
So, who should we believe now — the author or the AI that claims to have identified AI-generated writing?
When the origins of texts become uncertain
"We will have to learn to live with doubt," says Hannes Bajohr, a professor of German literature at the University of California, Berkeley.

blocks.caption: Hannes Bajohr, professor for German Studies at the University of California, BerkeleyImage: Jen Siska

blocks.text: He has spent years examining how AI is changing both writing and reading. His prediction: If the origins of texts can no longer be reliably established, we will have to evaluate them differently. What matters will be their quality alone, rather than whether AI was used in the writing process.
Nina George, a best-selling author and honorary president of the European Writers' Council, is unwilling to accept this.
At the Frankfurt Book Fair, she was awarded the Friedrich Perthes Prize in recognition of her commitment to issues including AI and copyright.

blocks.caption: A leading advocate for European authors' rights and copyright reform: Author Nina GeorgeImage: Sabine Kieselbach/DW

blocks.text: George has addressed the European Parliament and the German Bundestag, and speaks and writes tirelessly about the dangers of AI models. It is perverse, she says, that an author should suddenly have to prove that their writing is human. The focus of her campaigning remains the large corporations' self-serving mentality and the protection of copyright.
Can anyone become an author with AI?
But what if an author sees AI not as an enemy, but as a tool that makes writing easier?
American author and artist Luke Stoffel deliberately used AI in his memoir, "How To Win One Million Dollars" and "Shit Glitter," and was open about doing so.
"I'm dyslexic," he says in a video interview. "I've always written and made up stories, but I never dared to take them any further."

blocks.caption: Luke Stoffel openly talks about his use of AI in writing booksImage: Privat

blocks.text: It was only with the help of AI, he says, that he was able to fulfill his dream. The technology drew his attention to weaknesses in his writing and suggested a marketing strategy that actually worked.
Then, in May 2026, he received an award from the Independent Book Publishers Association (IBPA) for the book.

For South African author Coral Hart, AI is actually the foundation of her business model. Publishing under various pseudonyms, she releases more than 200 different novels every year, spanning romance, thrillers and mystery, all independently published.

She sees herself as an ideas person, as well as an editor and publisher. Although none of her books has yet become a bestseller, the business is profitable. According to Hart, each of her books reaches more than 5,000 people.
Many publishers already working with AI

New York-based author Luke Stoffel considers the entire debate hypocritical. Many publishers have been working with AI tools for some time. He's certain that "right now, a million-copy bestseller is being printed that was created with the help of AI. The author won't admit it, and then there'll be a scandal."
It is entirely possible that the scandal surrounding Thélyson Orélien is precisely that story. But we may never know for sure.
For now, the battle against the tech giants continues. Even the companies themselves are increasingly concerned about losing control.

At the very start of the fair, the German Publishers and Booksellers Association issued an appeal to policymakers in Berlin and Brussels, calling for stricter regulation of artificial intelligence, more urgently than ever before. More than 150 publishers have already signed it.
But for now, it remains just an appeal. And the question of what authors themselves should be permitted to do with AI will undoubtedly continue to fuel debate in the future.
Reading 2.0: How AI is changing our books
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: US imposes sanctions aiming to 'dismantle' International Criminal Court
articles.summary: The US has announced new sanctions on the International Criminal Court. It's the latest in a series of steps by the Donald Trump administration as it seeks to "dismantle" the intergovernmental…

image.caption: The US has had the ICC on its radar more or less throughout the second Trump termImage: John Thys/AFP

blocks.text: US President Donald Trump's administration imposed sanctions on the International Criminal Court (ICC) on Friday, hours after one of its former judges won the Nobel Peace Prize.

This comes as the US has in recent months made no bones about pursuing what Secretary of State Marco Rubio has called a "sweeping campaign to dismantle the threat posed by the International Criminal Court."
The United States and Israel had both strongly opposed the court's arrest warrants for top Israeli officials, including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

Since 2020 and the back end of Trump's first term, the US had also opposed investigations into military actions in Afghanistan that "deprioritize" alleged US wrongdoings, focusing on the Taliban, but can nevertheless include them.
What did the State Department say about the ICC sanctions?
"President Trump will never allow the International Court to prosecute Americans," Secretary of State Marco Rubio said in a statement.

"That is why, today, the United States is sanctioning the International Criminal Court. We will ban transactions with this rogue court, cutting off their resources and crippling its ability to operate," he said.
The ICC said the US sanctions aimed to obstruct an "independent" international court supported by more than half of the UN's members.

"The court will continue to fully discharge its mandate, with independence and impartiality, acting only on the basis of the law and the evidence, for the sake of the countless victims of grave crimes," said ICC President Tomoko Akane.
What is the ICC?
The International Criminal Court is an intergovernmental organization and international tribunal based in the Dutch city of The Hague.

It's the only permanent international court with the theoretical jurisdiction to prosecute individuals for international crimes like genocide, crimes against humanity, war crimes and illegal aggression.
The ICC was set up in 2002 and is underpinned by the Rome Statute treaty.
More than half the countries in the world, 125 in total, are full parties to the Rome Statute, having signed and ratified it.
Several of the world's most significant powers — not least China, India, Russia, the US and Israel — do not recognize the court's jurisdiction.
There is, however, a grey area in that the court accepts challenges from ratified members against individuals from countries that do not recognize the court.

That is why high-profile arrest warrants against Russian officials, including President Vladimir Putin, and Israeli officials, including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, have been issued in recent years — following respective complaints from Ukrainians and Palestinians.
What were the prior signs of Trump administration pressure on the ICC?
The US has been increasingly critical of the ICC during Trump's second term.

Rubio has often led the charge, for instance, writing an opinion article for the Wall Street Journal in mid-July this year saying, "America never agreed to a world tribunal that can override our own courts and the Constitution."

He argued it was possible for US "soldiers, police officers, Border Patrol agents and elected leaders" to be "dragged before an international court" and tried by judges "from random countries across the globe."

Just over a week later, on July 25, Venezuela's new administration — transformed after the US abduction of Nicolas Maduro in January — announced that it planned to withdraw from the Rome Statute and the ICC.

In response, the US State Department welcomed "the new Venezuelan government's partnership on American-led efforts to dismantle the corrupt and worthless ICC," calling on "all members of the ICC to withdraw from the Rome Statute."

A few days later, the military junta in Chad announced that it was withdrawing from the ICC. It said it had done so after a US request, with Washington urging other African countries to follow in the Russian-backed junta's footsteps.
The recent sexual misconduct scandal surrounding the ICC's chief prosecutor Karim Khan, who was dismissed in July, provided more ammunition the US could aim at the court.
In August, the US imposed sanctions on the ICC's president, Japanese judge Tomoko Akane, and Abdoulaye Seye, a Senegalese trial lawyer at the court.
Sanctions launch was first anticipated during UN General Assembly
These signs had been accompanied in recent months by speculation that, before long, the US would sanction the ICC as an organization, not just members of it.

Last month, reports circulated widely that President Donald Trump might announce the sanctions during his speech at the UN headquarters in New York, with off-the-record sources in the US and the court's seat in the Netherlands saying they were preparing for the measures.
Trump ultimately leveled sharp criticism at the ICC in his address on September 22, calling it an "evil" organization, but at the time made no announcement of new sanctions.

articles.title: ‘Not as long as I’m premier’: Danielle Smith rules out 2nd separation referendum if Albertans vote to remain

image.caption: Alberta Premier Danielle Smith took questions from CBC News’ chief correspondent Adrienne Arsenault on Friday, with the Alberta referendum a little more than one week away. (Jared Thomas/CBC News)

blocks.text: Calgary·New

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith was definitive Friday when asked whether she’d commit to not holding another referendum on Alberta separation should a majority of Albertans vote to remain in Canada on Oct. 19.
Alberta would ‘pursue other things’ if immigration, constitutional questions rejected
“Not as long as I’m premier,” Smith told CBC News’ chief correspondent Adrienne Arsenault during a one-on-one interview in Calgary.

The premier’s line in the sand comes a little more than a week before Albertans will vote on 10 questions, including whether Alberta should stay in Canada, or whether it should begin the process to hold a second, binding referendum on separating from the country.
And it conflicts with the positioning of Alberta separatist leaders, many of whom say that they won’t give up the fight even if the vote goes against them.

items: 'Never giving up': Alberta separatist leaders say referendum vote won't end their fight

blocks.text: There will also be five questions tied to immigration and four tied to Canada’s Constitution.

On Thursday, Smith wasn’t clear on what she considers a strong mandate or threshold for the other nine questions. She has previously said 50 per cent plus one was what she considered a threshold for the separatism question.
Alberta Premier Danielle Smith took questions from CBC News’ chief correspondent Adrienne Arsenault on Friday, with the Alberta referendum a little more than one week away. (Jared Thomas/CBC News)
Asked again by Arsenault on Friday about the percentage for the other nine questions, Smith said “majority rule” seems to be the way most decisions are made.
“If they’re rejected, then you know what? I guess we’ll have to pursue other things,” Smith said. “Find out other things that Albertans are concerned about.”
Smith rules out 2nd Alberta referendum: 'Not as long as I'm premier'

Pollsters have said that numbers on the separatism question have largely been baked-in for years. A recent poll done for CBC News suggested 23 per cent of respondents said they’d vote to start the legal process to hold a binding referendum, while 72 per cent said they’d vote to remain in Canada.
But polls attempting to sort out support for the nine other questions have been decidedly more uncertain.

items: Albertans divided on immigration, while half still undecided on 9 non-separation questions: poll

blocks.text: 'Public enemy number one'
While a significant majority of Albertans polled have said they’re in favour of remaining in Canada, the same is not true of members of Smith’s United Conservative Party.
Polling has suggested that among those who said they’d vote for the UCP, 53 per cent said they’d vote for the separation option, while 40 per cent said they’d vote to stay in Canada.

Smith has also recently seen one of her caucus members, Red Deer-South UCP MLA Jason Stephan, say that he voted in favour of the separation option on the ballot. A UCP riding association in southern Alberta also formally urged a party vote to review the premier’s leadership.

Jason Stephan, a member of Alberta Premier Danielle Smith’s UCP caucus, said he voted in favour of proceeding with a legally binding referendum on whether Alberta should leave Canada during a recent town hall. (Lina Elsaadi/CBC)
Smith said that over the past months, she has been working hard to convince more people to vote to remain in Canada.

She said that, given constructive co-operation with Prime Minister Mark Carney, “Canada is working better than it ever has,” highlighting the West Coast pipeline, officially known as Pacific Link, as well as the repeal of various federal laws.
While she said she speaks to those who disagree with her, Smith said that doesn’t include separatist leaders.

“As you've probably seen, I'm kind of public enemy number one for that group,” Smith said. “They don't like the fact that I've taken such a strong position on remain. So no, I'm not in contact with any of them.”

One of those independence advocates, Jeffrey Rath, told the fifth estate that to get the referendum they want, UCP separatists must get rid of Smith “sooner rather than later,” and proceed to “have a special general meeting of the party to vote on her leadership the same way we did with [former Alberta premier] Jason Kenney."

items: The Alberta question: How separatists took hold of the province’s governing party

blocks.text: You can see more of Arsenault's interview with Smith tonight on The National.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Joel is a reporter/editor with CBC Calgary. In fall 2021, he spent time with CBC's bureau in Lethbridge. He was previously the editor of the Airdrie City View and Rocky View Weekly newspapers. He hails from Swift Current, Sask. Reach him by email at joel.dryden@cbc.ca

articles.title: Saudi coalition vows 'firm' response after airport attack kills 3
articles.summary: Saudi Arabia and its allied forces in Yemen vowed a "firm response" to Houthi attacks that target civilians. The kingdom's authorities said three Saudi nationals were killed in Thursday's attack on…

image.caption: Smoke and flames rise from the main international airport in Riyadh on October 8, in this screengrab obtained from a social media video.Image: Social Media/REUTERS

blocks.text: The Saudi-led coalition in Yemen launched strikes that destroyed targets used by the Houthis, a coalition spokesperson said Friday.
Major General Turki al-Maliki said three rocket launch platforms were destroyed, adding that Houthi attacks on civilians would be met with a "firm response."

The Saudi-Houthi conflict has intensified in recent weeks, with Saudi Arabian authorities having said Friday that Houthi attacks on Riyadh's main international airport on Thursday killed three Saudi citizens and injured several people of "different nationalities."

The King Khalid International Airport was targeted twice on Thursday, the kingdom's civil aviation authority said.The first attack aimed at airport facilities and the second targeted an aircraft that belonged to the Saudia airline.
Houthi attacks on Riyadh raise the stakes of reignited conflict
Hundreds of flights were canceled because of Thursday's attacks, according to flight-tracking site FlightAware.
The Indian Embassy later said Air India had suspended operations through to Saturday, while the Lufthansa Group said its airlines would suspend flights to Riyadh through to October 16.
The European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA) on Friday recommended airlines not to operate in additional portions of Saudi Airspace in an updated bulletin.
The EASA said recent attacks had demonstrated the ability and the intent of the Houthis to strike targets deeper inside Saudi territory, including the capital.
On Thursday, the Iran-backed Houthis warned employees at Saudi oil facilities that oil installations remain a target.
Why can't the Saudis defeat the Houthis?
The Saudi-Houthi conflict: What to know

The Houthis have fought a Saudi-led coalition since 2015, when the kingdom entered Yemen's civil war to reinstate the internationally backed government in Sanaa. Houthi rebels took control of the capital in 2014.
But ever since, the Saudi-led coalition has found it hard to turn the tide of the war that quieted under a UN-brokered ceasefire in 2022.
In the last weeks, the Houthis stormed down Yemen's coast, capturing a wide swath of territory that has given them greater control of the Bab al-Mandab Strait.

A Saudi-led coalition has pressed a counteroffensive against the Houthis fighters and recaptured several areas along the strait, Yemeni officials have said. But the fighting appears to be far from over.
Can Yemen's government turn the tide against the Houthis?

articles.title: New spate of stabbings, overdoses and fires at Australian immigration detention centres run by ICE-linked US prison firm
articles.summary:
Exclusive: Federal government under scrutiny as documents reveal serious security lapses at Melbourne and Villawood immigration detention centres

  • Get our

blocks.text: A new spate of stabbings, overdoses and drug use in Australia’s immigration detention centres has put the Australian government in likely breach of laws designed to protect staff and detainees, internal documents show.

Earlier this year, Guardian Australia revealed catastrophic security failings across Australia’s onshore immigration network since Management and Training Corporation – a US private prison company used by Donald Trump to hold ICE detainees – won the $2.3bn detention contract in late 2024.

The federal government has repeatedly attempted to take a stick to MTC and its local subsidiary Secure Journeys to improve its performance, including through financial penalties and a fiery meeting last year between the home affairs minister, Tony Burke, and the company’s global president.

But new documents seen by the Guardian show serious security lapses have continued since, including through a spate of eight fire-related incidents at Villawood immigration detention centre and violence and drug use at Melbourne immigration detention centre (MIDC). Those failings have again put the department itself in the crosshairs of Comcare, the federal work safety regulator.

The documents reveal a string of incidents at MIDC involving violence, aggression, illicit substances and improvised weaponry since August. That includes a violent altercation on 18 August between two groups that led to six detainees being hospitalised for “slashing and stabbing injuries made using improvised weapons”.
On 10 September, a detainee was found overdosed in his room, requiring staff to administer Naloxone, a drug that reverses opioid overdose effects.

The incidents at MIDC prompted Comcare to warn the government that it was failing to control the rising number of “incidents of this type at MIDC and across the broader immigration detention network”. That failure meant it was likely to be in breach of the law, the document said.

“I have formed the reasonable belief that the department is contravening section 19 of the WHS Act by failing to ensure, so far as is reasonably practicable, the health and safety of workers and other persons,” Comcare said in its notice. “In particular, the risks associated with violence, aggression, and the presence of illicit substances and improvised weaponry are not being adequately managed.

“While the department has advised that a range of actions have been undertaken to address these risks, it has not sufficiently demonstrated that the control measures currently in place are effective in eliminating or minimising the risks, so far as is reasonably practicable.”
Comcare said the information available indicates these hazards pose an ongoing risk of serious harm to workers and others in the centres.
A separate Comcare document revealed that a series of eight fire-related incidents had taken place at Villawood immigration detention centre between February and May.

blocks.caption: Fire damage to a room at Villawood

blocks.text: That’s despite prior warnings to government to intervene after previous fires lit inside Villawood exposed serious gaps in MTC’s preparedness. That includes one fire on 23 September 2025, when MTC staff rushed into a detainee’s room to save him from a fire without proper safety equipment, causing two workers to be hospitalised.

The regulator found the department had not conducted its own systematic review of “all fire and smoke control measures falling within its influence or control”, a likely breach of work health and safety regulations.
after newsletter promotion

“The occurrence of multiple notifiable fire incidents over a period of approximately four months, particularly after previous regulatory intervention concerning substantially the same risk, provided repeated and compelling circumstances requiring the department to review the effectiveness of relevant control measures,” the Comcare document said.

The Guardian previously revealed a series of incidents across the centres since Secure Journey took over, including escapes, staff injuries and sick detainees missing medical appointments due to a lack of staff to escort them.

Lyndal Ryan, national president of the United Workers Union, which represents workers in the centres, said the notices from Comcare show “the continuing dangerous situations facing workers and detainees inside detention centres, and Secure Journeys’ inability or unwillingness to address those issues”.
The union has continually raised concerns about understaffing in the centres, and Ryan said Comcare has made it clear that the department has the responsibility to pull Secure Journeys into line.
“The list of eight fires at Villawood over a four-month period are signs of the instability and chaos our members are witnessing almost every day,” she said.
A spokesperson for MTC’s local subsidiary, Secure Journeys, said:
“In response to your questions, I can confirm that Secure Journeys’ commitment to maintaining safe and secure operations, as well as both staff and detainee welfare remains our top priority.”
The Australian Border Force was contacted for comment.

articles.title: Districts of top House leaders, some Bulacan solons get top DPWH allocations -Tinio
articles.summary: The district engineering offices of the Department of Public Works and Highways that received the highest allocations in the proposed 2027 national budget include those of Ilocos Norte Rep. Sandro…

blocks.text: Published October 9, 2026 9:58pm

The district engineering offices of the Department of Public Works and Highways that received the highest allocations in the proposed 2027 national budget include those that cover the legislative districts of top officials of the House of Representatives, a House deputy minority leader said on Friday.

ACT Teachers party-list Rep. Antonio Tinio, in an online interview, said the top engineering districts with the highest allocations include those that are in charge of the districts of Ilocos Norte Rep. Sandro Marcos, Nueva Ecija Rep. Mikaela Suansing, and Speaker Faustino "Bojie" Dy III of Isabela.
He also mentioned the DPWH's second engineering district in Bulacan.

Sandro Marcos, one of the sons of President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos Jr., is the House Majority Leader, while Suansing is the chairperson of the House Committee on Appropriations that shepherded the budget bill through the House of Representatives.
The House on Wednesday gave second reading approval to the P7.2-trillion General Appropriations Bill. It is scheduled to approve the same on third and final reading on Monday.
GMA News has reached out to Dy, Marcos, and Suansing for comment and will post their side when it is available.

Tinio didn't refer to the Bulacan lawmakers, but those with jurisdiction in the area of the DPWH's second engineering district are Representatives Linabelle Ruth Villarica of the fourth district, Salvador Pleyto of the sixth district, and Arturo Robes of San Jose Del Monte City.
GMA News has also sought their comment on the budget data Tinio raised and presented.

"Overall, kung ira-rank natin ‘yung mga district engineering offices, ang may pinakamalaki overall ay Ilocos Norte 1st. Meron siyang total of P4.79 billion na DPWH projects," Tinio said in an online interview on Friday.

"Ang pangalawa, Nueva Ecija 1st district engineering office, P3.91 billion. Pangatlo, Bulacan. Bulacan second district engineering office, may tatlong legislative districts na saklaw ‘yan, P3.5 billion. Sumunod d’yan, Isabela. So may dalawang districts na saklaw itong DEO na ito, P3.1 billion," he added.
"Well, obviously, I'm talking about the majority leader, the chair of Committee on Appropriations, and the Speaker, 'di ba?" Tinio said.
As for the allocation for each legislative district, Tinio said, "Supposedly ang baseline per district is P500 million. Tapos puwedeng bumaba, tumaas o bumaba batay sa so-called formula."
But the deputy minority leader also disclosed that even party-lists have allocations.

"Yung party-list, as I've said, meron ding alokayson sa DPWH infrastructure projects, anywhere from P120 to 160 million. Pero again, puwedeng madagdagan o mabawasan 'yan depende pa rin sa lapit sa kusina," Tinio said.
When asked if the Makabayan Bloc in the House of Representatives also has allocations, Tinio replied, "Decision namin na walang alokasyon dito sa DPWH or infrastructure projects."

"Nagdesisyon kami na ‘yong medical assistance, yes. Dahil ‘yan ang kailangan ng mamamayan, lumalapit ang mga constituents at ang mamamayan sa amin. So rather than tanggihan at ituro sa iba, na doon lang kayo, eh di direkta na namin hinahawakan. So ganoon ‘yon. Pero nananatili ang posisyon natin na dapat walang ganoon," Tinio said. –NB, GMA News

articles.title: Pete Hegseth’s plan to livestream execution puts US in dubious company
articles.summary: Only Iran and Afghanistan routinely carry out sentences in public, with Saudi Arabia appearing to have ended practice

blocks.text: If the US defence secretary, Pete Hegseth, goes ahead with plans to livestream the execution of a soldier radicalised to extremist Islam who killed 13 people at a military base in Texas, his country will join a motley assembly of lesser powers and rogue actors who have conducted public executions in recent years.

Only two countries currently systematically carry out capital sentences in public: Iran and Afghanistan. In 2025, the Taliban authorities carried out six such killings and the regime in Tehran 11, according to Amnesty International.

In April last year, the Taliban executed four men accused of murder in three different cities. All were shot dead in crowded public sports stadiums. Such events were common when the hardline Islamist militia movement was in power in the late 1990s. Then as now, the Taliban claimed a due court process had been followed.

In July, two young men accused of killing police officers were hanged by Iranian authorities in the central square of Isfahan, Iran. Human rights monitors have reported about 30 public executions in Ithe country in the last five years, with an intensification in recent months after massive popular unrest earlier this year and the war with the US and Israel. Historically, many hangings have been carried out using a crane as a makeshift gallows.

blocks.caption: Protesters gathered last year in Paris and other cities around the world to demand an end to executions in Iran. Photograph: Siavosh Hosseini/LightRocket/Getty Images

blocks.text: Saudi Arabia appears to have ended the practice after decades of beheading convicted criminals in a square in the capital, Riyadh, and sometimes publicly in provincial cities.

Legal experts and historians argue that public executions perform different functions. If the rule of law is shaky or there is doubt about the efficacy of the criminal justice system, they offer authorities seeking to win support a way of convincing the community that criminals will be punished. Such public spectacles can also be a way of cowing a population through terror.
Armed militant groups have frequently resorted to public executions – often in an effort to assert their authority.

Islamic State, which ruled a swath of Iraq and Syria between 2014 and 2019, conducted thousands of executions for alleged offences ranging from homosexuality to theft. Many of the executions took place in public or were videoed. A large number were deliberately choreographed to provide a spectacle for broadcast to terrorise enemies and potential dissidents as well as to radicalise IS supporters and attract new ones.

In October 2025, as Hamas sought to reassert its control over the population of Gaza, it carried out a public execution of six men apparently accused of collaborating with Israel. In 2017, the group had executed three men accused of the same crime, partly livestreaming the event on Facebook.

blocks.caption: The planned public execution of Nidal Hasan would be the first in the US in many decades. Photograph: Reuters

blocks.text: The execution of Maj Nidal Hasan, a former army psychiatrist, at Fort Hood in Texas would be the first public execution in the US in many decades.

In the US, the practice of public executions was largely stopped in the 1930s, though in 2001, some survivors and victims’ relatives were allowed to watch the execution by lethal injection of Timothy McVeigh, convicted of the 1995 bombing of a government office in Oklahoma City.

Hasan’s execution has been scheduled for 3 December. Hegseth, who has the authority to decide the conduct of the killing, has said that “of course” it would take place at the same time and in the same place as Hasan’s attack 17 years ago and would use firearms, as Hasan did.
Hasan can launch appeals within the civilian federal court system that could delay the execution for many years.

In 2025, Amnesty International recorded 2,707 executions, the highest total globally since 1981, and an increase of two-thirds on the previous year. The sharp rise was mainly due to more than 2,100 executions by Iran, its highest number of executions in decades.
Amnesty said authorities had placed the death penalty “at the centre of flawed public security and ‘tough on crime’ narratives to assert control, project state power and score political points”.

“This trend was strongest in countries where the authorities have tightened their grip on power by restricting civic space, silencing dissent and displaying disregard for protections established under international human rights law and standards,” the campaign group reported.

articles.title: Alexander Cabrera is last witness of prosecution in VP Sara impeachment trial
articles.summary: The House prosecution panel on Friday confirmed that financial forensic analyst Atty. Alexander Cabrera is the last witness that they will present in the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara…

blocks.text: Published October 9, 2026 9:44pm

The House prosecution panel on Friday confirmed that financial forensic analyst Atty. Alexander Cabrera is the last witness that they will present in the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte.

House prosecutor Akbayan party-list Rep. Chel Diokno said this on the 37th day of the trial when asked by Senate impeachment court presiding officer Francis Escudero if the prosecution will still present the witness from the National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) after the testimony of Cabrera.
“Atty. Alexander B. Cabrera is our last witness, Your Honor, for our case-in-chief,” Diokno answered.

Impeachment court spokesperson Regie Tongol explained that if the prosecution will already be resting for Article 2, which alleges that Duterte should be impeached for amassing unexplained wealth, then it means that Article 3 would be tackled next.

“Pero alam ko na alam niyo na rin na nakatanggap ang impeachment court ng manifestation that formally manifest to the impeachment court na ido-drop ang Article 3. Hintayin po natin ‘yung ating Presiding Officer to take that up on Monday,” Tongol said in a press conference.

(But I know that you are also aware that the impeachment court has received a manifestation that formally manifests to the impeachment court that Article 3 will be dropped. Let’s wait for our Presiding Officer to take that up on Monday.)

The prosecution announced earlier today that it already filed a manifestation with the Senate impeachment court that it will drop Article III or the bribery charges in the trial of the Vice President.
The trial on Friday ended with the direct examination of Cabrera. The defense will proceed with the cross-examination of the witness on Monday next week. –NB, GMA News

articles.title: ICE says officer shot New York man because they believe their lives were in danger

blocks.text: N.Y. mayor calls ICE 'rotten to its core' after agents shoot man

Outrage is growing in New York City after federal immigration enforcement agents shot a Dominican man in his car where a five-year-old child was also present. 'What happened today was an outrage,' said Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who also called for ICE to be abolished. The Department of Homeland Security described the man as a 'criminal illegal alien' with a prior grand larceny conviction and a history of other arrests, a claim the man's lawyer denies.
The Latest

items: A U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agent shot and wounded a 28-year-old Dominican man who was in a car with a five-year-old child Thursday.
The shooting drew outrage from New Yorkers, including Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who called for the release of the wounded man and the end of all ICE enforcement in the city.

In a news conference this morning, U.S. Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin said Mamdani’s comments were political theatre and an incitement to violence. A senior ICE official said agents opened fire because they believed their lives were in danger.
Mullin said ICE agents weren’t aware there was a child in the car.
ICE agents have fired their guns during more than a dozen vehicle stops since last year, killing at least four people.

articles.title: Ethiopia warns Eritrea it will defend itself after troops cross border
articles.summary: Truckloads of Eritrean soldiers have been seen driving into Ethiopia, which has reportedly responded with drone strikes.

blocks.text: Ethiopia has accused Eritrea of an "all-out invasion" of its northern Tigray region and warned it will defend itself, days after residents told the BBC Eritrean troops had crossed into the country.

In a letter to the UN Security Council, Ethiopia's foreign minister called it a "blatant act of aggression that engages Ethiopia's inherent right to self-defence", following reported strikes on Eritrean troops in Tigray.
Eritrean Information Minister Yemane Gebremeskel responded by saying it was facing "an unprovoked war of aggression" from its neighbour.
Fighting broke out between the government and the party that controls Tigray, the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), two weeks ago.
Both blame each other for violating a 2022 deal that ended its civil war. Ethiopia says Eritrea backs the TPLF, which it denies.
During the two-year civil war, Eritrea was a key ally of the Ethiopian government, having fought alongside them against the TPLF.

But relations between the two neighbours have since deteriorated - largely over the Ethiopian prime minister's ambition to take ownership of one of Eritrea's Red Sea ports - leading to the severing of diplomatic ties last week.
Accusing Eritrea of violating its sovereignty, Ethiopian Foreign Minister Gedion Timothewos said Eritrean forces had advanced up to 60km (37 miles) into Tigray.
Ethiopian drone strikes reportedly targeted Eritrean forces in the Tigrayan town of Adigrat on Wednesday and Thursday, amid fears of a wider regional war.
US-based conflict monitor Acled said "Eritrean troops and ammunition" in Adigrat were hit by "multiple drone strikes" overnight.
One resident told AFP news agency "there were many, many drone strikes", and that some Eritrean lorries had been destroyed.
Another witness said Eritrean forces appeared to be retreating north after the strikes, AFP reported.

Dated 8 October, Ethiopia's letter to UN Security Council members read: "In this time of difficulty, when Ethiopia is left with no other option but to defend itself, we count on your understanding, support, and solidarity."
But while Ethiopia accuses its neighbour of supporting the TPLF, Eritrea has blamed the conflict on Ethiopia's leaders, and accused them looking for a reason to seize Eritrean territory.
On Friday, Eritrea's information minister called the accusations levelled against Asmara as "duplicity in their most extreme forms".
In a post on X, he said Ethiopia was "openly working to bring about regime change in Eritrea by providing shelter and support to certain mercenaries who claim to be opposition".
Eritrea gained independence from Ethiopia in 1993, but ties were only normalised in 2018, when Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed came to power.
This latest unrest follows months of tension and the launch of new alliance of armed groups in Ethiopia - including the TPLF - in September.
Last week, TPLF forces withdrew from Tigray's main city of Mekelle, which is 115km (71 miles) south of Adigrat and is now under army control.

articles.summary: Confessed drug war perpetrators are also expressing interest in sharing their stories, according to the Truth Commission. “We are getting calls and interest even from former perpetrators, so maybe…

blocks.text: Published October 9, 2026 9:16pm
Confessed drug war perpetrators are also expressing interest in sharing their stories, according to the Truth Commission.

In a "24 Oras" report from Mariz Umali on Friday, the Truth Commission held its fourth session earlier in the day. The Commission aims to document and seek out what happened during former president Rodrigo Duterte’s war on drugs.

“We are getting calls and interest even from former perpetrators, so maybe against the backdrop of what has already been documented, but former perpetrators are also now expressing interest in telling their stories," Commissioner Al Fuertes said.
While the Truth Commission stressed that it is not a prosecutorial body that could directly file a case, they are listening to the victims and survivors, which could be key to reopening their cases.

“The challenge is, and this is what the Commission intends to do, is to really pressure the government to take the lead in pursuing justice for the victims because the victims, they need all the help they can get,” Commissioner Carlos Conde said.
It has been six years since Lorna Pepaño lost her son. Her neighbor had told her that her son Christian was gunned down.
“Nakita ko na po yung anak ko, nakabulagta. May malay pa naman siya, sabi niya, ‘hindi po ako yun’... pero tinuluyan pa rin siya,” Pepaño said.
(I saw my son lying there. He was still conscious; he said, ‘it was not me’... but they still killed him.)
Pepaño said it was a case of mistaken identity.

Now, she hoped that she could find justice for her son who, by her account, was a good and prayerful man. She also expressed hope that there would be no more killings like the one that happened to her son and other victims. —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Is China seeking to restrict Taiwan's cultural presence?
articles.summary: From coffee competitions to literature awards, Beijing appears to be working to limit Taiwan's international cultural and political impact on its own terms.

image.caption: Taiwan Travelogue follows a young Japanese writer visiting Japanese-colonized Taiwan in May 1938 on an official government-sponsored lecture tourImage: Pete Speller/Avalon/IMAGO

blocks.text: When Taiwaneseauthor Yang Shuang-zi's Taiwan Travelogue won the 2026 international Booker Prize, it marked a historic breakthrough on the global stage. But behind the triumph lay a sharp geopolitical reality.
On stage, English translator Lin King voiced the anxiety looming over Taiwan.

"In 2022, when Russia invaded Ukraine, I made the explicit decision that rather than translating Sinophone works indiscriminately, I would only translate writing from Taiwan for the foreseeable future. I will continue to do so until the day comes that my homeland's sovereignty is no longer a provocation or a punchline — until no English speaker feels comfortable saying to me, 'I really should come visit you in Taiwan while it still exists.'" King said this in her acceptance speech.
Literature and politics

Taiwan Travelogue follows a young Japanese writer visiting Japanese-colonized Taiwan in May 1938 on an official government-sponsored lecture tour. As she and her Taiwanese interpreter explore local street food together, a subtle intimacy unfolds between them. It is written in a narrative that centers Taiwan's history rather than Beijing's preferred Great China framework.

"Literature and politics are directly connected. Politics determines the allocation of resources, and the allocation of resources determines which works get pulled out, held up high, and defined as 'good literature.' The idea that politics can just be kept out of it doesn't exist," Yang told DW.

A few days after the Booker Prize was announced, China's Taiwan Affairs Office reacted that, "Writers from both sides of the Taiwan Strait should firmly uphold a national standpoint, respect historical facts, and squarely face the immense suffering inflicted upon the Chinese people ... by Japan's war of aggression and fascism."
"From China's perspective, they do not want to see Taiwan's voice gain prominence." Yang said.

Her book demonstrates that Taiwanese culture is shaped by multiple historical strands — including Indigenous, Japanese colonial, and local Han influences, rather than being merely a "branch of Chinese culture."

During Yang's German book tour this October, an event in Literaturhaus München sparked controversy when her interpreter significantly shortened certain statements concerning Taiwan, China and historical politics. The interpreter later admitted oversights and shortcomings in the interpretation but denied deliberately deleting content due to political stance or the political situation in Taiwan.
Taiwan and China

Beijing claims Taiwan as a Chinese province and has long threatened to use force to bring the island under its control. Taiwan's democratically elected president has rejected Beijing's assertion that its laws apply to Taiwan.
Since 1949, Taiwan has functioned with de facto independence, maintaining its own government, military, and legal systems while facing ongoing military pressure from Beijing.

blocks.caption: Taiwan's democratically elected President Lai Ching-te has rejected Beijing's assertion that its laws apply to TaiwanImage: Taiwan Presidential Office/AP Photo/Picture alliance

blocks.text: China's international overreach?
In the past, China's monitoring of Taiwanese international engagement has reached far further than words over a literature prize.

"The target of suppression and harassment primarily include outspoken individuals, exiled activists, diaspora community organizers, alongside their family members and close affiliates back home. From the PRC's (People's Republic of China) eyes, these groups are a threat to regime security, as they are able to amplify the dissenting voices and alternative stories of China to the West," said Dr. Yan-ho Lai, a senior fellow of Georgetown Center for Asian Law.

In April this year, Taiwanese barista Lin Shao-hsing, also known as Bala, won the 2026 World Latte Art Championship, but soon after, all mentions of Taiwan as they relate to Bala's win were removed from the official World Coffee Championships website.

It now credits Bala's win to "Chinese Taipei," a term which is often used in international competitions, like the Olympics, to refer to Taiwan. The term, however, is almost never used in Taiwan. The vast majority of people in Taiwan identify as "Taiwanese," while only 2.5% identify as Chinese, according to a 2026 poll by National Chengchi University's Election Study Center.

In 2024, China allegedly planned a car collision during Taiwan's vice president Hsiao Bi-khim's visit in Prague. Czech intelligence officials told local media that the incident was part of a much larger and escalatory plan by Chinese diplomats and intelligence officers working out of the embassy in Prague.

In early October this year, the FBI says authorities arrested a California woman for allegedly spying on the son of Taiwan's president at the direction of Chinese officials. According to the US Department of Justice, the woman traveled to Seattle in 2025 under instructions from Beijing to monitor the president's son and his family, capturing photos, video footage, and license plate information.
During a press conference on October 6, China's Ministry of Foreign Affairs said it "consistently opposes the hype surrounding so-called 'Chinese spies' and the smearing and vilification of China."

"It reflects the ambiguity and limitation of international law, that PRC using soft power to restrict the visibility of Taiwan may not directly fall into international law arena as Taiwan is not recognized by international bodies as a sovereign state party." added Dr. Lai.
This article was edited by Kate Martyr

articles.title: Art for freedom: Maria Kalesnikava in Bonn
articles.summary: The Belarusian musician and civil rights activist Maria Kalesnikava held the keynote speech on the importance of art at the 2026 Beethovenfest in Bonn. She also visited DW.

image.caption: Maria Kalesnikava continues to fight for freedom Image: Sebastian Gollnow/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Maria Kalesnikava knows all too well how authoritarian regimes repress art: The Belarusian flautist and activist spent five years in detention as a political prisoner, three of which were in solitary confinement.

Speaking at this year's Beethovenfest, she said: "A person's external freedom can be taken away, sometimes almost entirely. Their freedom of movement, contacts with other people, and access to information can be limited." She pointed out that it is, however, much harder to control what has already become part of one's memory, imagination and inner experience. "And it is precisely in this that I find the explanation for why culture is so important for a free society and why authoritarian systems so often view it with distrust" she concluded during the keynote speech.

blocks.caption: German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul welcomed Maria Kolesnikova at the Federal Foreign Office in December 2025Image: Amrei Schulz/AA/photothek.de/picture alliance

blocks.text: A key figure of the Belarusian opposition, the artist and political activist was arrested by the regime of Alexander Lukashenko in the summer of 2020, after the regime had violently suppressed the peaceful revolution for democracy and freedom. Across the country, mass protests and a democratic civil rights movement took place after the controversial presidential election on August 9, 2020.

Kalesnikava recalled how, during her imprisonment, she had carried her world and her experiences, with her all along. This enabled her to remain free, and not to feel like a victim. To Kalesnikava, this is precisely the power of art and also the reason why all dictators — whether Stalin, Hitler or Putin and Lukashenko — hate independent arts and culture, even if it's not overtly political.
During a panel discussion in Bonn, Kalesnikava stressed this point directly:

"The question often arises: what are we defending in Ukraine? Why do we need so much money and new weapons? For me, it is completely clear: the war Russia started is not just against Ukraine. It's a war against European values and European culture. It is a war against our civilization." Kalesnikava realized this immediately when she heard about the Russian war against Ukraine in February 2022, while she was imprisoned.
Music saved her

Kalesnikava was released and has been living in freedom again for ten months now — a miracle that she didn't think was possible and an achievement of international diplomacy. The fact that she emerged and returned to her life full of resilience is thanks in part to Beethoven and Bach, as Kalesnikava, who studied the flute and earned a degree in early and new music in Minsk and Stuttgart, recalled. "I spent a lot of time in complete silence. But this silence was almost never empty, because music constantly played in my head," Kalesnikava said in Bonn. "We musicians know this state very well — sometimes a melody or a musical phrase gets so stuck in your head that it's simply impossible to get rid of it. In normal life, this can even be annoying. In prison, I realized for the first time that this could bring great happiness."

blocks.caption: Maria Kolesnikova appeared on the Russian-language DW program "DW Novosti," on October 2, 2026Image: DW

blocks.text: During her visit to Bonn, the Belarusian activist also visited DW and appeared as a guest on the DW Russian language show "DW Novosti." Kalesnikava currently lives in Berlin following an invitation by the German government, where she is also recovering from the horrors she experienced. She sees it as her responsibility to remind the world about what is happening to more than 800 political prisoners in Belarus, as well as the importance and fragility of free artistic expression. On October 2, 2026, she held her keynote speech at the Beethovenfest in Bonn as part of a conference titled "Cultural Events as Political Spaces?," organized with the support of the German Federal Cultural Foundation.
The concert hall as a space for freedom

More than 200 representatives from concert institutions and music festivals from across Germany came to the newly renovated Beethovenhalle in Bonn for the final weekend of this year's Beethovenfest. Together, they debated innovative forms and formats for music, as well as issues that stretch far beyond the music industry and urge on to think outside the box.

blocks.caption: Steven Walter, artistic director of the Beethovenfest, spoke about the importance of music and freedom at the conference in BonnImage: Michael Staab/Beethovenfest

blocks.text: "Arts and culture are not responsible for taking on specific opinions from political parties, or for making explicitly political statements," Steven Walter, artistic director of the Beethovenfest and host of the conference, told DW. "What art always creates, however, is spaces for encounter, and places where people can tolerate ambivalence. And that is such an important part of our society, that we're able to handle making collective experiences." To Walter, this is precisely where arts and culture come in, as artists create spaces for independent thought, subjective interpretations, as well as doubts. "Perhaps it's true that there is something like a DNA of freedom in the nature of art," Walter explained in an interview with DW.
The most successful Beethovenfest in years

The festive closing of the 2026 Beethovenfest took place on 3 October, which is also German Unity Day. The BBC Philharmonic Orchestra, under the baton of conductor Anja Bihlmaier, performed Johannes Brahms' "A German Requiem," an iconic piece that evokes reconciliation and trust.

blocks.caption: At the closing concert of the Beethovenfest, Anja Bihlmaier conducted Brahms's Requiem with the BBC Philharmonic Orchestra and the Audi Youth Choir AcademyImage: Nekame Klasohm

blocks.text: After four weeks of Beethovenfest 2026, the festival recorded the highest number of visitors in a decade. Around 35,000 people came to experience, celebrate and discuss art together at more than 100 concerts and events.
This article was written by Andrey Gorezky, translated from German and edited by Sarah Hucal and Tenzin Sekhon.

articles.title: Sara Duterte impeachment trial Day 37: Bribery article dropped, financial records examined
articles.summary: The impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte concluded its 37th day with the prosecution wrapping up the presentation of its last two witnesses, as well as the dropping of the bribery article.

blocks.text: Published October 9, 2026 8:59pm

The impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte concluded its 37th day with the prosecution wrapping up the presentation of its last two witnesses, as well as the dropping of the bribery article.
The session on Friday resumed with the defense’s cross-examination of the Bureau of Internal Revenue (BIR) Office of the Commissioner's chief of staff Atty. Anne Loraine Garcia-Marquez.

Defense counsel Kristine Ferrer presented to the court the letter of authority issued by the BIR to Duterte and her husband, Atty. Manases Carpio. While private prosecutor Erwin Matib raised that the information was supposed to be confidential, Ferrer said that her clients gave permission.

There was also a brief disagreement on when the BIR could assess and file tax records in a fraud case, which Garcia-Marquez clarified: upon the discovery of fraud, the BIR has 10 years to assess the case.
Outside of the impeachment court, House prosecutor Keith Flores confirmed that they were dropping the bribery article against Duterte, citing time constraints.

During the interjections of the senator-judges, a few raised concerns about the Duterte couple’s financial records. Senator-judge Risa Hontiveros said that a Ukrainian company remitted money to Cale88 Foods Corporation, one of the businesses linked to Carpio. Meanwhile, Senator-judge Joel Villanueva raised concern over Cale88’s P150 million in sales in 2024 while only having two workers.

One of the biggest revelations of the day, however, included the testimony of the prosecution’s last witness: forensic financial expert Alexander Cabrera. While the defense questioned why Cabrera was allowed access to confidential documents, the prosecution maintained that lawyers were allowed to make use of experts.

Cabrera then delivered a report alleging that Duterte and Carpio had P817.87 million in unexplained wealth. He had pieced together, through the various tax and financial records provided by the prosecution, that the vice president had grossly underdeclared her and her husband’s income.
The defense has yet to cross-examine Cabrera and will question him on Monday. —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Poland: Lifeline for Ukrainian refugees confronts donor fatigue and online abuse as anti-Ukrainian sentiment grows
articles.summary: A Ukrainian woman who fled the war in her country built a lifeline for refugees in Poland. Now her organization faces donor fatigue, funding cuts and rising hostility as support for Ukrainians in…

image.caption: Nastya Podorozhnya was a 24-year-old Ukrainian graduate living in Poland when Russia invaded her native country in 2022. She decided to use her knowledge of Poland to help Ukrainian refugees arriving in the countryImage: Adam Easton/DW

blocks.text: Hours after Vladimir Putin announced his "special military operation" in Ukraine on February 24, 2022, Russian troops began attacking Kyiv's Antonov Airport close to the home of Nastya Podorozhnya's family.
Nastya was 24 at the time and living in Krakow in neighboring Poland, having recently graduated from the city's Jagiellonian University.

Alarmed by the news from Ukraine and fearful of what was coming, Nastya rushed back to Ukraine two days before the invasion to be with her family and help her sister and her three children cross the border to safety in Poland.
Helping compatriots fleeing Ukraine

Nastya realized she could use her experience of living in Poland — how to get a doctor's appointment or simply buy a tram ticket — to help the flood of mostly women and children arriving in the country.

blocks.caption: After Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022, refugees flooded across the border into Poland. In the months after the invasion, there was an outpouring of support from Polish peopleImage: Krzysztof Kaniewski/ZUMA Wire/IMAGO

blocks.text: Poles were offering help and food at the border, but some people sought to take advantage of the vulnerable arrivals.

"I spoke to activists engaged in anti-human trafficking and they said what was happening at the border in the first weeks after the invasion was like Christmas, Easter and birthdays rolled into one for traffickers because people were so easily trusting the volunteers," Nastya told DW in a two-bedroom apartment in central Krakow her organization uses to provide shelter to vulnerable women refugees escaping domestic abuse or trafficking.
Hotline still fields 100 calls a months
Named Martynka, after Nastya's youngest niece, the organization also runs a hotline. It has received more than 5,000 requests for help since March 2022 and now gets about a hundred every month.
Her small team provides psychological and moral support in four languages as well as legal assistance and counselling.

blocks.caption: Podorozhnya's organization, Martynka, runs a shelter in Krakow for vulnerable women and children refugees escaping domestic abuse or traffickingImage: Adam Easton/DW

blocks.text: "One of the very young women who lived with us for a long time was drugged by her boyfriend who she met as a teenager when she escaped the full-scale invasion and after years of relationship she found out that he has been drugging her and selling sex with her to other people" she said.
Nastya said she was motivated to help partly because of a traumatic experience of her own. While studying in Krakow, a Ukrainian man tried to rape her outside of her dormitory.

After a long and difficult legal process, during which police detained the suspect before releasing him, he was eventually found guilty of violating Nastya's bodily autonomy and given a restraining order.

"This terrible, traumatic experience not only gave me horrible PTSD, which later on sort of helped me be empathetic and understand survivors with PTSD, but also it put me through the system of justice and how survivors are being treated," she added.
Aid cuts and donor fatigue
Since 2022, around 100 women and children have found shelter in the apartment. Her team's work relies largely on donations from international organizations.

blocks.caption: Nastya Podorozhnya holds a box that was handmade by one of the women who stayed in the shelter Image: Adam Easton/DW

blocks.text: But cuts to USAID have led to increased competition for grants, while donor fatigue has forced the team to cut its one-to-one therapy sessions.

"Ukraine is not in the headlines anymore," says Nastya. "The international attention has moved elsewhere. For all of summer 2026 we have been running a very challenging fundraising campaign. It is so hard to convince people to donate to a Ukrainian organization right now. There is something called exhaustion, donor exhaustion, fundraising exhaustion."
The UNHCR's acting representative for Poland, Czechia and Slovakia, Jun Shirato, confirmed the difficult situation in the aid sector.

Speaking to DW in Warsaw, she said that funding cuts last year have forced UNHCR to scale back its staff in Poland by two thirds from 120 at its peak in the months after the invasion to 40 now. The UNHCR has now closed three of its regional offices opened in Krakow, Lublin and Rzeszow after Russia's invasion of Ukraine. Its sole remaining office in Poland is in Warsaw.
Changing attitudes to Ukrainians
Nastya's fundraising efforts increasingly meet with online abuse, too.
Attitudes toward Ukrainians in Poland have changed. In the months after the invasion, many Poles opened their homes to refugees, including Nastya's sister and her daughters.

blocks.caption: Historical disputes between Poland and Ukraine — in particular surrounding the role of the Ukrainian Insurgent Army in the Volhynia massacre during World War II — are fueling hostility toward Ukrainians in PolandImage: Marek Antoni Iwańczuk/NurPhoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: The situation is now very different. Earlier this year, new rules restricting access to child benefits and free healthcare for refugees who don't work were introduced.
In the first half of this year, reports of hate crimes committed against Ukrainians in Poland rose by a third according to Polish Police statistics.
Historical disputes fuel tension

At the same time, historical disputes between Poland and Ukraine, have resurfaced, fueling further hostility toward the Ukrainian community, which accounts for more than three quarters of all foreigners living in Poland.

In May, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's decision to name a military unit after the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA), which took part in the murder of tens of thousands of Poles during the Second World War, triggered outrage in Poland.
Polish President Karol Nawrocki stripped Zelenskyy of Poland's highest state honor, the Order of the White Eagle.

While Poles focus on the UPA's massacre of Polish citizens, many Ukrainians view the UPA and nationalist leaders like Stepan Bandera as heroes because they fought against the Soviet occupation after the war.

blocks.caption: A pro-Ukrainian demonstration under the slogan 'Don't Be Indifferent' opposing xenophobic attacks on Ukrainians was organized by the Committee for the Defense of Democracy in 22 cities across Poland this summerImage: Klaudia Radecka/NurPhoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: "This week we are supporting a family of Ukrainians whose car was completely destroyed. No windows left in the car and with spray paint someone wrote 'Bandera people go back where you came from,'" said Nastya, adding, "I think it is so devastating and I've recorded a video about it. We have hundreds of comments there, of people wishing me death, wishing me to go back where I came from. It is very tough emotionally."
Animosity stoked by Russian bots
Nastya said the hostility is also driven by Russia using online bots to stoke tensions between Poles and Ukrainians.
"They do not want us to be together, or to remember who our common enemy is. They don't want Ukrainian refugees to integrate or feel welcome," she said.
Despite the strain, Nastya remains optimistic that she and her team can continue their work.

"For some reason I am — and this is the weirdest thing. I love my job so much. I want to do this beautiful thing. I would easily send my mother, my sister, my best friend to Martynka for support. I know there are few organizations that could provide such wonderful help."

blocks.text: Published October 9, 2026 8:35pm

Financial forensic analyst Alexander Cabrera, a witness presented by the prosecution, on Friday revealed that P11.35 million worth of checks was supposedly paid to the dentist of Vice President Sara Duterte.

On Day 37 of the impeachment trial, House prosecutor Rep. Chel Diokno presented parts of Cabrera’s summary report, which highlighted certain banking behaviors of the Vice President and her husband, lawyer Manases Carpio “that may warrant further review and investigation.”

In the report, the witness noted several check payments with the payee's name being blacked out under a BDO checking account. He said he was able to list the names of the payees because they were still visible.
One of the names listed was Lourdes Lebosada, who supposedly received check payments amounting to P11.35 million.
Cabrera said that Lebosada, whom he identified as a dentist of the Vice President, was a partner of Carpio in Cale88 Foods Corporation.
“Si Ms. Lourdes Lebosada po ay ito po ang partner ni Atty. Mans Carpio sa kanyang business na CALE88. 47.5 percent po ‘yung kanilang ownership sa CALE88,” the witness said.
(Ms. Lourdes Lebosada is Atty. Mans Carpio’s partner in his business, CALE88. She holds a 47.5 percent ownership of CALE88.)
“Ang total po ng tseke na binayad po kay Ms. Lourdes Lebosada ay P11.35 million na sa palagay ko po ay hindi po ‘yan bayad sa pasta,” he added.
(The total amount of the checks paid to Ms. Lourdes Lebosada is P11.35 million—which, in my opinion, is not payment for dental fillings.)
Defense counsel Kristine Ferrer reacted to the statement of Cabrera, but Diokno himself immediately volunteered to have it stricken off the record.
Senate impeachment court presiding officer Francis Escudero then issued a reminder to the witness.
“The witness is reminded to kindly avoid unresponsive additions to the answer he will give to questions propounded by counsel,” Escudero told Cabrera.
The witness apologized for his remarks.
Diokno likewise asked Cabrera for a basis that Lebosada is the dentist of the Vice President.
“Meron po kaming nakitang Facebook post ng Lebosada Clinic kung saan magkasama si Dr. Lebosada at si VP Sara,” he answered.
(We saw a Facebook post from Lebosada Clinic showing Dr. Lebosada and VP Sara together.)
The photo of Lebosada and Duterte was flashed on the screen during the trial. —LDF, GMA News
